subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I referred to' the lack of team work'and' the need of better understanding among the many elements in Canada. When the House rose I was dealing with the argument advanced by some hon. members thus: The United States has high protective duties, the United States is prosperous, therefore high protective duties bring prosperity. In this connection I referred to the situation during the past winter in the highly industrialized city of Detroit, where the Ford motor plant was running but three days a week, and thousands of unemployed were almost on the bread line.
Referring to conditions in the United States and Canada I drew the conclusion from personal interviews with residents of the United States that the happy conditions there that we so often hear about were due not so much to a highly protective tariff as to certain other factor's, namely:	the tremendous financial
advantage gained by the United States by her late entry into the World War; the commendable reduction of some five million dollars in taxation; the immense building boom suspended during the war period and running up to some five or six billions of dollars; also to their system of financing, the very reverse of that practised in Canada, whereby credit instead of cash sales is encouraged. Fully ninety per cent, I believe, of the sales in real estate as well as business contracts, indeed almost-every commercial transaction is performed on the basis of a small cash payment down- ten, fifteen or twenty per cent-and the balance on paper. Further, there is the fact that apparently everybody in the big cities, doctors, lawyers, workers in the factories, and even nurses in the hospitals, subscribed to this financial practice.
The nature of practically every commercial transaction in the big industrial cities in the United States is well illustrated by this familiar example. A purchaser in the city of Detroit can go into the shop of a Ford dealer, -pay $12.50 down and promise to pay $5 a week, and drive out a fully equipped Ford car. Such a system in the final analysis is costly, wasteful, and vicious to the country at large. As the inevitable result we find the big industrial cities of the United States in the very midst of an inflated condition, with the rural districts experiencing a corresponding depression, due to the inflated values of everything -the farmer has to buy and to world market prices for everything he has to sell. In other 167i
words, the big industrial districts of the United States, which have attracted so many of the best of our young manhood during the past few years, are experiencing a situation very similar to that experienced in western Canada some years ago-unbounded optimism, easy credit, inflated land values, immigration pouring into the coun.ry, and men and women in every walk of life leaving the beaten paths of stable industry in an effort to get rich quick and at any cost-all the earmarks of seeming prosperity.
I will not attempt to refresh the minds of hon. gentlemen of this House with what ultimately followed such a financial practice, the results are too vividly in the minds of our people to be easily forgotten. Is such a system of finance sound? Is this the system ihat we are asked to strive to emulate? Given the same or similar premises, similar results are certain to follow, and with mathematical precision. If the industrial centres of the United States do not soon take stock, cease their fictitious trading with one another, and build on the more permanent basis of the stable prosperity of the country as a whole, then should any serious deflation occur, and it has occurred in the United States, the same unfortunate results, as we experienced in western Canada some years ago will follow. A house divided against itself cannot stand. Great Britain, the United States of America, the Dominion of Canada, France or any other country cannot go forward to permanent prosperity unless as a united people-united we stand, divided we fall. Developing this thought further, the Farmer's Advocate editorially says:
A movement is on foot in the United States to oring about a better understanding between industry nnd agriculture and conferences with this end in view ore held from time to time. The organizers look at it in this light: "Better results mean better times for manufacturers; better markets for farmers, better times for farmers; better markets for manufactured goods, better employment for labour." It is realized on every hand that the first step in the right direction is a "better understanding."
And that applies as well to Canada as it does to the United States. It goes on:
There is too much meaningless criticism offered in place of constructive suggestion, while both industry and agriculture are often the victims of demagogic attacks that are sometimes not even correct in theory. Considering the lack of understanding between classes and industries, between rural and urban people, and between labour and employer, it is remarkable that so much progress has actually been made.
Is it not t;me that the various organizations representing agriculture, manufacturing, finance and labour held fewer meetings by themselves and took a little time off to get acquainted with the other fellow's viewpoint ar.d the other fellow's conditions?
The Budget-Mr. Brethcn

As showing the need of a better working understanding among this great family, the Canadian people, I am reminded of the story of a young man whose trousers were too long. He went to mother and requested her to shorten them, but mother was too busy. He went to sister. Sister was too busy. Thrown upon his own resources, he decided to do the job himself. He took a generous slice off each leg, and hung the pants away for Sunday. Later mother regretted that she had not acceded to his request, and she also took a slice off the already diminished trousers. Sister's conscience bothered her and she repeated the operation, and when the young man on Sunday glanced ruefully at the abbreviated pants he remarked, "What this family needs is less operation, and more cooperation."
The politicians of France and the United States are putting everything they have in the way of indications of prosperity in the front shop window. Great Britain is plugging away in the background, but still going down to the sea in ships. Canada is divided. Some of us are working earnestly to bring about permanent prosperity on the basis of "equal opportunities to all and special privileges to none," while others are just busying themselves flashing 4.4 beer in the window or sulking in the cellar of pessimism. Is it any wonder that our Canadian boys turn from this drab picture of steady Canadian progress to the flashy picture of American boom and bustle and seeming prosperity?
But why should we be downhearted? The pound sterling is crowding the top perch with the American eagle. The Canadian dollar is at par, and John Bull and Jack Canuck, with the earnest patriotic support of every Canadian citizen, will some how paddle through.
How can we help to bring about happier conditions in Canada? By taking a few leaves from the book of our friends to the south. Put some of Canada's real assets to the fore. In this connection I should like to pay a compliment to the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Hammell) who refusing the other night, to be led aside into mere partisan debate, proceeded to put before this House and the world the revenue producing possibilities of the tourist traffic of Canada. We are all acquainted with the importance of the Swiss watch industry-everybody has heard of the Swiss watch-a great industry. But when compared to the tourist traffic of Switzerland the relation is $15,000,000 for the watch industry to $300,000,000 for the tourist.

traffic. Of course the Swiss people are a sane, frugal, efficient people. A story is told by a traveller of Swiss efficiency. When up among the mountains in that country one day, he came to a herdsman's cottage. Through the open door be saw the mother in the home with a book from which she was singing, in one hand, the other hand working a chum, and her foot rocking the cradie; and as the traveller looked into that window he soliloquized "What an illustration of efficiency; mind, eye, voice, hands and feet all working." But to his amazement when the woman in reply to his summons left her chair he saw she also had been pressing a Swiss cheese. I repeat, let us put the assets, the real assets, of Canada to the fore; put them in the front shop window. Let us tell our wealthy American friends, who annually spend hundreds of millions of dollars in sightseeing the world about this wonderful country at their very doors; about our sparkling lakes and rivers filled with the gamest, sportiest fish in all the world; its ease of access by railroad, by motor, and launch through scenery unsurpassed; about her snow-capped mountains, crystal streams, and hidden lakes which I have heard world travelled Americans describe as unsurpassed even by the Alps themselves. Here is a source of revenue whose fringe has scarcely been touched. I will support a largely increased expenditure for development here. Let us tell the world about our fertile fields, an empire in extent; our No. 1 northern that commands a premium on any market; about the wealth of our forests, our fisheries and minerals. Let us tell them about our wonderful water powers developed and undeveloped, and how they operate the wheels of industry; about our sturdy, reliable Canadian workers; our stable system of financing and sound economic practices in commercial transactions. We have been knocking Canada before the world long enough: let us boost some.
Let us take another leaf from the book of our American neighbour: Reduction of federal taxation. By a system of economies in small things as well as by eliminating expensive duplications in the service the United States has been able to reduce her federal tax from $54 to $27 annually. Since the war the United States has reduced her debt by over five billions.
How has this been accomplished? By old fashioned thrift, actually saving the pennies rather than talking about saving the millions: by co-ordination in the public service. To illustrate what can be accomplished here I should like to refer to the situation when President Coolidge became governor of the

The Budget-Mr. Brethen
state of Massachusetts. When he entered that office he found departments which aggregated 118 in number. He was successful in getting a bill through the legislature which allowed a reduction to not more than 20, and was given three years to do it in. The number was reduced to 18, and the thing seemingly impossible was actually accomplished in less than one year. Friends and enemies alike, said, "This is the death knell of your political future. These disgruntled partisans that have been turned out of office will spell your defeat." He came into office as governor of Massachusetts with the majority of 17,000, and was returned with a majority of 125,000, proving that the great mass of the people will support any government that has the moral courage to attack and correct this duplication and wasteful expenditure in the public service. Reduction of taxation by avoiding every unnecessary expenditure. How this may be brought about is well illustrated by the inaugural ceremony that has recently taken place at Washington. Formerly the outlay upon such occasions amounted to about
8100,000.	This year it cost but 85,000. This saving may not have pleased the elite at Washington, but looked good to the people who pay the taxes. President Coolidge has this to say:
I am interested in this policy of economy not because I want to save money but because I want to save people.
Another saving was effected through the creation of the bureau of the budget, This was referred to yesterday by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. LeSueur) in detail, and I take this opportunity of again congratulating that hon. gentleman upon his contribution to the debate. General Lord, who succeeded General Dawes as the director of the budget at Washington, has this to say: "Little or no saving was achieved in the public service prior to the budget." Since its inception the government has been enabled to reduce taxation some two billion dollars annually according to President Coolidge's statement in Washington, on January 26.
Reduction in taxation, federal, provincial and municipal, can only be accomplished when the government receives the whole-hearted support of the individual elector. The people can no longer reasonably expect to continue to receive lavish expenditures for public services from the government, and at the same time enjoy any drastic reduction in taxation. It can't be done I I know of no surer way of bringing this home to the people than by the practice of refusing every request for the expenditure of public money that cannot be
ear-marked "solely in the public interest." "Resolve every dloubt in favor of the taxpayer." New post offices such as the one referred to by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) at Penticton, or the building of a wharf similar to the one at Belle River, whose existence was dependent solely on the return of a government supporter, would not be considered legitimate under this policy.
I have no personal grievance with anyone in the civ-1 service, and any words I have to say concerning that service will be directed against the policy and not against the individuals. I would suggest, in order to reduce taxation, a vigorous cutting-down of the civil service. This would not be a popular movement right here in Ottawaj but the government that had the moral backbone to effect such an economy would have the lasting gratitude of the people of Canada. The most effective way to accomplish such a reduction would be to remove the " haven of rest " idea with which the service is enveloped and place the service on a business basis. Lengthen the hours in the inside service from an average of less than six hours a day to a commercial eight-hour day. I believe by this means a real saving of possibly 810,000,060 annually can be made. The departments would not suffer any in efficiency, and such economy in the public service would be appreciated by the over-burdened tax-payer who works eight, ten, twelve or fourteen hours a day. If such action interferes with any section ci the Civil Service Act I would scrap or amend that section. The Civil Service Act was made for man and not man for the act.
Another suggestion would be the co-ordination of the departments. Will any hon. member offer any serious objection to the uniting, say, of the office of Solicitor General with that of the Minister of Justice? In a little by-play ui the debate the other day we learned that one of the best arguments for retaining the office of Solicitor General was that the now right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) at one time filled the office very ably. After the practical demonstration given by the sixty-seven-year-young Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in administering three departments, and acting as prime minister simultaneously, why should we be nervous if a 814,000 per year minister were entrusted with the combined offices of say Secretary of State and National Defence or Trade and Commerce? Great savings were accomplished in the United States along these
The Budget-Mr. Bret hen

lines. The people of Canada will appreciate a saving here.
I have never been very critical of the Senate, believing that with some minor reforms the upper house could well serve a very useful purpose. After a larger acquaintance with the working of parliament, with all due respect to the hon. gentlemen of that august body I am frank to admit, however, I am a convert to the idea of abolition. At present the good services that might be performed by the Senate in initiating good legislation and checking ill-advised legislation are largely offset by the practice of the elected representatives of the people in the House of Commons using the upper house as a smoke screen behind which they may hide in dealing with questions that may be of peculiarly lively interest to certain sections of our people. I believe every hon. gentleman now adorning the Red Chamber whose ability and physical condition would permit could serve his country better as an elected representative of the people in the House of Commons, and I have no doubt he would be welcomed as such. The British North America Act is evidently not perfect and an amendment to permit of such action would I believe meet the hearty approval of the people of Canada.
I doubt if much saving can be accomplished under the present practice of administering the departments of the government. The system savours too much of the cost-plus species of remuneration, with the inevitable result, gradually growing departments with higher administration costs. To me the only feasible method of reducing the ever-growing cost of departmental government is by way of a reduced allotment for each department by a body independent of government heads of the departments. I have no doubt that under such a system the head of each department would accommodate his work to the reduced expenditure, without any serious loss in efficiency, the same as the farmer and others have had to do under falling revenue.
Now I come to the consideration of this House itselfeconomy like charity should begin at home. I am heartily in favour of -he suggestion of many hon. gentlemen that i;he membership in this House should be materially reduced. This would seem an opportune time to give this matter serious consideration, in view of the expressed intention of considering at a near conference amendments to the British North America Act that would enable such changes to be made. Another change that is quite within the powers of

parliament and which I seriously recommend to members of this House is a reasonable reduction of the indemnity. While many good arguments can be advanced against such action, the truth remains that no drastic economies can be effected without the members of this House demonstrating their willingness to give a lead. Some say that with any reduction there would be no inducement for good men to enter public life. Answering this I should like to say "the lure of .the dollar can never attract; (the best men in Canada like the call of service." and I am sure no hon. member would suffer any permanent inconvenience when the good effects of such action are measured. The indemnity is not a salary but is supposed to be given to secure hon. members against financial loss. I recognize that members coming from the extremes of Canada, on account of their inability to give personal supervision to their business, suffer a greater financial loss than the member within a stone's throw of Ottawa, and therefore I would favour as fair and reasonable the payment of indemnity under a graduated scale or a zone system. Coming from Ontario I can suggest such a change with more freedom than could an hon. member from those parts of Canada who would be favourably affected by such an arrangement.
I do not purpose referring to our uncontrollable expenditures such as interest on national debt, pensions, and so on, further than to say that while some hon. members of the late government might be seriously criticized for their lack of vision in failing to reduce the capital expenditure during the period of good times following the war, the fact remains that these debts are with us, we must bend every energy to prevent them expanding and devise some means for their substantial reduction.
I have suggested some practical economies in the public expenditure that can and will be appreciated by every taxpayer in Canada. I would now like to refer for a few minutes to methods that might be employed to raise the necessary revenue with the least hardship to the people at large. What then should be our sources of taxation?
First:	Death duties carefully and stiffly
graded. This is the fairest of all taxes. When a man has had a life use of the money which the country has helped him to make, the country has a right to a share of it at his death. Of course, the interests of the widows and orphans must be safeguarded to a reasonable extent.

The Budget-Mr. Meightn
Second:	A graded income tax, beginning
well down and after a certain sum-say $10,000 a year-is reached, rising very sharply on large incomes. This is getting the money from where it exists. But I would make a distinction favourable to incomes reinvested in industrial enterprises over the latent or dormant income. Such a tax on a man's income is easily collectible and it is preferable to the tariff which is a tax on the poor man's needs.
Third: A sales tax which might be largely excuse in its character, bearing most heavily on luxuries and on such Canadian manufactories as enjoy the highest protection. Automobiles, for instance, would be considered as in such class.
Fourth:	A tariff for revenue. This, of
necessity, must be flexible and levied as far as possible on the non-necessities of life and luxuries. Tariffs are usually costly taxes, troublesome to collect and, in my opinion, an implement of taxation warranted only by dire necessity. When levied as protective, tariffs are unjust and ruinous taxes; they are a privilege granted to the few to bleed the many; they drain the country without filling the exchequer; they are heaviest on the best citizens, the men who are rearing worthily families whose needs have to be supplied; they are harsh on the poor. These are taxed out of all proportions to their means with every purchase. It is the purchasing power of the mass of the people that makes trade prosperous. It is the worker's needs supplied that makes work for workers.
I have been rather surprised during this debate to hear our friends to the right advocating almost with one accord reciprocity with the United States-reciprocity of tariffs, not of freer trade. Our Liberal-Conservative friends are not always protectionists; sometimes they are more Liberal than Conservative, and a few nights ago they w'ere almost Progressive in their leanings. A certain private bill was proposed by the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) which was to extend for six years a certain patent enjoyed by a manufacturing concern in Montreal. When it was strenuously opposed by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Wallace) and others in this part of the House, to our surprise the only apparent support that came from anywhere in this House for the company seeking this particular protection came from that doughty protectionist, the sponsor of the bill. He was like " a voice crying in the wilderness." I am opposed to protective tariffs. They have been given a fair, reasonable trial in Canada for well-nigh fifty years. Successive
governments, as was showm by the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson) have made insignificant, downward changes; yet when we point to the impoverished farmers throughout the country, when we point to the strikes of labouring men for higher wages, to seasonable unemployment and to the suspension of protected industries, our protectionist friends in this House say this is all due to a reduction or threatened reduction of the tariff. Such a charge I defy my protectionist friends to sustain. On the contrary they but discredit themselves by advancing such a baseless argument and by seeking to avoid responsibility for conditions, for which they are clearly and undeniably responsible.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that if the>e is any man in Canada who really believes that, under a democratic form of government where the people rule, where laws should be made for the good of all, any party has the right to impose taxes or to put burdens on one class in order to benefit another class, then that man is unworthy of a place in the free country in which he lives.
I have tried honestly to answer the question: What is wrong with Canada? and to offer some humble suggestions by' way of remedy. In so doing, I have endeavoured to avoid unduly hard or destructive criticism, believing that Canada needs at this time, as in the war-lime crisis, the united, unbiased, whole-hearted, patriotic efforts of every member of this House to bring Canada through.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate
has this year extended to an extraordinary length, and I know all hon. members are relieved to be certain that it will close tonight. I am not making any reflection on the length of the debate, although it is well known that, as regards this side of the House, we were prepared to close last week. The budget debate in Canada serves a purpose which is not there to be served in many other countries. We are a very widely scattered people. We have great diversity of interests, physical conditions and occupations. The budget debate is the medium oy which the opposing views of many sections are expressed and brought together. I do not believe severe strictures on the length of the debate, therefore, are warranted; but at the same time it is possible to overdo everything, and I would have preferred had this debate closed sooner.
My contribution, if it can be called such, will not be lengthy to-day. We on this side
The Budget-Mr. Meighen

have on the order paper a notice of motion in my name which we have endeavoured to move and have discussed, but so far without-success. This notice of motion has to do with what is the transcendent question in Canadian politics to-day, namely, that of the best fiscal policy under	the
conditions of the world at this time. The notice of motion covers this field and this only, and I thin'k it will save the time of the House and contribute to orderly debate if I leave its discussion to the time when I may be able to move the motion.
I am going to attempt to analyse our financial position and to do so with all the clearness I can. I do not feel that I can speak with any pontifical authority, but I will do this for hon. members who do me the favour of listening:	I will give my authority
for each statement which I make, and leave the House to judge whether it is dependable or not. The result will be nothing very cheering so far as Canada is concerned, especially for our taxpayers. And while I believe that it is due in considerable degree to inefficiency, lack of control and lack of definiteness of purpose on the part of the government, I want to make it clear at the beginning that in my judgment the consequences are traceable in far greater degree to unsoundness of fiscal policy, to unsoundness of fiscal practice on the part of the administration, and to still greater seriousness of their fiscal threats.
I had intended making some reference, as a member of the late government, to remarks which fell from the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault); but on looking back over past debates I find that everything which he so recklessly alleged was irrefutably answered in 1917 in his own hearing, and to the material of which answers he made no reference. It was there 4 p.m. shown that, so far from there being any waste in respect of the matters to which he referred, each and every article was supplanted by another without a dollar of cost:	the Ross rifle by the Lee-
Enfield, rifle for rifle; the Oliver equipment by the Webb equipment, each for each; that neither of these was used one single day, so soon as it was possible to get another to take its place; and that far from its having been possible to have the substitution made earlier, so great was the scarcity, especially in rifles, that the British government were compelled, though they did not favour the Ross, to place large orders in this country for that very rifle. It is very hard to understand how an hon. member could drag these musty subjects into the debates of to-day and do so

with a good conscience, having regard to present conditions in Canada.
I pass now to a review of the year's results, and from that I shall move to a review of the full results of the past three years and a quarter. There is in the minds of many hon. members confusion, at all events there is very little in the way of agreement, as to what is disclosed in the budget speech of thi3 year. I do not think I can recall two hon. members who have given to the House the same deductions from the budget presentation. If there have been any single group who have agreed it would be quite a number, by no means all, of hon. gentlemen opposite, who draw a deduction which is manifestly wrong and which not one of them in a real encounter would venture to sustain. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) argues that the budget presentation is clear. Strange indeed it is, if such is the case, that hon. members of this House cannot tell what the result of it is; and stranger still is it that no one erred more frequently than the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George himself.
The budget presentation is not either complete or clear; it fails in the -main purpose of a budget presentation, a purpose which the hon. memlber for St. Lawrence-St. George endeavoured, I think conscientiously, to supply, but which it should not have been necessary for anyone to attempt at all to supply, if the budget speech had contained the one great element which should be its first essential. Hon. members to my left have repeatedly urged that something be stated which is clear, which they will understand, which other than accountants can understand. It is suggested that this is not possible. Why is it not possible? When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) presented his budget two years ago I complained that it was not complete; but no one in this House found any difficulty in deciding upon its results. The same was true of the budget he presented the year before; I never heard any complaint as to its not being clear. Nor was there any complaint of that kind in respect of any previous budget presentation so far as I can recall, though, years having passed, one may possibly have overlooked an instance. The reason that it is possible for the present budget to be obscure- is the fact that the finances of Canada to-day appear under two phases instead of under one; and it is obscure not because the bookkeeping of the country differs in principle, or differs at all, from the bookkeeping of previous years: it is simply because the government in presenting the results of the book-

The Budget-Mr. Meigkeu
keeping have concealed the result and facta from the public.
I have said that our financial affairs now run in two channels; everyone knows what I mean. We make two fronts before the world, first as Canada in its own account and secondly Canada as the National Railways. Each is our possession, the finances of each are our concern, and the debts of each are our responsibility. I am not complaining that the accounts are kept separately; no one would so complain. They should be. But they should not be kept separately for the purpose of concealing the result of one or failing to disclose the joint result of both. What is this joint result so far as 1924-25, the last fiscal year, is concerned?
If we look to 1922-23, the last vear of the Hon. Mr. Fielding's regime, we shall find that the result was given as a deficit of $31,000,000. He arrived at that deficit. Mr. Fielding-I must mention his name, if I may be forgiven [DOT]-took into account the whole of *'he finances of both phases, both of account No. 1 and of account No. 2. On this we are all agreed. In 1923-24, the first year of the present Acting Minister of Finance, the whole was not collected and a total result of the whole given the public. It is not fair, though, to say that all of one was removed to one side and the result of the other alone given as the result of the year. Part of one was given, and all of the other. Part of the railway result was included, that is to say, the cash advances, but not the assistance, the commitments in other forms; cash advances amounting to some $23,000,000-these the present acting minister included in his annual outlay in arriving at the result which he presented to the country, namely, a surplus of $35,000,000. I hope that, so far, I am clear. To arrive at that claimed surplus the Acting Minister of Finance placed all his receipts on one side, which was right; all the disbursements, ordinary, capital and special, of account number one on the other, and as to account number two, the railways, he included all cash disbursements, but no more. He did include what he had loaned in cash. He did add not only what he had loaned the railway in cash to his ordinary expenditure of the country, but he added his capital as well, and his special expenditure too. In a word, he included everything except the guarantees he made for the National Railways. Now I hope so far there is no difference of view; if there is, I am trying to state it accurately and I would be only too glad to be corrected or placed on the right track if I am wrong. This resulted in a surplus of $35,000,000. It is true the guarantees, which were not included, were 72V millions. With those included there would have been a deficit of 364 millions. Or, to put it in a word, the result of putting the two accounts together meant a deficit of 364 millions.

He will find that in ordinary expenditure there is $5,100,000 less than last year, but the budget speech does not compare the capital expenditure with last year's capital expenditure at all. Are hon. members surprised to know-it is some six millions more? The budget speech does not compare even the special expenditure this year with the special expenditure last year. This year's special expenditure is about $4,000,000 less, because no doubt of recession from the war. So, summing the three together, the improvement in expenditure less than the year before is approximately $3,000,000, or a little over. So we have $53,000,000 less revenue, and about $3,000,000 less expenditure-some $49,000,000 worse off in the. total, and this irrespective of the railways, than we were a year ago. Taking all together, irrespective of what the minister leaves out, we accept $1,823,000 as right.
Now what other obligations have we entered into during the past year? And may I say, especially with reference to some comment that has been made by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler)?- in arriving at our position we cannot, on the system we have followed for years, claim to have a surplus unless we have a surplus over everything. We have not done it for years. We never claimed a surplus in our time. We said we had a surplus over certain things,
but we showed clearly we had a deficit altogether. Expenditure on capital account was always included, has been for many years in this country, and because capital account is included in our expenditure as a country, why in the world should we distinguish it in our expenditure ah a railway? -the more so because whatever capital expenditure we put in now or for years to come, we cannot, if we are honest, call the return for that expenditure an active asset, of this country. For this reason: If we want to know where we are at, we must absolutely include every commitment until the day comes, if it ever does, when we can honestly consider our investments in our railways as active assets.
I stated that we were accepting the figure as $1,823,000, understanding that to one side were placed all the items I have referred to. Now these items are, according to the minister's own figures: $18,027,000 cash advance; $46,000,000 guarantees-National Railway bonds-and $18,000,000 further guarantees, aside altogether from another $17,000,000, which is for refunding. May I state my own view on this point? In arriving at our position, and in this I entirely agree with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), our endeavour should be to ascertain how much the National Railways have gone further into debt. Of course, to get how much further they' have gone into debt, we have to take off what debt has been paid. Now $17,000,000 of last year's guarantee was for refunding; $18,000,000 was not. So the total assistance to the railways is made up of these three items: $18,000,000, $46,000,000, $18,027,000, or a total of $82,027,000. In addition, there was $900,000 for the merchant marine, and $600,000 for Quebec harbour, making a grand total of $83,527,000. From this must be deducted the surplus claimed on the balance of our accounts; that is to say, ordinary revenue over ordinary expenditure, capital and special-$1,823,000.	This deducted we
find that there has been a net recession for the year of SSI,704,000. I do not think those figures can be honestly controverted. They take into account all refunding. This is the amount we have gone back this year-$81,-
704,000.
Now, it is claimed that if the government admitted $81,000,000, they would be putting themselves in a position unfavourable as compared with presentations made in previous years by the late government; that is to say, they would be admitting liability for guarantees of loans when the previous government did not admit those as part of the debt of
The Budget-Mr. Meighen

Canada. I am going to inquire into that contention.
In the first place, let me say that if we assume it as absolutely true-and I think I will show to the satisfaction of anyone it is not, but assume that it is-what difference does it make? We still have gone back $81,000,000 this year. All it would mean would be this, that we claimed to have gone back in certain former years less than we really did go back; that is all it would mean. So whether I succeed or not in showing that the comparison cannot be made to our disadvantage, it is established that we did go back SSI,000.000 this year anyway; and if the Prime Minister in his contention a year ago is right-that we did not include our guarantees even when they were not for refunding-all he succeeds in showing is that in those years we went back further than we admitted.
Now let us see if that is true. I do not know just how my hon. friend for St. Lawrence-St. George got some of his figures. I am sure he did not intentionally present them wrongly, but I could not follow some of his figures.

Now, I want to inquire as to what has been the result of the three years and three months up to April 1, of this year of the present administration. It is important so to inquire and I proceed to do so including both accounts of course. I proceed to do so taking into account all refundings and the way to get it
The Budget-Mr. Meighen

is this: To take the debt on the fust account as at the end of 1921 and take the debt on that account on 31st March, 1925. The difference is the increase or decrease as the case may be. Then in relation to the other account , the National Railways, take the debt at the end of 1921 and the debt at the end of March, 1925. Now, if I leave my statement that way it is not altogether fair. In getting the total increased obligations of the country it will not do to include the whole increase of the National Railway debt. All that it is right to include is the increase of the debt due to the public-due to the third parties; you cannot include the increase of the debt due the government, because of course that is not any increase of the joint debt at ali.
Now. what is the increase in the debt on the first account?-that is, the old account of the government of Canada proper. The Canada Gazette shows the debt on the 31st December. 1921, to have been $2,366,861,252.29. This government took office on December 29, 1921. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) shows the debt at the end of April to have been $2,431,487,112.88. The difference is $64,625,860.59. There can be no dispute of these figures. All the comment I have ever heard is this:	That when you
take the debt at the end of 1921, and add the debt for the three months succeeding, you are adding debt which was incurred under estimates prepared by the previous government. That is true. But the expenditure from the end of 1921, from the accession of tins government, was wholly under the control of this government, because when moneys are voted in estimates it does not mean that those moneys have to be spent. It is only authority to spend those moneys. The payments by this government after they come into office are their responsibility, and the responsibility of no other. The actual increase in debt is the $64,625,000 which I have just given.
Now I proceed to inquire where we stand in. relation to the railways. Certain figures have been put on Hansard by the Minister of Railways in response to questions put by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drasdon). These figures show an increase in the three years, not taking into account these latter three months, of $294,000,000. That is the increase of public debt and of government debt both. Those figures do not differ very much from those given in the reports of the company, but they do differ somewhat. They differ very considerably in the division of the increase between the public and the government. I hold in my hand the report of the National Railways for this last year.
cMr. Meighen.]
This report gives the debt due the public at the end of 1924 as $913,913,082.80. This is due the public alone. This will be found at page 29 of this report. In order to find out what was due the public at the end of
192,1	it is necessary to have recourse to two authorities. One is the annual report of the Grand Trunk, because the roads were not united then; and in the annual report of that company for the year 1921, at page 8, the following is given as the debt outstanding on the 31st December, 1921; $371,042,194.75. Now if hon. members will turn to the annual report of the Department of Railways and Canals for the year 1922-that is the report for the previous year-they will find that out of this amount there is due the government the sum of $76,965,322.10. Take this away from the $371,000,000, the total debt, and we have the amount due the public $294,064,872. This is the debt on the Grand Trunk at the end of 1921. Now we have to get the debt on the Canadian National Railways at the end of 1921. This appears in the report of the Railways and Canals department at pages 35 and 38. The figures are:
Canadian Northern	 $302,399,006
Grand Trunk Pacific	 157,699,714
So that adding the three figures together, the S294,000,000 on the Grand Trunk, $302,000,000 on the Canadian Northern and the $157,000,000 on the Grand Trunk Pacific, we have a total debt to the public at the end of 1921 of $755,115,592. We have $755,000,000 odd due the public at the end of 1921, $913,913,000 odd due the public at the end of 1924, and since 1924, until the end of March of this year $18,000,000 more has been added according to the statement of the minister which is correct as we all know, the $18,000,000 being new money from proceeds of the $35,000,000 issue made this year.
Then adding all these together, the $913,913,082 and the $18,000,000 we have $931,913,082 as the debt due to the public at the end of March last. Deducting the debt due to the public $755,115,592 on the 31st December, 1921, when this government took office, we find the increase in our debt as denominated, Canadian National Railways, $176,796,490. This is the increase in the one account, the increase in the other account is $64,625,860, and the two together make a total on both accounts of $241,423,350. Nor does this represent the total increase in the debt from December, 1921. To arrive at these figures there is included the $4,000,162 that has been added this year on account of the debt of Greece and Roumania. There was included as well some $8,199,333.31 last year and $8,938,260

The Budget-Mr. Meujhen
the year before which were rightly taken in as an asset, but which were just as much our assets five years ago as they are to-day- exchange adjusted as due us by the British government; and a similar amount the year before. I am not complaining at least in the case of the latter two items being included in our estimates to get at our right debt now, but what I say is that we cannot fool ourselves by thinking we are that much better off than we were. We are just exactly in the same position. They were our property then as they are now. Adding these, the debt that we have gone into since this government took office, after all refunding is allowed for, is $262,561,105. I do not think it can be successfully contradicted that that is the real position. I do not think I am in disagreement at all with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George in this respect.

speechtext:
I do not know why it
was necessary for my hon. friend to keep forever repeating his conclusion. It would have been enlightening if he had given us his method of arriving at it. I have given my method of arriving at the result just presented and I have quoted my authority at every stage. My hon. friend is entirely wrong as to his figures of a surplus. I commend, to him, more careful inquiry, more deliberation and less determination to get back into the good graces of the government.
What is the significance of all these returns? Has this House been prepared for the fact, which is admitted even in the report of the Minister of Railways, that in the three years, irrespective of what has taken place in the last three months, the National Railway debt to the public and the government increased by more than $294,000,000? Is it prepared for the fact, which nobody disputes, that, adding the last three months, it is now, according to the minister, about $312,000,000-or, according to the reports of the companies, about $327,000,000-more than it was just at the end of December, 1921? The increase to the public i3 colossal in any event; the increase in both is still worse. We have been supplied all along with data as to how the operating account was running. We were told through the year 1923: "It is improving." The operating account was improving. We were told through the year 1924: "It is getting worse." It was getting worse. But the operating account discloses only a mere fraction of the whole truth as to the National Railways and the real position we are in to-day.
The Budget-Mr. Meighen

Let me say a few words by way of persona! reference. I am not one who has been predisposed to criticize the National Railways. I have been assailed myself most severely for the part I took in amalgamating the roads under the government of Canada at the time they were amalgamated, especially, for the acquisition of the Grand Trunk. No one hoped more ardently than I did that the operation of those roads, controlled by the statutes which were submitted and passed by this House, would be a success. After the first two years' reports came down, the hopes that I had originally entertained were strengthened. When the Minister of Railways presented his report in the spring of 1922, I commented, as the House will remember, most favourably upon it and looked forward hopefully to the success of the system so amalgamated. In 1923, I followed in the same vein. It is certainly with a degree of disappointment, which I do not think anyone will sincerely question, that I now am compelled to say that the whole aggregate result to-day is discouraging. It is not that the disappointment is so great in respect ol the result of operations, but the disappointment, indeed, is keen when we have regard to the fearful pace at which, in these last three years, the capital account has been increased. I know the capital account was very considerably increased prior to 1921. When we took over the Grand Trunk railway particularly, it was in a dilapidated condition. The board of arbitration found that that company had been paying to shareholders dividends which should have been applied to their system, which should have been invested in rolling stock, in their line of railway, in maintenance and things of that kind. The condition of the road was such that millions had to be invested to get it into the shape in which we found it in 1922. Those millions, however were not as great as have been generally believed. They were given by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and they were given correctly; but everybody thought at the end of 1921 that these large capital investments would be over. Nobody thought all capital additions vould be over. You cannot maintain a railway without some enlargement of capital investment. In the year 1922, this policy was rightly, honestly pursued. The board of management of that year added to the debt of that railway in 1922 only the sum of $59,000,000, as is shown by the minister's return. This sum of $59,000,000 could have very little in it except the deficit inclusive of fixed charges and operation.

The deficit alone would be something over $50,000,000, so that the amount of capital investment in 1922 was relatively very small. The management at that time was under Mr. Hanna and the former board and it determined that we had gone as far in the way of investment as we should go for the time being; that our business was to take the property we had and make it go, to endeavour to get traffic enough for it to give returns to the people of Canada and not to continue the process of adding million by million to the capital debt of the system.

speechtext:
It is not a proof, no;
but it is a proof that the policy tha+ has b ien followed is unwise. Never under the conditions of these last three years was this country justified in putting 3327,000,000 more into the National Railways; even if you assume-which I will not-that the money is now represented by tangible assets, the policy was not the right one. We already had over $1,100,000,000 in that road and to-dav we have $1,492,000,000. And of that, $327,000,000 has been put into the railways since this government came into power. These figures, I say. are staggering; they have staggered the people of Canada. And this government under ths law of the land is responsible for all moneys provided for capital expenditure of the Canadian National Railways. Let no one forget that fact. The statute makes the government responsible for capital. I could point to investments of the railways that have not been sound; but I do not claim that under any management every investment that is

The Budget-Mr. Meighen
made will be sound. What I ciaim however is that the road has been run without financial direction, of a quality adequate to such an enterprise, ever since the end of 1922.
You may have a high opinion of Sir Henry Thornton or you may not; he has his critics and his friends, and he has many of both. But neither Sir Henry Thornton nor any other man in charge of a railway can be master of all the phases of this huge enterprise. Name me the president or general manager of any great system half the size of this who is surrounded with the class of men whom this government provided to manage a road .n which- including the Intercolonial and Transcontinental-we have invested nearly two billions of the money of the ; ecple of 5 p.m. Canada. This road's operations are twice the size of the titanic United States Steel Corporation; and I wonder if we would compare the directors of tne United States Steel Corporation with the Talbots, the Goughs, the Dawsons with whom this government supplied Sir Henry ThornTn at the end of 1922. Where is the man on that board-or rather, where was the man on that board, for I shall comment on rhe present board in due course-who was competent to render any real assistance to Sir Henry Thornton, assuming that he himself was competent, giving him every credit for what he has done, when the old board was changed at the end of 1922? Instead of Mr. E. R. Wood, instead of Mr. Riley, instead of Mr. Hobson, we had on the board, the men I have named. The consequences are now upon us. There has been a little improvement of personnel lately, I admit. I do not object vo, rather I commend, the appointment of two or three men, Mr. Gardiner, I think, was a good appointment; so was Mr. Brown. But these men have been only lately put on the board. Up to their appointment who was there on the board who held the slightest control over the financial direction of that colossal enterprise? No control from the directors, no control from the government-and Canada to-day finds itself $176,000,000 more in debt to the public in respect of the railways, and $327,000,000 more in debt altogether since this government has come into power.
Canada is not a country that can afford to go down hill at such a pace, and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is absolutely right when he calls attention to the inevitable end. Such a state of affairs cannot continue and the responsibility is on the administration, who having the power to control this tremendous outlay has failed to exercise that power. They have allowed millions to go into Scribe hotels, golf courses, 168
radio sets and all that sort of thing. If this country were going ahead it would not be so bad. If we were expanding and the population were growing, if there were sufficient traffic to supply both railways, with a surplus, these expenditures might be justified. But when there is only a limited amount of traffic available, to be spending the money of the Canadian people in tens of millions in a mad effort to get the traffic from the other enterprises is manifestly not wisdom. It is because of this policy that we find ourselves where we are to-day.
I said there was no expansion. Have hon. members observed what has been going on? Has there been any attempt at co-ordination or economy? I look at the Colonization department alone and I find that what in 1922 was about $160,000 has increased until now it is $770,000. And this in competition with the immigration efforts of the government. How can such a duplication of effort be justified? During the fiscal year 1923-24 the government spent $3,482,986 on immigration work, or $1,128,000 more than was spent during the year 1922-23. And with all this duplication we have an immigration of 111,000 as against 148,000 the year before. This year the Canadian National Railways' expenditure in colonization has gone up by 150 per cent; while, as I have stated, the government has spent $1,128,000 more on immigration. Yet, notwithstanding all that additional expenditure, to say nothing of the overlapping, we have received about 37,000 less in immigrants than we did the year before.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has been in the habit of telling us that when his government started this work they had to begin at the bottom of the hill; that the old government had allowed the immigration machinery to go to rack and ruin, and so the present administration had to start at the bottom; and the people must therefore wait until later figures would be available to see what the full harvest of the government's policy will be. Well, by actual count, they have announced nine policies in their three years of office so far as immigration is concerned. The figures however show that our immigration, as at the 31st of
March, was as follows in each of the years enumerated:
1920		 111.338
In that year our soldiers had not all returned.

1923		 72,887

speechtext:
It would make little difference anyway, because there has been a great increase in the immigration figures. But I got the figures from the department; and if the items referred to should not be included under the head of Immigration why did the department so include them?
Now, these are the consequences which we have to face. They are not very cheerful to contemplate, nor will recovery from them be very easy. I sometimes wonder how the government can justify the course it is pursuing. We have abundant resources, we are told; but abundant resources are not enough, unless we manage them for the benefit of the people of our country. All this talk about great resources is just so much air; what is essential to accompany resources is a policy which will develop them; and the government should see to it that the people of Canada shall get the benefit of the full harvest of that development.
We have been met year after year with admissions: things were not any too good, but they were going to be very good soon. One year we had one excuse; the next year we had another; the third year we had still another; and I wondered what was to be the excuse this year. I remembered that last, year the Acting Minister of Finance told us in his statement that with these reductions of duty on basic commodities, on the "instruments of production," there would be so much to buy and so much money to buy it with that our workmen would be employed overtime and our factories running night and day. This was the prophecy made in the closing words of the budget of last year. Instead of that, everybody knows-not only everybody here but the people throughout the whole country-that the very reverse

has been the fact; and I wondered what the Acting Minister of Finance would say by way of explanation when he came before rhe House this year with his budget. He looked about for some new excuse. The three best had gone; he had to have another. He looked across to Europe, and he said: "1 know what the trouble is; it is the reparations problem over in Europe. Europe is all mix:'I up; the people there cannot buy. The reparations trouble left them in chaos up to last year, but last year they got it fixed up by the Dawes plan, so now we are on the eve of expansion." Do hon. members really think there is the slightest thing in that? Do hon. members really think that is valid to the extent of one per cent? Is it difficulty in selling our exports that has been our trouble? Have we ever got as good prices in history, in time of peace, as we got this last year? I do not think we ever did, nor do I think we have ever found so ready a sale-that is, for our raw product, the production of which and the marketing of which was going to make us all so busy, all so happy, all so rich. On the contrary it is business at home that has become stagnant, the people at home who have become discouraged. I ask, with such policies as this government is pursuing-the National Railways running more or less wild, expenditure mounting up and revenue decreasing-what will be our position next year? Does the government anticipate that next year we will get higher prices for our products? If so, on what is that expectation based? Does the government expect that a contracted population is going to produce more than an expanded population? If it does nol expect these things, upon what does it rely to extricate this country from the mire of debt into which it has fallen?
Now, the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) in the amendment says this and this alone: that the essential thing for Canada to-day is reduction of taxation, especially of those taxes which bear on the masses of the people and which this government has increased-the sales tax, these nuisance taxes, and the like. Reduction of all taxes is necessary, but of these especially. The amendment says, as welt that there is disclosed in the budget of this year no evidence of that economy that will make such a, reduction possible. I ask, is there any hon. member of this House who in his heart of hearts thinks he can discover any such evidence in the budget of this year? Is there an hon. member to my left-and they are on trial in this debate as well as the rest of us-is there one of them who has not

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
stated in this House the very things that are stated in the amendment? Has there been one hon. member to my left who has uttered in this debate an opinion which conflicts with the statements made in the amendment? Are those statements not of importance? Is it not of value that this House should declare a fact-and it is a fact-so vital to the welfare of this country? If hon. members admit those facts, how is it that they are going to vote against them? Some hon. members have said, "These people to our right are protectionists." Well, there is no protectionist statement in the amendment. We have not diverged from our views-and I own it-on the subject of protection; we stand where we stood in office and we are going to stand there. Further, we are going to do everything in our power to get the judgment of the people of Canada on the issue. We have a statement of our faith in that respect on the records of this House'; there it has been since the first day of this session, and there it will stay until it is moved and discussed in parliament. But if we had included in the amendment a declaration with regard to protection, duplicating our other declaration of faith, hon. members to our left would have said: Oh, the rest of your amendment is all right; we are with you on economy, we are with you in reduction of taxation, but there is that protection declaration-we have to vote against you on that account. But this time they have no such excuse. This time the sincerity of their professions on this question are to be tested. This time the country is going to know whether hon. members to my left are more interested in continuance in office of this government than in the adoption of sound principles of public administration.
As for this government I can make no such appeal to them. They are interested in one thing, so far as I can see, and one thing only- the retention of power. But I do ask them to have some regard, before it is too late, to the actual condition of this Dominion. I do ask them to adopt principles and practices, both of administration and of fiscal policy; I do ask them to adopt such courses as will relieve the discouragement of industry, the lassitude of trade and the wastage of population which confront us now.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rules
of this House have been so arranged as to make possible a discussion on particular occasions of matters of great concern to the 168i
country as a whole, and at such times the House and the country have a right to expect that the topics which are the subject of consideration will be brought under review particularly by the party leaders in the House. It is customary on the occasion of the budget debate for all political leaders to discuss the budget proper. A time has been set apart for the discussion of railway problems. In order to permit of the fullest possible discussion, matters relating to railways are referred to a select committee of the House with power of examining in detail all the questions involved of calling witnesses and going into all the facts and figures and circumstances relative to the railways of the country. When the report of the committee is presented to the House, it is reasonable to assume that railway matters will then and there be considered and that every member will be prepared to discuss them. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when we come to discuss the budget, if we are to follow established precedent we have a right to expect from the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) a discussion, if not, above all else, at least in some measure, of the fiscal policy of the country. He told1 us this afternoon that he regarded the fiscal policy of the country as an all-important question. I think we will all agree with him in that, and I think it goes without saying that the time for the discussion of fiscal policy is when the House is assembled for that express purpose, namely, to debate the budget. Instead we have listened this afternoon to a discussion on the part of the right hon. gentleman which has had to do almost exclusively with railway matters.
We are told by the right hon. leader of the opposition himself that he does not intend to discuss the fiscal policy at this time. Well, Sir, I do not know what motive my right hon. friend has in mind in not wishing to discuss the fiscal policy, in not wishing to bring forward his own fiscal policy and have it made a subject of debate here, unless it be that he is either ashamed or afraid of his own offspring. On the eve of the assembling of this parliament my right hon. friend issued a manifesto to this country, a manifesto dealing with fiscal matters. When the government called parliament together early in the month of February, it did so with the hope and expectation that the business of the country would be expedited, that the convenience of hon. members would be consulted, and that, the government being prepared to bring down its measures rapidly as opportunity permitted, it would be possible for

May I say with regard to the present debate that I believe it is the longest budget debate that has ever taken place in this parliament. Certainly it is the longest that has taken place in the last thirty years, and over a budget that is in the main non-contentious. What has been the nature of the debate? Most of the time has been taken up by hon. gentlemen of the official opposition in saying that the government should have put the tariff higher, and by hon. gentlemen of the Progressive group in saying that they were not satisfied because the government had not made the tariff lower. As a government we are being condemned by hon. gentlemen opposite not because they agree. If they join together in a vote against the budget their vote will only have this significance, that we are being censured because at one and the same time we have not gone in diametrically opposite directions. That is the force of the opposition that has occupied a month and a half of the time of this parliament, the government is to be criticized because it has so sized up public opinion in Canada to-day and in this House that it seeks to avoid an extreme in either direction, and to do at the present time the
thing which the moderate, sensible people of this country wish to be done.
It may interest hon. members to have a review of the length of time that has been spent year by year over the last thirty years in debating the several budgets. In twenty-three years of the last thirty the debate on the budget has not occupied a longer time than ten days at the outside. In several sessions it has not occupied more than five days and in some sessions but one or two days. In 1896 it occupied twelve days. That was just before an election and probably at the present time some hon. members feel it is necessary to speak on the budget because they think there is a possibility of an election coming on in the near future. In 1915 the budget debate lasted thirteen days. In 1902 and in 1922 the budget debate lasted fourteen days. Last year it occupied nineteen days. In 1900, before the general election of that year, it lasted twenty-three days. This year the debate has run into twenty-four days. We began on the 24th March and to-morrow will be the 1st May. The time of the House, with the exception of a brief adjournment at Easter and the ordinary adjournments over Saturday and Sunday has been given continuously to the discussion of this budget.

May I now
come to what in other particulars has been the nature of the criticism directed against the government. It has been in part along the line taken by the right hon. leader of the opposition this afternoon. First of all, there has been criticism of the manner in which the public accounts of the country have been made up. In the next place there has been criticism of the method in which the budget has been presented and the time at which it was introduced, and finally there has been the amendment of the ex-Minister
2640	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) and the different points referred to therein. I think in these particulars we have summarized fairly well the nature of the opposition which has come from hon. gentlemen opposite. May I say that I think it ought to be possible for hon. gentlemen in this House to debate public questions without either impugning the honour of ministers of the crown or the integrity of government officials. It is because hon. gentlemen opposite, including my right hon. friend this afternoon in the course of his remarks, have descended to that level, that I wish to take the strongest possible exception to the nature of the pronouncements they have made against the government and one of its honourable members, as well as against members of the public service of the country. My right hon. friend last year-and hon. members opposite have done the same thing this year -insinuated that the government in some way caused the public accounts to be made up in a different fashion from the form in which they had been made up hitherto. In fact, the sole point of my right hon. friend's remarks this afternoon is that the government has not taken into account in connection with the discussion of the government services as such and what relates to the government services as such, the railways and facts and figures relating thereto. There has been a direct statement-I will not call it an insinuation, although it started as an insinuation, and, as in the case of many other things oft repeated, those who repeated it have come to believe it themselves, it comes now to a direct statement-that the government has changed the method of making up the public accounts so as to deceive the House and the country. Hon. gentlemen will recall that over and over again we heard the statement that we had not included in our public accounts as contributing to the net consolidated debt the guaranteed and unguaranteed amounts which the railways had expended and which they say we should have included, and further that by not so doing we were altering the method of bringing the public accounts before the people of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were confronted with the sworn statement of the auditors who in their day audited the books of this country, found that while they might make that assertion a few times they could not make it indefinitely, and so they have abandoned it as my right hon. friend abandoned it to-day, and have come now to make the statement that it is not the books of the country that have been altered, but it is the method of the presents-. fMr. Mackenzie King.]
tion by the Minister of Finance of the accounts of the country.
Let me come to the statement of the books of the country. In the year 1920, the then Minister of Finance, the present member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) called in a firm of accountants from the city of Toronto to go over the books of the Finance department to see if they were kept in a proper way and to audit them. I think it was a wise and desirable course to adopt. There had been large expenditures during the war. The minister wished to have a sense of security that in these vast outlays there had not been too much in the way of confusion; and he brought in a firm of auditors and gave them not only the task of auditing the books of the Finance department but gave them also the further task of straightening out the accounts of the Finance department in such a way that they would more readily compare in form with the methods adopted by great financial institutions or railway companies and industrial concerns. I will read to the House the statement that appears in the report of the Deputy Minister of Finance in the Public Accounts for 1920. It is as follows:
In carrying out the policy of making the balance sheet simple and illustrative its usual form has, under the personal supervision of Mr. George Edwards, F.C.A., C.B.E., of the well-known firm of Messrs. Edwards, Morgan and Company, Chartered Accountants, head office in the city of Toronto, been revised and set up in a manner more in conformity with those of banks, railway corporations and other financial institutions. Mr. Edwards and his firm have given considerable attention to this revision without remuneration. The revised balance sheet will undoubtedly be favourably received by outside business concerns.
Then there is the certificate of the firm of Edwards, Morgan and Company, chartered accountants, dated Ottawa, December 1, 1920, which appears in the Public Accounts 1920, at that time:
We have examined the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada (shewn herewith) as of March 31, 1920, also the expenditure and revenue account for the fiscal year ended on the said date, and have verified the same by reference to the Dominion ledgers. We certify that the above-mentioned statements accurately set forth the matters therein referred to, and are as shewn by the said books.
Edwards, Morgan and Company,
Chartered Accountants.
That is the firm this government retained to examine the public accounts and books of the Finance department last year, after hon. gentlemen opposite had said they were made up in a different fashion. We asked them to certify to parliament as to whether or not any change had been made in the manner of presenting the public accounts. This is the certificate which that firm has given, a firm

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
which I wish the House to remember was retained by hon. gentlemen opposite in the first instance, and which was requested by this government to certify whether there had been any change in the method by which the public accounts for 1924 were made up. This certificate appears in the Public Accounts of this year:
We have examined the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada as at March 31, 1924, and we certify that the balance sheet conforms to the balance sheets of previous years in not including in the net debt of the Dominion, issues of the Canadian National Railway Company and companies included in its system, which carry the guarantee of the Dominion of Canada. Such guaranteed issues are shown year by year as indirect liabilities.
