With that certificate before us, can any hon gentleman any longer argue in this House or in this country that the present government has sought in any particular to deal dishonestly with the House or with the public in separating the railway accounts from the rest of the public finances? I marvel at hon. gentlemen opposite daring to suggest such a thing. It is not patriotic. It is not honest. It is not true. Talk of deceiving the public-that is the way to deceive them. I say that it cannot again be questioned that, as regards the railway accounts, this country from the beginning of confederation down to the present time has kept the railway accounts separately with respect to guaranteed and unguaranteed amounts, and if this government were to change that method, it would only serve to bring confusion into the whole national situation by making impossible comparisons between the cost of government to-day with the cost of government in previous or succeeding years and the cost of national control of railways, a matter which is being given a fair trial at the present time.
Let me say a word in regard to this matter of the control of the National Railways and the bringing of their accounts into the government accounts. First of all, I would ask hon. gentlemen: Who was responsible for having the Grand Trunk railway system being made a charge upon this country? Who brought into being the National railway system as we have it at the present time, or rather not as we have it at the present time, because this government has organized by legislation efficiency out of the chaos left by the previous administration?
Hon. gentlemen opposite were the ones who, by act of parliament, decided that this bankrupt railway system should not be allowed, as has been done frequently in the United States, to go into liquidation, but instead should be bought at a particular price in the condition it was in and made part of the National system. It is very fine for my right hon. friend and his friends to turn round now and try to indict this government and this party for enormous expenditures which, he says should not have been added to the debt of this country, when as a matter of fact we have had no responsibility whatever in the initiation of that policy.	We have a
responsibility in the matter of carrying on the control of the railways, and I shall endeavour to show,	as	I continue to speak, how we have sought to discharge that responsibility and what we have done in that connection. It will reflect very favourably, I can assure the House, as compared with the methods of my right hon. friend during the short time he had control.
The point I wish to make here is that the National' railways were turned over to the government, and when this was done, the government had to decide upon one of two policies. I am going to submit this to the fairness of the hon. members of the House and of the country. The two policies that were possible in connection with this vast railway system were: Either to administer the system as a part of the government business of the country under the control of a minister of the crown who would be responsible for everything that was done, who would have the complete direction and control and who would have to give an accounting to the country; or to take the National railway system entirely out of the control of politics and entrust it to a president, board and a set of officers, who would be assured that they would be given a free hand and that there would be no political control at all from the government's point of view. Those are the only possible alternatives. We adopted the latter, believing that that was most in accord with public opinion, that it would give, as nothing else possible could give, a fair chance to the National railways to show whether they would pay or not. But I ask hon. members: Having done that, having parted with control, in deference to public opinion, and I might say, in accordance with the unanimous wish of this House, because there is not an hon. gentleman opposite but said that that was the policy that ought to be adopted, are we to be held responsible and the government blamed for all the expenditures, all the debts, all the difficulties that arise in connection with the
2&12	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
National Railways? If we are to have responsibility, then we must have control; but if we have not control, we cannot be held responsible at the same time for the methods or consequences of administration.
I think the country is pretty well satisfied, despite whatever my right hon. friend may say about Sir Henry Thornton or the gentlemen who surround him, that Sir Henry Thornton was the ablest executive it would have been possible to find anywhere. If the roads can be made to pay at all, they can be made to pay better under his direction and guiding genius than under the direction and guiding genius of any other person these gentlemen can name. The government will take responsibility for the appointment of Sir Henry Thornton. That was our responsibility. We took our time; we made inquiries in as many directions as possible; we moved cautiously; We considered different railway executives and when we had come to the conclusion that we had found the one man that we really believed possessed the qualities to make the National system a success, if it could be made a success, we took the responsibility of offering him the appointment. If he had failed, ours would1 have been the responsibility for the poor executive we had chosen. In the first talk I had with Sir Henry Thornton, I told him that the responsibility would be upon him and his officers for the running of the road; that there would be no interference in the nature of political control with them so far as it was possible for me or any of my colleagues to prevent it, that they would have a free hand. Sir Henry Thornton was equally frank in saying that he would not undertake the responsibility of administering a system as vast as that on any other basis.
Having parted with and given to Sir Henry Thornton that right of control, and the country having endorsed that proceeding, is it right to say that this government must bring into its public accounts to-day the whole accounts of the Canadian National system when such a course has never been adopted before at any time and when sudh a procedure would serve only to create confusion? The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) never for one minute claimed that the surplus he spoke of or the figures he gave to the House related to other than ordinary government business as is so understood. He made it perfectly clear to the House that there was to be considered by this parliament at this time the ordinary government business; that there was the railway business also to be considered

but at the appropriate time. If we understand that there can be no room for difference between us.	I agree with the
view that every dollar of public expenditure that the railways incur is an expenditure of which account should be taken in estimating the finances of the country. But there is this vast difference between the railway and the ordinary business of government. The railway is in the nature of an industrial enterprise, conducted from a financial .point of view for the purpose of profit or gain. The business of the government is not of the same character. The National railways are an industrial corporation, taken in hand by the state for a short time or for a longer period, as time may disclose, but this administration is a wholly different kind of business from the administration of the affairs of a country. I think hon. members will agree with that; I am sure the country will. This financing as done in calendar years, ours in fiscal years ending with March 31. From now on, so far as my discussion of the matter is concerned, I shall keep to the line which the Acting Minister of Finance adopted, which the officials of his department advised him to adopt, which hon. gentlemen1 opposite adopted when in office, and which will have to be followed in future if we are to avoid the sort of confusion which has been thrown into the debate to-day by the speech of the leader of the opposition wherever we fail to keep separate the ordinary business of the country from the finances of the railway system.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
before recess I was endeavouring to make clear that the government in the presentation of its financial statement to the House had no desire other than to give to the House and to the country the fullest information on the financial situation, and that we were following in our budget presentation this year and last year, the methods followed in previous years by this administration and by previous administrations. I was pointing out also that we felt it would not be in the interests of the government services, in the interests of the railways, of the public, or of parliament, to occasion confusion by changing these methods in such a way as to bring all the railway business into the discussion of the fiscal questions involved in the presentation and consideration of the budget address. I want to

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
repeat that in what I have to say to-night about the finances, answering my right hon. friend, I do not intend to take account of railway finances at all except to refer to the expenditures made during the time we have been in office as compared with those made under the administration of my right hon. friend and his party. There has been no desire, in the presentation of the financial statement, in any way to mislead or deceive the country. The government wants the country to understand that it is keeping the whole railway situation separate and distinct from the general finances. We are prepared to admit all that the committee that has been specially appointed to look into the railway situation find to be the deficit of the railways year by year after having had an opportunity of examining expert witnesses and getting all the facts. We have no desire to conceal anything. Our policy with respect to the National railways is to give government ownership a fair chance-as fair a chance as it is possible to give it in the face of the tremendous handicaps that the National system has fallen heir to through the manner in which it has come into being. In other words, this bankrupt system was taken over by our predecessors and it has to be carried on by us; I doubt very much whether government ownership is getting or can possibly get a fair trial under an inheritance of that kind. However, it is in no way the fault of this administration that the inheritance is what it is. We are responsible for taking circumstances as we find them and doing the best we can to give the railways every possible chance. That was our policy as enunciated when the government came into office; it was stated as our policy when we made our appeal to the people, and it is the policy which we intend to follow in dealing with these railway matters. We do not intend to confuse the railway situation with the other business of the country, that is to say the ordinary business of government.
As I have pointed out, the criticism of the opposition against the government has been, first of all. as to the method in which the public accounts have been presented. I think I have made it very clear that there has 'been no alteration in the method of presenting the accounts. There was the further charge, or insinuation, if it was not a charge, that the Acting Minister of Finance had presented his figures in a way that was different from the method ordinarily followed. I wish again to assert that there has been no change in that particular. The method followed by the minister, as must be apparent to anyone
who will give the matter careful study, is on all-fours with the method always followed by finance ministers in presenting their financial statements to the House. The custom is this: The Finance Minister first of all states what his total revenues are. He deals with the preceding year, then he deals with the year which he is presenting 'his estimates. In dealing with the preceding year he states what his revenues have been; then he goes into the matter of ordinary expenditure. He sets out the ordinary expenditures, then certain outlays on capital account, then outlays on special account. These are presented as a first statement, set off against the revenues. In addition, he presents another statement of indirect liabilities which are a charge upon the public debt of the country which go to maJre up the total net consolidated public debt. These figures include cash advances made by the government to railways, loans or cash to such institutions as harbour commissions, payments on account of the merchant marine-in other words, services that are not regarded as part of the ordinary services of the government, but involving advances which, nevertheless, constitute liabilities and which have to be taken into account in estimating the net consolidated public debt. Now, that is exactly what my hon. friend has done; in all particulars he has presented his statement in the usual way. Then, he has said there are in addition, the railway finances to be taken into account.
The right hon. leader of the opposition insinuated, if he did not directly charge it, that the Acting Minister of Finance, in bringing down the budget before we had entered upon the new fiscal year, had some ulterior motive in view. My right hon. friend sought to leave the impression that this should not have been done; that he was surprised at the precipitate manner in which the government had brought on the budget; and the inference thrown out was that the Acting Minister of Finance for reasons best known to himself wished to have the budget over before the figures of the year were complete. Well, I want to tell my right hon. friend that in presenting his budget the Acting Minister of Finance was careful in every particular to underestimate the revenue of the country and to overestimate the expenditure. Had he waited till the fiscal year was ended, he would have been in a position, as I am to-, night, to present a much more favourable statement to the House of Commons.
Before giving to the House the figures, let me correct the false impression my right hon. friend sought to create as to the method of
2644	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
procedure and the time at which the budget should be brought in. My right hon. friend knows very well that the [DOT] proper thing to do is, if possible, to bring the budget in and have it discussed before the old fiscal year is over and the new fiscal year to which it also relates begins. Our fiscal year for many years ended on June 30th, not on March 31st, as it does at the present time. It was in 1906 that the change was made to March 31st, and from 1890 down to 1906, with the exception of the one year, 1905, the budget was brought into this House before the expiration of the fiscal year on every occasion. Remembering that the fiscal year from 1890 to 1906 ended on June 30, the budget on one occasion during that period was brought down in January, once in February, six times in March, three times in April, three times in May, and twice in June before the month was out. After 1906 the budget was brought down before the end of the fiscal year in 1907, 1908, 1910, 1911, 1912, 1915 and in 1916. In fact, it is only of very recent years that it has been as late in coming down as we appear to have witnessed it here. In 1919 it was brought down on June 5, very late; in 1920, it was brought down on May 18, also late, the business of the country being somewhat delayed as a consequence. In 1921, 1922, and 1923 it was brought down in May. Last year it was brought down on April 10, and this year it was brought down on March 24.
The government, if anything, is entitled to credit for having endeavoured to expedite the business of the House by bringing the budget in at a much earlier stage. Indeed, if it had not been, as I pointed out this afternoon, for the manner in which debates were protracted before the budget was brought in, the government was ready a fortnight before, as I stated to the House at the time, to present the budget, and the budget making allowance for a period of nearly a month for the purpose of its budget debate, might well have been out of the way before the Easter recess and we would then have been free after the Easter recess to get along with the other important measures to be dealt with by the House.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are making inquiries from time to time as to when certain particular measures are going to be introduced. How is it possible for the government to say what it is going to be possible to do this session when we are confronted with the kind of protracted discussion that we have met with in the last two months? I will have something further to say about that before the debate concludes, but I just wish to make

plain to hon. gentlemen opposite that the government has been ready to proceed with its business expeditiously, has had its measures in readiness and has been awaiting an opportunity to get them before the House for discussion at as early a date as possible. If some measures fail of discussion the fault will not be with the government, but with the circumstances that we have been unduly hampered as all hon members know, in the manner in which I have described this afternoon.
Now let me give the figures of my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance. He presented his budget on March 24th, and today is April 30th. The fiscal year having ended on March 31st it is now possible to give with greater accuracy just exactly what the revenues and the expenditures are likely to be for the past year. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance gave as his estimate for ordinary revenue $344,000,000. Now the figures which I shall give at the present time I am assured are still an underestimate; they are still erring, so to speak, on the safe side, so that when the final statement is given, when all the revenues are in, they may be expected to run beyond the figures which I now give. The latest estimate is that the ordinary revenue will be not $344,000,000, but $344,700,000.
Now as to the expenses of the government. My hon. friend has considerably over-estimated here. He gave as an estimate for government services $342,177,000. As a matter of fact, the expenses for government services will not exceed $339,884,000.
The surplus which he estimated on government services, and I ask hon. members to note that he laid no claim to this being a surplus on the score of the net consolidated debt, it being stated that it was a surplus only on the ordinary business of the government, was $1,823,000. The latest estimate indicates that there will be a surplus on government services of revenue over expenditure of $4,816,000, or an increase above what my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance gave the House of $2,993,000.
Now of other receipts of which my hon. friend made no mention, namely, receipts by way of special revenue, a total of $725,000 has come into the treasury.
Other expenses-this is the part that goes to make up the total debt-my hon. friend estimated would total $19,527,000. In that he included the cash advances that would be made to the railways. As a matter of fact, these other expenses, instead of totalling $19,527,000 will probably not total $11,602,000; in other words, my hon. friend over-

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
estimated expenses there to the extent of $7,925,000. In statistical form the figures are as follows:

These figures disclose that the increase in the net consolidated public debt of Canada for the year 1924-25, made up as the net consolidated debt of Canada has been made up from the days of confederation down to the present time, will not exceed $2,059,000, and this in the year following the budget in which the government made the large reductions which it did in the customs tariff, removed a large proportion of the sales tax, and relieved the people of this country from a very considerable tax burden.
Now what have my hon. friends opposite to offer? They have criticized our method of financing; what have they to offer in place of it? The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) in his amendment says we ought to reduce the sales tax and other levies. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said that we ought to reduce the income tax, and he was also a member of the previous administration, a former minister of the crown. Then the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) made another statement. He said that the $700,000,0(Xbodd worth of imports into this country should never have come in, that we should have manufactured all the things represented by those imports at home. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition says that his remedy is " protection, protection, more protection; put up the tariff" and his former
Minister of Finance says that to the extent of $700,000,000 the goods that are coming in and that yield a revenue should be kept out. The government, in the opinion of my hon. friends opposite, ought to lower the sales tax, lower the income tax, and give up customs duties, and still carry on the business of this country, two-thirds of which is in the nature of uncontrollable expenditure, two-thirds of which is in the nature of money which has to be collected by the government, acting more or less as a collecting agency, to pay the interest on the public debt, to pay for pensions, to pay bondholders, to pay subsidies to the provinces, and to meet different items over which the government has no control whatever. It is easy for hon. gentlemen opposite to talk about reducing taxation all along the line, but you cannot reduce taxation all along the line in this general fashion and at the same time carry on the government of Canada. Conditions in this country are different from what they have been at any preceding period in the country's history; and sources of revenue are required without which we might possibly be able to get along were it not for the conditions resulting from the war.
Now may I come to the suggestion which the ex-Minister of Finance makes in his amendment, and which the right hon. leader of the opposition says affords common ground on which both the members of the Progressive party and his own followers can vote against the government. I will read the amendment as it has been moved:
Moved by Sir Henry Drayton, seconded by Mr. Baxter:
Conditions in Canada urgently demand reductions of taxation, especially of the sales tax and other levies which have been increased by the present government, and the House regrets that the financial statements now presented show no evidence of the economy necessary to make such reductions possible but rather disclose an alarming increase in the public debt.
An examination of thalt amendment will disclose that for the most part it is in the nature of mere generalities and platitudes, intended, as the right hon. leader of the opposition frankly admitted this afternoon, to Tarry the support of both sections of what he speaks of as the opposition, and that for the rest, it contains statements that are not only misleading but which are untrue. It refers to "an alarming increase in the public debt." Now the increase in the public debt this year, as I mentioned a moment or two ago, will not exceed between two and three million dollars. That is the alarming increase that my hon. friend speaks of, and that in the light of the fact that the government has saved to the
2646	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
country some $30,000,000 odd of taxation, as the result of the tariff changes made last year. I think I shall be able to show that in other particulars the statements set forth in this amendment do not deserve the support of hon. gentlemen, at any rate those of the Progressive party.
In the first place what do the statements as brought down show? My right hon. friend this afternoon said he would review the government's situation during the last three years. Well, I will take the last three years and I will be a little fairer than he is. I will compare our record of the last three years, not with the previous three years, but with the previous two years, and I state to the House that the record shows that with respect to financial matters there has been an improvement, first of all, on ordinary business account; in the second place, in respect to the railway accounts, and in the third place, with respect to the combined debt including all the accounts that can be possibly brought together. In all these particulars this government's record of three years of expenditure will show less in the way of expenditure, less in the way of public debt, than does the record of two years of the time when my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition was for the most part leading the government. What is the first fact in regard to ordinary business from the exact figures? The truth is that the previous administration in two years added $174,000,000 to the public debt. That is what hon. gentlemen opposite did in the two years 1920-21 and 1921-22. Hon. gentlemen will Observe that so far as the period of the war was concerned it ran from 1914 to 1918. Then there was the period of demobilization; I am allowing two years for that, 1918-19 and 191920. So that I give only the period of 192021 and 1921-22 for hon. gentlemen opposite. In those two years they added, as I have said, to the public debt of this country, taking the figures of the debt at the beginning of the period I have mentioned in comparison with them at its expiration, the sum of $174,000,000.

1923-	24, it stood at 2,417 millions; and in
1924-	25, it stood at 2,419 millions, or a net decrease in the three years since 1922 of $3,000,000. This is what the ex-Minister of Finance calls "an alarming increase in the public debt". I want again to make it clear that the government is not trying to make the claim that the net public debt of this country in the three years we have been in office has been reduced $3,000,000 taking into account the deficits of the railway. I say it has been decreased by that amount leaving out of account the railway situation which we will discuss by itself and for which we will take our responsibility. Let me say also that the above showing has been made in spite of the enormous burden that was left to us by our predecessors when we came into office. Hon. gentlemen opposite know there were many obligations entered into by them which had been left unfulfilled and which we had to meet, obligations that should never have been incurred but which we found on the doorstep when we came into office.
Then what is the position in regard to the railways? I am going to quote from the figures prepared by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). I do not think any hon. member of the House will feel that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has tried to underestimate the railway situation and the seriousness of it. I think he has estimated it accurately, as far as I have been able to check up the figures. I have gone to considerable trouble with regard to all the figures I have given to have them verified by officers of the Finance department and the statistical department of the government; and in giving the figures I am presenting to the House to-night I am speaking with the full sense of responsibility which I have in having to speak in the name of the government. Those are the
figures at which hon. gentlemen financed

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
these bonds. I have sought to have an estimate made of how much the country loses in income tax on them. As I say, we have to meet the interest charges annually, and yet hon. gentlemen who are responsible for the issue of these bonds say that the conditions of Canada demand a reduction of taxation. Let us see how much income tax is lost on these tax exempt bonds? My right hon. friend said the other day that he did not think it was possible for an estimate to be formed showing what would be lost in that way. That is not the opinion of the officers of the Finance department who are accustomed to dealing with these matters and who think they can form a reasonable estimate, and I have the following as a basis which more or less errs on the safe side. The rate of income tax on $1,000, when the total income of the individual is over $100,000, but does not exceed the next division is $630. When the total income is over $200,000, but does not exceed the next division, the tax is $714. When the total income is over $500,000, the tax is $745.50. When the total income is over $1,000,000, the tax is $766.50. If the average income of holders of tax paid bonds exceeds $100,000,-and that is regarded as a fair estimate-the loss of revenue during the calendar year, 1925, would amount to $18,487,958. This is estimated by onc-half being held by individuals, totalling $15,846,821, and one-half held by companies, totalling $2,641,137, making a total of $18,487,958. I am prepared to say that this statement may not be accurate. It is merely an estimate, but it is an estimate which financial men of experience believe to be a fair and reasonable one. It helps to show one more of the difficulties that the government faces in having to meet the financial situation when called upon to reduce taxation.
Not only did the late government finance the entire cost of the war without levying a dollar of taxation for the purpose; not only did they issue these tax exempt bonds on which there is an annual interest charge of $50,000,000 to be paid and which is costing the country in loss of income tax some $18,000,000 odd to which I have referred; but if one looks at the method of financing of hon. gentlemen opposite, he will find that the method they adopted both during and especially since the war was to issue long term loans at high rates of interest, unnecessarily long terms and unnecessarily high rates of interest. These loans cannot be called in. They fall due at a particular time and they carry till then these high rates of interest. Let me give to the House the figures with respect to some of these loans. I will not take all of them, but I will ask the House to pay particular attention 169
to the last loan of hon. gentlemen opposite in comparison with the first loan made by the present administration. I shall not discuss loans issued during the war period, interest rates on which were high; but I shall come at once to the period subsequent to the war, subsequent to demobilization, to the time when my right hon. friend was Prime Minister of this country and when the hon. member for West York the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), who has presented this amendment to the House, was handling the finances of Canada. In October, 1920, my right hon. friend's government floated a guaranteed loan of $25,000,000 running for twenty years. The rate of interest was 7 per cent and the annual interest charge is $1,750,000. This issue sold for 96.20. In December of the same year the same right hon. gentleman floated another guaranteed loan of $25,000,000. The rate in this case was also 7 per cent and the annual interest charge is $1,750,000. This loan sold for 94.05. In February, 1924, the present administration floated a thirty-year guaranteed loan of $50,000,000. This loan bears interest, not at 7 per cent, but at 5 per cent, and the annual interest charge is $2,500,000. This loan sold at 97.81. Thus the interest charges which we are at present paying and will continue to pay until 1940 on $50,000,000 issued by hon. gentlemen opposite are exactly $1,000,000 greater than the interest charges on a like amount issued in 1924 by the present government. If we admit that interest rates in the meantime have declined, the issuing of long-term bonds when the interest rate was at its peak of 7 per cent, amounts to a glaring instance of financial incapacity.

Now let me make a further comparison, because I want hon. members to see wherein it is difficult for any government to attempt to go much further in the reduction of taxes under existing circumstances.
We have to meet out of our taxation these special obligations that I have referred to as being in the nature of uncontrollable expenditure, the interest on the war debt, provincial subsidies, part of the railway deficits and the like, all of which are met out of the $294,000,000 revenue raised by taxation. We have left after we have imet this uncontrollable expenditure about $99,000,000 to carry on the regular business of the country or between $10 and $11 per bead of population. Comparing that with 'the last year of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's administration this $99,000,000 of taxation has to do the work which in 1911 required a net tax revenue of about $81,000,000. The population having increased since then, it means that to-day there is actually a lower per capita cost in dollars, in spite of a rise of some 50 per cent in commodities and service. Or take the last pre-war year of Sir Robert Borden, 1913-1914. In that, year $127,000,000 was collected. From this must be deducted provincial subsidies amounting to $11,000,000, leaving taxation for Dominion purposes of $116,000,000, as compared with $80,000,000 odd in the last year of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's administration, or an increase of more than 43 per cent in the tax burden of the Canadian people in the first three years of the Conservative administration.
Comparing Sir Robert Borden's last year with the present administration, $116,000,000 tax revenue was required in 1913-1914 to do the work which our $99,000,000 of taxation revenue does to-day, despite the increase in the cost of commodities and services.
The hon. member for West York in his amendment blames us for the addition of $13,000,000 to the public debt this year. As a matter of fact, as I have already shown, there has been an addition of only $2,000,000. Compare that with what he added. We have added $2,000,000 to the debt in 1925, and the hon. member for West York, after collecting $75,000,000 more in taxes than we did, added

in 1921, $92,000,000 more to the debt than we did; in other words there has been a total improvement in the finances in this one fiscal year, over that year of his administration of $165,000,000.
I am sorry to take up the time of the House with these figures, but I think they are necessary in order to show clearly the position of the present administration in its endeavour to deal with debt, with taxation and with matters of economy, and I submit that when one considers the handicaps under which we have laboured1 since we came into office, the economic conditions of the country and the unsettled condition of the world, and the vast obligations we have been called upon to meet, this is as good a showing as any administration under like circumstances could possibly have made.
What I have said with respect to these matters of public debt, taxation and economy in referring to the amendment of my hon. friend from West York are equally applicable to what in part my hon. friend the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) said in the amendment which he introduced into the House, but which under the rules of the House was not permitted to be moved. I hope that my hon. friend will feel, having before him at the present time figures which he had not in his possession at the time his amendment was drafted, that perhaps the government is entitled to more consideration than was given it in the form of his original draft. He referred to one other matter, which is a matter of great importance, and that is the question of the cost of living. I would like to have gone into that, but I have spoken at considerable length, and I think I will reserve for another time the remarks that I have to make in that connection. But I would like to point this out to my hon. friend and hon. gentlemen opposite, that the cost of living in Canada has been considerably reduced since the present administration took office. The cost of living has been reduced, first of all through the reduction of taxation to which I have just referred, a reduction which amounts to a difference in payment of taxes of $3 per head as against $4 per capita when we came into office.
The cost of living has also been materially affected for the better by the changes which were made in the tariff last year-the removal of the duties on implements of production to a very considerable extent, also the sales tax thereon which has had the effect of cheapening materially the cost of production in the basic industries, and as hon.﻿2655

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
members know, whatever affects materially any of the basic industries will affect all the subsequent industrial life of the country. I might add also the changes made in the tariff in the two preceding years not only on implements of production but on many articles of daily consumption, food, clothing, and the like affecting the homes of countless numbers in our land.
The cost of living has also been affected by the reductions we have made in the income tax by means of increased exemptions in the case of families, first of all in our raising the exemption to $300 per child and then later increasing that amount to $500. thus making a considerable saving to a large number of families.
In addition to that, the sales tax besides being removed from the implements of production as,mentioned, has been completely taken off a large number of commodities, commodities that enter into the daily needs of a large number of families. We have sacrificed a considerable amount of income in that regard. True, we found a certain rate of sales tax. We added to that for a time, and reduced it in part again, but we also made perfectly free large numbers of articles that enter into the ordinary consumption of the great body of the people.
In addition to that we removed the duties from the coverings usedi exclusively for covering goods not subject ito sales tax, these include cheese boxes, butter boxes, fruit .packages and the like and constitute a very material reduction which also has its effect upon the cost of living. We also have given a 10 per cent discount upon preference rates where goods come into Canada via Canadian ports.
I would further submit that the great development that has taken .place in trade under the present administration has had the effect [DOT]of giving the average citizen more in the way of purchasing power and a man's cost of living has to be estimated, as it were, in terms of two quantities, the price of the things he buys, and the money he has to purchase them with, and if trade is more extensive as it certainly is, I submit that the lot of the average man in this country through increase of purchasing power has to that extent improved.
I would like to give just one brief summary in respect to the cost of living which has been carefully .prepared by the aid of statisticians in the government service, and which will help to indicate what has taken place. In September, 1921-which I will compare with September, 1924 as well as March. 1925, so that it will not be thought that I am choosing particular months, and I take September, 1921, because it was the time my right hon. friend was getting ready to make his appeal to the country-in September, 1921, the cost of living as based upon a family budget of foods, fuel, lighting and rent, was 159.3 per cent of what it was in 1913. In September, 1924, the index number had fallen to 147.2, and in March of 1925 it was 148.4, or a decline of about 11 points since September 1921. Foods, which had been at 161.1 in September of 1921, were 140.4 in September, 1924 and 142.6 in March, 1925. All the foods in the budget except mutton, rice, tea and coffee were lower in September, 1924 than in September, 1921.
Again, the retail index number of fuel and lighting, which includes coal, wood and coal oil, was 189.0 in September, 1921, 175.9 in September, 1924 and 175.4 in March, 1925. While rent shows little change since 1921, the retail price of clothing has fallen from 167 in September of 1921 to 155 in March, 1925.
These index numbers, however, do not tell the whole story. They do not include some of the most notable of the achievements of the present government in the reduction of taxation. Thus, for example, they dlo not include reductions in the rate of income tax. Yet, to take a very ordinary case, the married man with an average family of three children .and an income of $3,500 a year, who in 1921 paid $36 in income tax to the government of that day, is to-day entirely exempt therefrom.

Now, Mr. Speaker, it had been my intention to-night not to debate the question of finance but to discuss the question of the tariff. I thought that this debate would be largely concerned with matters of fiscal policy, but as
