the right hon. leader of the opposition has not discussed those matters, has run away from all tariff discussion, I shall defer until some other time what I had intended to say in that regard.
There is one point however, which I wish to make perfectly clear to hon. members of the House because it has been one that has been differently viewed in the course of this debate, and that is with respect to the reference contained in the speech of the Acting Minister of Finance to the intention of the government to have an advisory board to advise the Minister of Finance on taxation whether in the form of customs duties, or excise duties, income tax or in other forms. Hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party advocate a tariff commission. They purpose to appoint independently certain gentlemen who will be given power to make examinations on their own account and make recommendations to the government. Should the government in power be that of my right hon. friend if that government were to act in accordance with the terms of his manifesto, it would not be obliged to carry out those recommendations; the commission may make recommendations but that is all there is to it in that regard. The proposal for such a body takes away from parliament altogether the settlement of the fiscal policy. Now, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is utterly impossible to remove from the arena of the House of Commons the settlement of the fiscal policy of the country. Parliament necessarily concerns itself amongst other things with the business of taxation and from time immemorial has exercised the right of imposing taxation. That right should never be handed over to any tribunal of men, no matter whom they may be, but should always be in the hands of the representatives of the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about appointing a commission representative of manufacturers, of labour, and of some other class. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that in this House of Commons we have representatives of manufactures, we have representatives of labour, we have representatives of agriculture, we have representatives of all the classes that go to make up this country, and this is the place where the voice of the people thus represented should be heard. What the government feels is this: That in order to discuss intelligently these matters of the tariff, these complicated questions of taxation-and in view of the conditions in which this country and the rest of the world finds itself to-day, there is greater need than there ever was of expert advice and guidance,-that the Minister of Finance should have attached to his 
department experts, men of great experience, who will command the confidence of labour, of the manufacturers, of the farmer, who will be so trained that they will be able to go through the various tariff schedules and indicate the effect of existing tariffs upon industry and upon revenue, indicate what the effect of certain changes will be upon industry and upon revenue, so that when the Minister of Finance comes to the government or comes to the House with his budget he will be in a position to give the fullest and most accurate information it is possible to have with respect to the basis upon which taxation is made.
My hon. friend the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) thinks the tariff should be revised so as to bring in a larger amount of revenue. As to that I am in entire accord with him. We believe that the tariff should be used for purposes of revenue; it should not be used as my hon. friends opposite contend for purposes primarily of protection. The two things are entirely different; the two objectives are different. We join issue with hon. gentlemen opposite on this. They say we want a tariff for protection. Protection of what? Certain special industries. Then they go on enlarging, and enlarging, and enlarging, until what is the result? They want to include all the industries, and then after they are all included the costs all round will be raised by a corresponding amount. What they really want is the protection of certain special interests for the benefit of those whose capital has been invested in them. They say they want protection in the interest of labour. How is labour going to gain? Will not the wages of labour continue to be settled as they are to-day through competition in the labour market? Is there any guarantee that if two, or three, or four manufactures get special protection while capital may secure its extra monopoly profits the labour in those industries will be paid any wage other than that which competition of those available for these particular industries, may determine? Talk about protection! What about the women of this country who are not engaged in the specially favoured industries, who are nevertheless the heads of families and that to-day have to provide for needs of the household? Do they not need protection? Do not they and all other women need some protection with respect to the commodities they have to buy? What about all the younger element of the country? What about those who are in the civil service of Canada? What about those in the learned professions, what about those who go to make up the great numbers performing the clerical work of the country? What

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
about all these classes? Are they not to be considered? Are you going to limit the protection to special interests in which some specially favoured happen to have capital invested on which they want to make a higher rate of profit? Our position is that if you are going to have protection then protect the people as a whole and not merely a favoured few. Have your tariff so arranged that it will help to bring in revenues to the country in a manner which will relieve taxation not add to it and thereby serve the best interests of the people at large.
That is the intention with respect to this tariff board to which I have referred. There are in the government service at the present time gentlemen who have very full and accurate statistical knowledge; some with regard to trade, some with regard to customs, some with regard to income tax and the like. That information ought to be made available to the government and to the particular member of the cabinet on whom it devolves to bring down the budget to this House. We propose by this means to get such information as we can obtain; but we propose also to supplement the clerical staff that may be used for this purpose with two or three expert advisers who will give all of their time-not part of their time, as these other gentlemen will be expected to give-to studying taxation problems, tariff schedules, schedule after schedule and the like; studying the effect, as I have said, of the existing or a proposed tariff on a particular industry, and the effect of the tariff upon revenue; the effect of depreciated and appreciated currencies and kindred topics. They will not be appointed for an indefinite time but they will be appointed for a year at a time, and the appropriation will be made by this parliament. The minister will be responsible for those whom he appoints. What we will seek to bring into our tariff discussion will be more light and less heat so that in discussing these matters we shall be able to do only what is most in the interest of the people as a whole.
Now may I conclude what I have to say by making a reference to the subject of trade. But just before I d'o, let me make this reference in case I should overlook it. It has been intimated to me by some hon. members that they would like me to state what the government is going to do with certain measures that have still to be brought forward. On that point may I say this: The government brought on this session, as I have already intimated, early in the month of February, the first week of February in fact, in the hope that we would get through business at least before the hot
weather came. We brought on the session when we did believing that it was in the interest of the country to have the public business put through with despatch. We believe the people do not want the public money wasted in lengthy discussions involving prolonged sittings of this parliament. As I intimated in the early part of my remarks this afternoon we believe there has been and is a deliberate attempt to protract the session, and in view of that fact it would be impossible as I stand here to give any assurances as to what measures can be brought down and put through at this particular session of parliament. We have some very important legislation still to introduce. There is the railway rates legislation, which is important, and which we ought to have been discussing a month ago. There is the legislation respecting the Home Bank depositors which is important. Hon. gentlemen opposite have asked me two or three times about the alternative vote. I promised last session that it would be brought down, and it will be brought down and we will proceed with it. These are measures which will take considerable time. The Grain Act has been drafted. The minister made mention earlier in the session of his intention to bring down that measure and I hope we will be able to put it through. As to some of the other measures, rural credits and the like, I am unable to speak definitely until I see how the work of the session progresses: but I want to say this, and I want to make it perfectly clear: This government does not intend to stay here through the summer months trying to carry on the business of the country'; and if for no other reason than that hon. gentlemen opposite wish us to go in two opposite directions at one and tlhe same time, or because hon. gentlemen directly opposite want to prevent by undue discussion a campaign from being brought on, I will say here and now that if for these or any other reasons the government finds it impossible to carry on the business of the country in an expeditious and in a satisfactory manner, I shall not for one minute hesitate to ask His Excellency to dissolve this parliament and give us a chance to appeal to the people. So far as the business of this country is concerned, I believe that the people of Canada have the same view that the people of Great, Britain and the people of the United States apparently have had; they want to see in power a government that will not be faced with uncertainty in its proceedings, and that will not be faced with embarrassment because it is surrounded by groups at variance with each other; they

The Budget-Mr. Mackenzie King
want to see in power a government with a strong majority that will be able to carry on the business of the country without fear and without favour in any direction, and I can tell hon. gentlemen opposite that when the time-comes to appeal to the country, it is on these lines the appeal will be made.
I have given an outline of the manner in Which the government has endeavoured to carry on the business of the country. I have shown that, despite the obstacles we have had to contend with, the heavy legacy of public debt and other financial obligations, our majority of one, the unsettled conditions throughout the country and the world, a divided opposition, a Senate which is politically hostile to us, and embarrassments of different kinds, we have been able to make a record of which any administration might well be proud. Not only that, but I have only to give to the country the figures that I hold in my hand with respect to trade development to show how Canada has prospered during the period the present government has been in office. I shall quote these figures, and with that I shall conclude. What are the figures with respect to the trade conditions of the country?
In the fiscal year 1920-21, when hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, the trade imports exceeded the exports $30,000,000. The result was that in November, 1920, $1 of American money required an exchange of $1.20 in Canadian money. In 1921-22, for nine months of which my hon, friends were in office, the exports exceeded the imports by $6,000,000. The result was that in November 1921 one American dollar was worth $1.09 Canadian money. In January, 1922, immediately after the change of government the American dollar commanded only $1.05^ in Canadian money. In 1922-23 the exports of Canada exceeded the imports by $142,000,000. In 192324 the exports exceeded the imports by $165,000,000, and now the 30th April has come and I am able to give the House the exact figures with respect to the last fiscal year. We find the exports last year have exceeded the imports by $284,000,000, the largest favourable balance of trade that had ever been known in this country, with the possible exception of the period of the war.
Again I wish to say to hon. gentlemen opposite,-and here I speak more particularly to my friends of the Progressive party-the government has been able to accomplish this in no inconsiderable part through the cooperation which has been accorded us by hon. gentlemen belonging to the Progressive party, and in spite of the difficulties which have been put in our way by hon. gentlemen directly

opposite. We have endeavoured while seeking to carry on the economic side of the work of this country also to do another work which is perhaps even more important. We have sought to remove, as far as we were able to do it, all that there was of discord and division among the people on racial, religious or sectional grounds in different parts of the country. We have worked steadily for national unity, and hon. gentlemen have helped' us in that. Last year we made considerable changes in the tariff which I think I am right in saying benefited more than any other part of the Dominion the part of the country from which the majority of hon. members of the Progressive party come. In doing that we were not only helping hon. gentlemen opposite, but we were helping all parts of Canada. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House stood solidly with the government in helping to bring about changes which we believed were for the good of western Canada, and whilst improving conditions from an economic standpoint would help to make for the furtherance of a spirit of national unity throughout the Dominion.
This year, as far as the tariff goes, we have thought it advisable to permit an unobstructed view of the effect of our changes of last year, so that the country will have an opportunity of seeing that they need not be alarmed with respect to tariff changes, with respect to the reduction of duties on agricultural implements or other commodities, where made after mature consideration, and in accordance with a policy that goes to make for the welfare of the country as a whole. We believe that the country is being steadily reassured, and it is for that reason among others that we have thought it inadvisable to make any change of a material character. One change we have made, continuing our policy of last year, a change designed to benefit some of the fishermen of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts engaged in a basic industry which did not come in for as full consideration as others at the last session. We have beside 'lowered the duty on bituminous coal three cents a ton. Not much has been said of that, but it gives some benefit to the consumer. The household consumers of coal use bituminous coal, they do not use slack. We have raised the duty on bituminous slack coal, and why? Well, for two or three reasons. In the first place at the time the duties were fixed it was never thought that bituminous slack coal would begin to enter into effective competition with run of mine bituminous coal, which is a product of the mines not only in the Maritime province but in Alberts well. The gov-

The Budget-Mr. Warner
eminent of the day did not- believe it would result in the customs being defrauded and in purchasers being defrauded, as has certainly been the case, because we know on account of the difference in the tariff, slack coal is being brought into this country, paying a lower rate of duty, than mixed with run of mine and sold as run of mine, with the result that the purchaser is defrauded in what he pays for and the government defrauded in duties as well. We have felt further that there is one part of our Dominion which to-day has been having a hard struggle; no one can deny that. The Maritime provinces have had and are having a hardl time. We were not without hope that our action in this particular would put new faith and comfort into the hearts and minds of the people of the Maritime provinces and for no class more than those who are engaged in the hard work of mining coal in connection with the primary industries of that part of our country. We felt this was helping on as well a great national policy of self-sufficiency in the matter of our coal supplies in this country. Those were great national reasons transcending, I believe, all other reasons. I ask my friends of the Progressive party: Are you not going to be magnanimous enough to sink any little feeling you may entertain with respect to some theoretical maximum on tariffs and stretch to our friendh in the Maritime provinces the same helping hand they stretched out to you in good faith and good fellowship last session? You have an opportunity to do so on this budget. You have an opportunity by your action on this budget to show that in your outlook you are something more than sectional; that you have a broad vision; that you are thinking first of Canada as a whole, not only of the particular constituency from which you may come. Nay, rather, may I say this in justice to your constituencies? I should feel pretty badly if I thought that any group of men and women in western Canada in the constituencies from which you come would not respond to attitude of that kind and would not rather condemn you if you failed to assume it. You have your chance on this budget and it is for you to say. I again appeal to my lion, friends. It has been from this larger point of view, from the point of view of national interest as a whole,, national economy, national well-being and national goodwill, that the government has taken the stand that it has on the tariff question at this particular session.
Let me conclude with these words. In the short time that we have been in office now
some three years or more, we have reduced the public debt. We have reduced expenditure. We have reduced the taxation of this country. We have reduced' the cost of the public service. We have reduced the cost of living. More than that, we are able to point to a vast increase in the trade of the country, reflecting improved conditions of industry, to an improvement in our credit enabling us to borrow in the worlds money markets at business rates of interest. Not only has our money been at par for some time past but if you will look at this evening's paper, you will see what I had the pleasure of reading to-night in large letters across the centre page:	"Canadian dollar quoted at a
premium." Above all this we have achieved a growing national unity. Having regard to these and other circumstances, I think the government is entitled to ask from all or at least hon. gentlemen who have promised honourable co-operation in the government's efforts to serve the country's interest a ready measure of support of the budget now before the House.

subtopic: COMPARISON OF FINANCE, FISCAL YEARS 1924-25 AND 1920-21
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tariff has been emphasized more than any other phase of this debate, and so I will offer a few remarks on that first. The tariff is important, but at the same time we realize that some other subjects are also important although, perhaps, not very much has been said about them during the course of the debate. As regards the emphasis placed on the tariff, it appears to me that to my immediate right the emphasis has taken the position almost of preaching blue ruin on account of small reductions that have been made in the tariff. The people who sent me here want a lower tariff than we have at present, and I think they are quite reasonable in not expecting that reduction to be brought about all at once. At the same time they want progress made all along that line. Our friends to the right have been all the time using the United States as an example for Canada to follow. I know something about conditions there from experience and in other ways as well. The idea is held out that the prosperity in the United States has been brought about by the highly protective tariff which they have had continuously. My opinion is that the United States have become prosperous in spite of the tariff rather than on account of it. I lived there long enough to form that conclusion from experience. The statement has been made that the United States have three times as high a tariff as Canada has. It makes a difference how you undertake to figure that tariff. I
The Budget-Mr. Warner

want to read just a little from a clipping taken from the Ottawa Citizen and I think it is a pretty good authority under the circumstances under which it was taken:
Early in the session, Mr. Stevens, of Vancouver, spoke of the United States "with a four thousand mile boundary and a tariff three times as high as ours." This information was given as an argument for the increase of the Canadian tariff to equal that of the United States, accompanied by the understanding that conditions in the United States due to higher tariff were more satisfactory than in Canada.
A little further on in the same editorial, we have this:
For his benefit, as well as for the information of students of tariff affairs generally, the following comparisons may be quoted from Imperial sources. For the year 1924 the per capita rate of duty in Canada was $14.65 and in the United States $4.86.
I think that is a fair way of looking at the tariff; we must consider it from the per capita point of view. These calculations have been carefully checked on the data furnished by the above-mentioned reports. As a matter of fact, if the year 1921 is taken, the comparison shows in all three of the above that the Canadian rate is higher than in the United States.
Our friends to the right in stressing the tariff have gone beyond what they ought reasonably to expect, and I wonder if they really want the sort of tariff that they are talking about. I was a candidate in 1917 as well as in 1921 for election to this House and in both those campaigns the Conservatives apologised for the high tariff which they had had in that part of the country where I was running; and some of them went so far as to declare that a reduction was necessary. And the only way they could justify the tariff then in force was to say that it was no higher than the tariff that had been in effect at any other time under the Liberals. I will not discuss that point as it has no bearing on the present question. However, hon. gentlemen have emphasized in this House their claim that the reduction of the tariff will mean the ruin of this country. Just what their object is would not seem to be quite clear, but it strikes me that they have been making a desperate effort to prevent this government from reducing the tariff to a greater extent than they have done. What effect this move on the part of hon. gentlemen will have on their supporters back home I do not know, but that is what they have evidently been doing. As I see it, there would appear to be in the minds of hon. gentlemen some idea of party advantage in stalling the government in their endeavour to reduce the tariff, and then turning round and telling the people throughout 	i
the country that the government had not carried out their pledges.
Now, the Progressives want a lower tariff and perhaps most of them will vote against the budget on that account. I can see that this will place the government in a very undesirable position; I can quite readily understand that. But whether hon. gentlemen vote against the government because they want a lower tariff, or whether they vote against the government because they are anxious to stall them for the purpose of conveying to the country the impression that this administration have failed to fulfil their pledges, the vote in either case will be an adverse one. It does seem to me
10 p.m. that we could put in our time to better advantage than by talking for the purpose of furthering party interests; I think the country is in too serious a condition for us to carry on a debate for four or five weeks merely for party purposes.
I shall say just a few words now about the tariff commission. Parliament cannot dodge its responsibility for dealing with the matters which members are sent here to consider. I do not want to be put in the position of opposing a tariff commission, but I should like to know just what is intended in this connection. I think we have some assurance from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and from the government benches that this tariff board is not to decide what shall be done in the way of changing the tariff; its purpose is merely to gather information. If the board is to obtain information and come to a decision as to how industries in the country will be affected by tariff changes, either up or down, and if its function is to be simply advisory, then it would seem to be a good thing to have such a body to advise parliament. Ever since I can remember, the tariff has been a political football in the United States and this country, and I do not think that it is the best thing for any country to allow its fiscal policy to be treated in that way. I believe that the people are entitled to full information in regard to tariff matters; they should know what their tariff is and how its changes would affect them. But under the conditions that have existed in this country, how are the people to know just what the exact state of affairs is? This tariff question is largely comparable to religion; a man may hold any religious belief he pleases; he can prove that his opinions are right in bis own opinion by the Bible; he can take the Bible to prove any position he chooses to assume. Similarly, a man can belong to any party at

The Budget-Mr. Warner
all and support any kind of tariff policy he wants to, with the party information and the party statistics with which he is supplied. But I do not believe that it is to the advantage of the country to have the tariff handled in that way; and if we had a board that would provide the proper information which we could depend upon I think it would be a good thing; we should then be able to arrive at conclusions a great deal more satisfactorily than we can without such a board or some similar body to supply us with information.
Now I come to another subject which I wish to discuss to some extent; I refer to the question of raising revenue in this country. The revenue-earning power of the tariff would appear to me to be rather doubtful; and we never know how much we get out of it nor how much it costs us for what we get. Let me for a moment or two refer to the question of direct taxation. The organization that has sent me here to serve as their representative believe in direct taxation. I do not want to be understood as opposing the idea of direct taxation, but I want that direct taxation to be fair, if it can be made so; and that is the idea I want to emphasize in my remarks on this subject. If direct taxation is fair and we know how much we have to pay in connection with it, then we are ready for direct taxation instead of this conundrum, the tariff, as a method of raising money.
I wish to refer for a moment to the question of milk and cream tickets. I have here a letter from a gentleman who is secretary of the National Dairy Council and who is counsel for that organization, and I would like to put it on Hansard. It is as follows:
In answer to your request for information I beg to say that, acting as counsel of the National Dairy Council, I secured a ruling last year from the Department of Customs and Excise, to the effect that a cream ticket which was not addressed to a bank was not a cheque and was not subject to the law requiring a stamp upon cheques. However, the department decided that a cream ticket was a receipt and that therefore, if the cream ticket amounted to $10 or more, the law requiring a two cent stamp on a receipt of $10 or more applied, and a two cent stamp had to be put upon the cream ticket. Acting as counsel for the dairy interests, I advised to this effect.
The practice of paying for each can of cream by issuing a cream ticket, which is followed by the creamerymen in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, is not followed in Ontario and Quebec. In these two provinces the dairy farmer is paid every two weeks by a cheque or express order. This used to be the practice also in the prairie provinces, but some time ago it was changed to the cash system, which has been found most beneficial to the western farmer and the merchants in the western towns. These cream tickets which may be sent by mail to a farmer a hundred miles away from the creamery are treated as cash by the merchants and the banks and therefore have
been of material assistance in times of stress, by keeping money in circulation.
Another practice that exists in the prairie provinces, which is not generally followed in Ontario and Quebec, is the paying of cream on grade. There are three principal grades, being special, first and second. The farmer who ships special, gets a better price than is paid for first grade, and the farmer who ships first grade gets a better price than is paid for second grade. The result is that cream is shipped frequently and in comparatively small volume. This practice results in a better quality of butter being made and it has been encouraged by the cash system of payments through cream tickets.
From my knowledge of the dairy industry, I am satisfied that the system of cash payments through cream tickets is a decided improvement on the system of half monthly payments and therefore I sincerely hope that nothing will be done to prejudice the system now existing in the west.
I have read this letter in order to show how this system grew up. It is the opinion of creamery men that under this system a better grade of butter is produced than can be produced under the system that was formerly followed. I take it that the secretary of this organization, which acts for all the dairymen of Canada, is a good authority on this subject. We want the dairy business to grow. This government have been doing all that one could expect any government to do to encourage the dairy business, but if they impose this extra burden upon it the result will be very detrimental to those who are engaged in it. I have here a wire from the Alberta Dairymen's Association, through their secretary, representing all the creamerv men and dairymen in Alberta; I have also a letter from him. I shall not read either the wire or the letter, but they would be good reading and contain information that it would be well to have on Hansard. I have also a letter and a wire from the chairman of the producing section of the Alberta Dairymen's Association, who speaks for all the producers in that province. It is the view of all these men that the business cannot stand the extra burden that it is proposed to place upon it in the form of this tax. I have also communications from private creameries- from the Edmonton City dairy, the Woodland dairy, the Wetaskiwin dairy and the Camrose dairy. I have a statement by the manager of the Wetaskiwin dairy that I would like to put on Hansard; I judge that he is a pretty good authority on this subject and that the figures he gives may be taken as approximate. Speaking to the Kiwanis Club of Wetaskiwin, he said:,
In 1919 about 13,000,000 pounds of butter were made in Alberta, while in 1924 this figure was increased to 22,000,000 .... In 1922 the Dairymen's Act of Alberta was passed, making the grading of cream compulsory. Saskatchewan and Manitoba have followed Alberta's
The Budget-Mr. Warner

example in this respect, and to-day the butter from the prairie provinces has a place on the world's markets second to none.
That is what we are aiming at; we want to turn out the best product that can possibly be manufactured, and the ticket system helps to bring that about. It can only injure the industry if these tickets are regarded as cheques instead of receipts and are all required to have a two cent stamp. I said at the outset that I was in favour of direct taxation if it was fair, and I believe the stamp tax, properly applied, is a fair tax. But a different situation is created if, in accordance with the minister's proposed amendment, these tickets are treated as cheques instead of receipts. We have men delivering small amounts of cream to those dairies every day for which they would receive one or two dollars, so you can see at once that if you put a 2-cent stamp on five of these cheques there will be a tax of 10 cents to pay on amounts as low as ten dollars. That is surely an unfair amount of taxation to place on that business. On the ordinary ten dollar receipt a man has only to pay a two-cent tax, whereas the man taking his cream to the dairy will pay the very same tax on an account of one or two dollars.
Now I come to the cheques. Suppose they issue cheques. Very few of these accounts are over ten dollars, and most of them are below that. On an ordinary business cheque for fifty dollars you only have to pay a two cent tax, but you might have to pay fifty cents if you were in the dairy business and took fifty dollars worth of cream to the dairy. There is no other business this tax strikes so hard, on account of the budget calling these receipts cheques and requiring them to be stamped the same as the ordinary cheque. If these accounts were paid in bigger cheques it would not be so bad, but hardly any of these accounts reaches ten dollars. The dairymen all say that they are willing to put on a two-cent stamp if the account goes over ten dollars, but you can see what a handicap the tax will be to the business if a two-cent stamp is required on every ticket, however small, and I want to tell the government that I do not believe they are going to get the revenue they expect from these tickets, because the dairymen will be compelled to go back most likely to payment every two weeks or once a month
I have here a number of letters that I shall not put on Hansard as time is passing, but they all go to show that the dairy business cannot stand this tax, and they will have to adopt some other method. The government

are going to get these creamery men into a lot of difficulty. They will simply have to avoid this stamp tax in some way because they cannot afford to pay it, and it means they will have to change their system. The government in that case will not get the revenue, but they will fall into discredit with a whole lot of farmers who want the cash system that is now in operation continued. The creamery-men cannot undertake to give cash to each man who brings in his cream. That is out of the question, because not one man in twenty takes his own cream in to the creamery; he gets someone else to haul it in for him, and some of it is shipped a hundred miles. These cream tickets are as good as money to the farmer because the merchants or anybody
will	take	them in as	cash	knowingthat	the	creamery men	will	make itgood;	so	it is really a	cash	system.
But you cannot take money out of the bank and pay actual cash to the producer who sends in his cream to the creamery, because he does not go to the creamery himself. We do not want a handicap ito be placed on this industry from a lack of knowledge of what this tax will mean, and that is one reason why I am taking time to explain the system to the House to-night. These gentlemen who are in the business certainly know what they are talking about, and they know another thing, that they will not be to blame if they have to go back to the two weeks or monthly payment system, and that will be a step backward. The cream will have to be kept too long so it will not make good butter. The man who is getting these cash payments in the west certainly needs these certificates every day in order to carry on his household expenses and support his family. Now why do we need to put a two-cent stamp on this dairy certificate? What is the reason we have to do it? It has not been made clear to me yet, but what has been made clear to me on investigation is that there are already some exemptions allowed. For instance, when a man clips a coupon from a bond and deposits it in the bank he does not have to put a stamp on that. I am not going to say that that is not wise provided we can afford it, but I do say that it is not fair to exempt the coupon clipper and to tax the dairyman, upon whom you are depending to build up this country in every part of it. There are other exemptions I might mention. One dollar will pay the maximum amount of revenue that you have to put on any cheque,, even if it amounts to $100,000. All amounts over $2,500 are exempt

The Budget-Mr. Warner
Now, Mr. Speaker, and gentlemen, hon. members of this House, when you allow those exemptions is it fair to tax the small man who is producing a little cream to take care of his family through the summer season, and many of them are now depending upon it for the winter as well? If you want to be fair, if you are going to tax the cream ticket, I say tax the man that puts a bond coupon in the bank, and put a tax of two cents on every fifty dollars when a cheque is drawn no matter for how large an amount;
I do not care if it is a cheque for $100,000. A man who can afford to write a cheque for that amount can better afford to pay the tax than the small dairyman.
You might say that the creamery men should stand this tax. But it is like any other business, there is a certain amount of overhead, and this tax will be charged in their overhead, and the small producer will have to pay it. It will not be the consumer who will pay it in this case, because the world's market makes the price for butter, and the rest of the butter at home will sell at the price butter will bring in the world's market, less the cost of transportation there, so the tax will come back to the small man. It may not break the dairy business, but it will be a handicap on the business, and I claim that it is an unjust tax. If there were other businesses that were exposed to so much expense and had so many small accounts to pay then perhaps there would not be so much objection. The dairy business is growing, and I have a number of statistics here that will indicate the growth. Our butter is being regarded with more favour on the world's market. In the British market, in Japan and in other parts of the Orient, and in a general way all over the world, our butter is establishing a reputation for itself. With the new system now in vogue, in view of the system of cash payments and the small amounts of cream going into the dairy while it is sweet, our dairymen are able to compete with the dairy products of any other country in the world's market. The fact that our butter is getting such a good name for itself is a strong factor in enabling our. product to compete with the butter from other countries and secure a top price. We have not yet exported in any great volume, although it is increasing satisfactorily and we hope that given proper treatment the business in future will enormously increase. Before I leave this subject I must say that this development in the dairy industry has been brought about as the result
of information furnished by the Department of Customs by their classing milk , tickets as receipts, it has not been brought about through	any violation of the	law.	To-daythe industry is not asking for any special favour;	all it is asking	for is	even	handedjustice and a fair deal.	That	is all	we are
asking for and we think that as dairymen we are entitled to it.
Now,	Mr. Speaker, I	have	several notes
here dealing with matters on which I wished to speak, but the time is going faster than I realized and I cannot take them all up. But I do want to mention the subject of rural credits,	I have not heard much on that
question this session. Nevertheless throughout the country the people are looking for something along that line to be done at this session of parliament. Reports on the subject were presented in 1924 and 1925, by a commissioner employed by the government to investigate the feasibility and the possibility of a rural credit system. I claim that in those reports we have information enough to enable us to make a start on that line. This subject was investigated by a special committee appointed to consider agricultural conditions in Canada, and Dr. Tory, the commissioner in question, states in his report that he has followed very closely the suggestions offered by the committee on Agriculture based on the evidence that the special committee took. We also have his statement that he has followed very closely the recommendations of the committee on Banking and Commerce. In the second report on agricultural credits made last year to the Minister of Finance, and printed as sessional paper No. 142 there is a resolution passed by the Banking and Commerce committee. I quote from the report:
This resolution was concurred in by the House of Commons on Friday, July 18, 1924. Subsequent to this action instructions were received from the Acting Minister of Finance to complete the investigation suggested by the resolution of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce referred to above.
Now, there are many quotations that I should like to put on Hansard if I felt that I had the time, but in view of the lateness of the hour, and the fact that a number of other gentlemen wish to speak, I shall read only a further quotation or two from Dr. Tory's report:
In Canada we have invested in lands under occupation approximately $2,250,000,000, upon which there is live stock valued at about $1,000,000,000. In addition, the average crop production for the five years ending 1923 was $1,230,000,000. It is respectfully suggested that the time has come for the creation of financial organizations which will think in the terms of this industry, aiming specifically and definitely and without excuse
The Budget-Mr. Warner

The Budget-Mr. Warner

the government was imposing such a low tariff it was going to ruin the whole country on account of the 22 per cent of Progressive members who were dictating to the government. I do not think any party in this House have come as near to having their way as the Conservatives have. They are trying to prevent the government from giving a lower tariff, and have succeeded. The people throughout Canada want a lower tariff; they have sent a large majority of members here who are in favour of a lower tariff if they represent their constituents as they should. Hon. members to my right have prevented the govern-meat from going further with their lower tariff policy. As the saying goes, the government are between the devil and the deep sea. At the same time it has been the Conservatives with a few Tory-Liberals added who have preached the ruination of this country on account of a very little bit having been cut off the tariff at last session. If they wanted a higher tariff, why did they not have it when they were in power and could get it? They did not have a very much higher tariff than the Liberal party, and they made the claim in 1917 and 1921 that they would be just as low tariff people as the Liberals if they had a chance. We are not, as I say, taking a hand in the political fight. We do not feel that we came here to carry on any political fight. Our people have told us over and over again that we are here to represent them, we are here to support the government when they are doing what we can afford to support, to help to carry on the business of the country in a proper way and to oppose measures which are not in the interest of those whom we represent. We are not sent here to build up any party machine nor to strengthen any party machine that is already built up. If this debate has lasted longer than it should have, I believe the country will understand that that is due to the political propaganda that has been carried on.
The soldier settlers in our country are appealing to members of parliament in some way to take enough off their indebtedness that they may be able to make good and hold their farms. I am in favour of immigration to our country, but I want to see the right kind of people coming here and I do not want to see money wasted in bringing in the wrong kind of people. We have a great big country that needs many more people in order that we may carry it on economically and profitably. We have in Canada these 
soldier settlers, a class of settlers that we cannot afford to ignore, and we should give them an opportunity to make good. They have already suffered loss, and if their equipment and stock have shrunk in value until they will not return the money paid for them, you cannot expect the soldier settlers to carry on under those conditions, because most of them had1 no capital outside of that furnished to them by the government. They are, therefore, up against an impossibility, and if necessary I would be in favour, instead of spending all our money to bring other settlers into this country, of spending some of it in helping the soldier settlers that we already have here- sufficient at least to enable them to make good. These men have done their very best; and if in some cases they have not come up to the standard! that we might expect of them, that is no reason why we should treat shabbily those who have exerted their best efforts. I do not think we can afford to close this session of parliament without doing something to reduce the indebtedness of these men, whose position at the present time is simply impossible.
I have just one word to say with regard to the Hudlson Bay railway; I certainly think that undertaking shodld foe carried through to completion. The people in my part of the country 'are more interested in this matter than they realize. They have not been pushing very strenuously for it because they have had their eyes to the west; they have been looking to western shipping. But I think that this Hudson bay proposition is cf more importance to them than they realize just novr, and in order to save the investment we have already sunk in it we should go ahead and finish the road I think we have sufficient information on which to take action.
I have said little about ths tariff inasmuch as I felt that these other problems were more important, but I would make just a brief comparison between the United States and Canada. Notwithstanding the great difficulties we have to put up with in Canada, it is my opinion that none of (hem is great enough to render this country unprofitable for any immigrant who wants to come out to this part of the world and establish a home where he can live comfortably on a farm. In my opinion, such an immigrant would find it more profitable to come to Canada than to go to the United States. I am not saying this as a guess ; after the experience of a lifetime in the two countries I have come to this conclusion. I do not suggest that this would be true unless we did our part; we must do our best to

The Budget-Mr. Jones
lighten the burden of taxation in every possible way. I can see that the government has so much in the way of fixed charges to contend with that it is a difficult problem for us to reduce taxation in Canada. But at the same time we must do everything we can to relieve the people of this burden to as great an extent as possible, and we must help our people to produce by lowering the cost of production. This is imperative if Canada is to be made a prosperous country. This is not a country in which money can be picked up along the roadi; you have to work for it. But when this is said, I think that people have in Canada a chance which is greater than can be found anywhere else in the world. That is my opinion, although I do not forget that difficulties do exist. But the more we can and do help ourselves, the more the government can push forward production by assisting the people in the way of reduced taxation and reduced cost of the implements of production. I must apologize for the time I have taken up, but I feel that the subjects I have touched upon call for some consideration, and I shall leave these few remarks with the House.

speechtext:

Just for a few moments I wish to refer to conditions in my constituency. Agriculture is the chief industry that is followed there. Over fifty per cent of the entire dairy products of the Maritime provinces is manufactured and put up in the constituency that I represent. I do not think that can be successfully contradicted by anyone, because the statement has been made for a number of years down there on different occasions, and I have never known anyone to say that it is not correct. Our farmers at the present time are not very prosperous on account of unsettled conditions, the high cost of living, the great burden of taxation, and especially on account of the very high freight rates on all the commodities they purchase and on the products they have to place on the market. Our dairy farmers have to import large quantities of bran, shorts, middlings and other feeds to keep their stock at a high-prodticing standard, and their manufactured product of butter, cheese and milk has to be transported a considerable distance to the larger centres and shipping points.
The farmers of this country need protection about as much as any other industry. I noticed in an American paper just a few days ago that the president of the National Dairy Council of the United States, Mr. M. D. Munn, appeared before a committee of the government at Washington urging that the tariff on* butter from Canada into the United States be raised from eight to twelve cents. Mr. Munn states that they manufacture in the United States more than two billion pounds of butter, and that they import about twenty-five million pounds, which is a very small amount compared with the amount they produce themselves. He goes on to say, however, that that amount is enough to upset their market and at various times in the year to break their price from five to seventeen cents a pound. We are under the same conditions in this country, especially in the Maritime provinces. Whenever our butter and eggs get up to a fair price there are large imports coming in from the United States, whilst our tariff against their products is less than half what their tariff is against ours.

In the province of New Brunswick, the next largest industry to agriculture is lumbering. In the constituency I represent about 75,000,000 feet are cut annually. That amount was cut down considerably during the past year on account of over-production the year before and the slow sale of lumber during the year, due also to the competition that we meet in the New England states, the city of Montreal and other large centres by importation from the Pacific coast. This industry is very badly handicapped, and knowing conditions as I do, I might say that of the large number of operators and manufacturers of lumber on the north shore of the province, I do not believe there are more than two or three whose business is not for sale at the present Pme. The hon. member for Northumberland, NJ3. (Mr. Snowball) is a large operator and has been ever since I can remember. The name of Snowball is very well known in the Maritime provinces but the hon. member's firm is doing very little business this year, in fact it is only operating a portable mill where it has two very large stationary mills. The hon. member in question, during his speech earlier in the debate said that conditions were not extra good in New Brunswick, but quoted newspaper clippings to show that business was improving and that conditions were better than they had been. I have been in business at the place where I am located for the past thirty-five years, and I have never known conditions on the farm, in lumbering, and in industry generally, in that district, to be in such a sluggish and bad state as they are at the present time. To prove this statement I wish to refer to a speech delivered in the New Brunswick legislature on April 8, and the quotation is taken from the Telegraph-Journal, a newspaper printed in the city of St. John. N.B. The gentleman who made the statement in the New Brunswick legislature is Mr. J. D. McKenna, president of the Telegraph-Journal. I am only going to read the headlines placed on the speech; I shall not weary the House by reading the statement itself. One headline is;
Vision provinces, enduring most hideous annexation form in movement to U.S.
Then another one:
King's legislator tells House young people are leaving country by thousands and asks broad minded men devise new methods.
This does not bear out the statement made by many hon. gentlemen who claimed that conditions in Canada are good, and that conditions in the United States are worse than

The Budget-Mr. Jones
they are here at the present time. I do not think statements of that character made in this House, would bear the light of investigation. To further demonstrate that conditions are not as they were represented to be by the hon. member for Northumberland, I wish to read an extract from an address delivered by Mr. J. A. McLeod, general manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia, in the city of Toronto. Every person in this country knows that the Bank of Nova Scotia is one of our good, solid, substantial banks and that dependence can be placed upon the statement of its officers. Mr. McLeod, in the address in question, said:
Last year we referred to the onerous taxation which was pressing upon industry in Canada. There has been no improvement in this situation during the year. If business is to be revived, we feel that some relief from the burden of taxation will have to be given. We fully realize that the cost of the war has to be met, but we do not believe that our governments, by which we mean the Dominion, provincial and municipal authorities, yet realize the seriousness of the situation. New obligations continue to be incurred which are bound to result in increase of taxation rather than decrease. There should be such economy in all departments of government as will permit of some reduction of taxes, in order to encourage the business man to go ahead with new projects in the expectation that he, and not the tax collector, will reap the whole benefit of his industry. The British and United States governments have already made substantial tax reductions, but the tendency of Canadian taxes has been steadily upward. If we are to maintain and develop our foreign trade, our producers and exporters must not be handicapped by a heavier scale of taxation than applies to their competitors in other countries.
Another of our great problems in the Maritime provinces at the present time has to do with the old story of freight rates which have been very much increased. I realize that under conditions as they exist here to-day this is a very hard problem to deal with, but I believe that something could be done in this direction which would tend to relieve the present situation. Just at this point, and to contrast the conditions prevailing in the United States with those existing in Canada I wish to read the following clipping taken from the Financial Review and published a short time ago.
Railroads Break Freight Records American Lines Attribute Increase to Manufactured Goods
New York, March 20-(United Press).-American railroads during the first ten weeks of 1925 handled the greatest volume of freight ever carried at this season of the year-9,000,328 cars having been loaded from January to March 7.
That is 144,858 cars higher than the previous record established last year.
These figures were announced at the meeting of the directors of the American Railway Association here to-day.
The bulk of the increase has come from manufactured products or commodities used by the manufacturing industry. Since most agricultural products moved last Fall and early in the winter, there has been a decrease in the loadings of those commodities.
On March 1, 1925, railroads had 4,988 serviceable locomotives in storage compared with 3,800 on March 1. 1924.
You will observe that the movement referred to is not the movement of a large quantity of wheat or other natural products; it is a shipment of manufactured goods produced in the United States. It is not my intention to dwell on this matter very much longer except to discuss to some extent matters affecting the Canadian National Railways. In dealing with this branch of the subject I wish to say that I am not inspired by any feeling against the Canadian National Railways. Being a resident in the Maritimes and living on the main line of the National system I have always been a supporter of it and have tried to give it all the business possible. My firm-you will excuse me for this personal reference-gives the Canadian National Railways about 250 car loads of outward freight every year, and about 80 car loads of inward freight, besides freight in less than car load quantities and other business, so that any reference I may make to the National railways is not of a personal nature. I am prompted to speak as I do because of what I would term the most gross extravagance that has prevailed on the National railways under the management of Sir Henry Thornton. When that gentleman was appointed president of the National Railways I certainly wasivery hopeful that we would see a change in conditions, but as time goes by apparently the management is going from bad to worse. We were assured at the time Sir Henry Thornton was appointed that he would be above political influence, and would not stand for any political interference so far as the management of the road was concerned. I think that everyone in this country at that time believed that Sir Henry Thornton would not stand for any political interference, but after following Sir Henry Thornton in his different trips to tihe Maritime provinces, and keeping tabs on him in the rest of Canada, I believe that Sir Henry is a very clever and astute politician, and that he is paying about as much attention to the polititoal side of the question as was done by -certain officials in the days of the management of the old Intercolonial in the Maritime provinces.
I am glad the Secretary of State (Mr. Co-pp) is in his seat, because I intend to refer to another matter now. Last December there was a provincial by-election held in the city of Moncton for the seat rendered vacant by the elevation of the Hon. C. W. Robinson to the Senate of Canada. That vacancy existed for

some time, I suppose they considered the seat in Moncton as perhaps a little doubtful, although my hon. friend the Secretary of State in the last federal election had a majority in the vicinity of seven thousand' in his constituency.

It was public talk in the city of Moncton. I was discussing the matter of the attitude of the management of the Canadian National Railways, and I said at the beginning that I believed there was the most gross extravagance going on, especially under such conditions as we are confronted with in Canada to-day. I am only going to mention a few of them, and the first will be the Scribe hotel in Paris, the grant of $3,000,000, the Union club ini London, 11,500,000, and the radio broadcasting stations. It is not only what the cost of the installation of radio stations will be, but their upkeep for all time to come, and of course it is going on all the time. Then we have the golf courses, parks and operation of hotels, and the question of rolling stock on the Canadian National Railways. The first year of Sir Henry Thornton's management of the railways was 1923, and a question was asked of the Department of Railways and Canals regarding the building of new steel cars for the Canadian National. In 1922-1923, being Sir Henry Thornton's first year, he had not got well established in the business, and no new steel cars were purchased, but in 1923-1924 we find that 154 steel cars were bought by the Canadian National: in 1924-25 we find 65 steel cars, or in the two years 219 steel oars were purchased, at a cost of about $15,000,000. I claim these expenditures unwarranted and extravagant under present financial conditions. There are hundreds and hundreds of good first class and other cars which could be used. All they need is a coat of paint and a little reipairing of the upholstery to make them all right under conditions such as we are confronted witih in this country at the present time. I dlo not believe the people of this country will approve such extravagant expenditures.
Another matter is the use of private cars. I am not opposed to some private cars. I believe in the use of private cars for presidents of railways, or perhaps for cabinet ministers if they do not abuse it. For managers of railways the private car is just as essential as an office at headquarters, (because in going from one point to another in a division they can carry on business just the same practically as in their offices. But what I object to is this:	I have heard mention made of
trips that Sir Henry Thornton made in the Maritime provinces, and in fact in the rest

The Budget-Mr. Bird
of Canada, not merely in private oars but in private trains of eight or ten cars, just as if he were going up and down the country on a joy ride. I object to this expenditure on the Canadian National Railways, because when patrons of the road in remote sections ask for trifling concessions, they are invariably denied their just demands on the plea of economy.
I will close with just one more reference to a matter that was referred to iby a number of other hon. members at this and other sessions of parliament. It was referred to this session by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), and it is the matter of representation in this House. I would support and do everything I possibly could to have a reduction in the number of representatives. It is too large. Canada, with a population of eight or nine million people, is certainly overgoverned and there is too much expense in every way. A reduction in the membership of the House would necessitate a reduction in the cabinet by at least one-third, and I believe you would get more effective and better work if the present cabinet were cut in two.
I am also in favour of a reduction in the indemnity, and if the resolution that was on the order paper for a couple of years had ever come to a vote, it was my intention to support it. I believe the session could be shortened up very much, yes, by at least one-third. A lengthy session may be all right for members from Quebec who live in the vicinity of Montreal and that section and members from Ontario who live near Ottawa, but members coming long distances, from the west and the Maritime provinces, are here for five or six months listening to debates on academic questions that get us nowhere.
The Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King), in his closing remarks referred very feelingly, I thought, to our friends the Progressives in regard to the budget. He told them it was up to them whether they would support him or the amendment of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). He said that if he did not have a good substantial majority, he did not see anything left for him to do, but resign. I do not know what our friends the Progressives are going to do in this regard, but the best thing for them to do if they have any interest in the welfare of this country, would be to oppose the present budget and give the Prime Minister a chance to dissolve parliament, go to the country and receive the condemnation he so richly deserves.
Before I take my seat I wish to say that the Prime Minister favoured me with a speech
in my constituency during the campaign of 1921 when he spoke in the opera house in the town of Sussex. There he referred to my right hen. leader as an autocrat. He stated that business was going to the wall; that the cost of living was high, and that if the electors of Canada would only elect him and his party, we would see a great change in conditions in this country. In making his address here to-night, he said that he had reduced the cost of living, but wherein, he did not say. The Canadian people have reasons to think otherwise. I do not know that he said he had increased the speed of the wheels of industry, but that matter will be decided by the electors when an opportunity is given them at the ballot box and the wheels drawing the chariot of the present administration to its down-fall will move with great velocity.
