Already I have had intimations that opinion in the west regards the minister's utterance as a smoke screen behind which the government can carry on its policy of delay in this matter. There is a time to correct that view, and when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) gives his statement, then the government may have an opportunity to make clear to the public
12 m. just what its policy is on this important matter. That is all I intend to say at the present time in regard to the Hudson Bay railway.
I want to say a few things touching the budget in general. A- large part of this debate has been taken up with a wrangling over our methods of government bookkeeping. It appears that we have developed a system of bookkeeping which is designed to justify the government that happens to be in power instead of throwing any real light on the questions before the public. From the debate which has been going on it is impossible to draw any other conclusion. It seems to me to be a system of bookkeeping worthy of a Chinese laundry. What the public needs is not an elaborate and confusing justification of whatever government happens to be in power; the public needs a straightforward,

The Budget-Mr. Bird
unequivocal presentation of the facts. Why not put the revenue on one side and the expenditure on the other and give the public a chance to see where the balance really lies? Some countries go so far as to put their annual statement forward in diagrammatic form, and that is a suggestion which I would pass on to the government, so that the man who runs may read and understand without every year having to be dragged through a maze of balances and distinctions that are meant to confuse him. I have been reminded during this debate of the old fashioned grocer who used to keep his accounts by means of certain hieroglyphics which no one understood but himself. It was all right so long as the grocer was an honest man; but how was any one to tell whether he was honest or not? And that is precisely true of our present way of accounting; it has never been meant to enlighten the public but rather to justify the government that happened to be in power. I believe that we have probably spent too much time discussing this matter and too little time discussing what is the real substance, the heart of the annual statement. After all the people are not very much interested in the kind of book entry that has been made; they are interested in the amount of taxes they have been paying and the way in which they have paid them. This year the government has taxed the people to the extent of $290,000,000, a stupendous sum, and the only satisfaction we have in contemplating it is that it is somewhat less than the amount last year. It would be premature to congratulate the government, because when you strike the average for the last three years, which is something like $323,000,000, two or three millions higher than it was when this government came into power-when you look at it in that way, while it may not reflect any discredit on the government it does reveal the plight of the taxpayer. I do not think Edwards Morgan & Company could make it any plainer -$291,000,000 taken from the people in taxes this year. But that is not the really important thing from the taxpayer's point of view -that is, from the point of view of the ordinary taxpayer, the ordinary consumer and producer. What they are interested in, perhaps more than the amount, is the incidence. They want to know just where the blow has fallen, and that is one thing that has been neglected in this debate-an attempt to show the public just how they have been taxed. Canada for many years has been notorious amongst democracies in the way the cost of running an expensive government has been loaded on
the shoulders of the consumer. What has happened in the last two or three years? It was bad enough before, but during the two or three years of a professedly popular government, what has happened? We find that in that time indirect taxation has grown from an already high figure of 67 per cent to 80 per cent. That is to say, 80 per cent of the cost of running this country to-day rests upon the shoulders of the consumer and of the producer. Eighty per cent of the interest on the war debt; 80 per cent of our war pensions; 80 per cent of the cost of this debate, rests upon the shoulders of the consumer, the workingman with a family, the soldier settler struggling on a bush farm, the pensioned soldier and his family living on a government pittance. I do not think we can find in this world a country that lays any claim to democratic development that so cheerfully lays the burden where it is most difficult for it to be borne. Search the world through, and I question whether you can find a country where the principle of ability to pay is so much neglected as it is in this Canada of ours. Whether you go to free trade Britain or to protected America, you will find that tlhis is true. In Great Britain 57i per cent of the taxes are raised by direct taxation, and in the United States 55 per cent; and if you add the estate duty it brings the United States figure up to the level of that of Great Britain, which proves that those two great democracies have been in step in evolving democratic forms of taxation. We in Canada are lagging behind, and the reason is because the governments we have had for a generation or two have not been concerned about legislating for the people as a whole, because the people as a whole during that time have not been represented. Their voice has not been heard here, and the annual budget for more than two generations has absolutely ignored the common people, with the result that at present we are raising by indirect taxation 80 per cent of the total cost of running our government.
Our friends to the right, .the Conservative*, are almost silent on this phase of the budge1!. -and very naturally so; it accords well with the ancient Tory practice of bolstering up a privileged few at .the expense of the many. But we do not look for that kind of doctrine from a Liberal government whose traditions are so opposed to that kind of taxation. The Conservatives have in their amendment made a gesture in this direction. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) when he was speaking addressed his remarks most particularly to this side of the House. He looked at
The Budget-Mr. Bird

us almost in a threatening manner when he was dealing with this question. Were we as Progressives, he asked, going to vote against an amendment proposing a reduction in the salee tax? Well, we Progressives, while we miay be simple men, are not so easily taken in as the leader of the opposition seams to imagine. It is very easy to see .through that amendment. A reduction in -the sales tax, coming from the Conservative party, simply means baiting the protectionist trap. The Conservative wants to lower the sales tax and the stamp tax and the income tax; where is he going to get his revenue? There is only one source left, and that is the tariff. 'Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird." He cannot expect the Progressives to be misled1 by such a simple device as that.
The Conservatives have not said very much about reducing the income tax, but I have noticed that certain papers for a long time now have been exerting a silent pressure in that direction, and it seemed to find an echo in the speech of the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). When that hon. member was speaking he compared the plight of the income tax payer in Vancouver with the plight of the income tax payer in Seattle. I would not question his figures for a moment, but the real significance of them is this: There is no doubt that the income tax payer in Canada is carrying a heavier burden than the individual income tax payer in the United States, but so is the consumer in Canada bearing a heavier burden than the consumer in the United States. The fact is this, that Canada as a country is much more heavily burdened than the United States as a country. We are groaning under a burden that the United States knows nothing about. The difference is this, that in Canada the burden is more inequitably placed than it is in the United States. In the United States the burden is fairly distributed; in Canada the burden has been shifted over onto the backs of the consumer. If you take the contribution of the average tax payer of the United States, you will find it amounts to $17.50; in Canada the average contribution is $6.50, which is a very vivid demonstration of how the burden is being distributed in this Canada of ours, and the result of that policy is written right across Canada. For some years there has been a tendency in this country, on the one side, towards an effiminating luxury, and on the other side, and I speak sincerely when I say it, a tendency to a degrading poverty, and that process has been going on quicker than some hon. gentlemen imagine. Dives has been having a little more purple and fine linen each year, a little more sumptuous 
living, while poor Lazarus has had just a few less crumbs to his share. You are faced every day of your life with business buildings and bank buildings that resemble pagan temples, and on the other side we have homes which resemble mediaeval hovels rather than homes, and yet there are some hon. members here who would still further denude the homes of the people in order that they might embellish still more the homes of the well-to-do, because that is what this system of taxation means.
I turn for a few moments to the question of the tariff, that time-worn topic in this annual debate. I notice that the two chief protagonists on these occasions are the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). When the ex-Minister of Finance was speaking, he twitted the member for Brome on his "ism," as he called it, but the ex-Minister of Finance is also smitten with an ism, whether he knows it or not, and I am afraid his ism is perhaps a little more wild-eyed and impractical than the other. The member for Brome has this advantage for his theory, that it has been associated for a long time with the fine traditions of good British common sense, but the ism of the ex-Minister of Finance, as I understand, was spun some years ago out of the brain of a German professor who promulgated the doctrine that it was a very fine and patriotic thing to tax the agricultural population in order to build up a strong productive power. That is real Frussianism, and I want to say that it is just as anti-social .as it is antiBritish in its spirit. The unfortunate thing is, Mr. Speaker, that humanity cannot live on theories alone, it does not- matter how respectable they are. When we are offered free trade on the one hand, and protection on the other, we are really not offered very much at all in a country like this, for this reason, that tlhe Canadian people for one oause and another have never been able to accept either doctrine. A medicine that the stomach will not retain is really no medicine at all, and yet for a good many years Doctor Liberal and Doctor Conservative have been called in to minister to an ailing country. Those nostrums are all that they have ever had to offer to an ailing Canada, and Canada for some reason or other has never found itself in the frame of mind to accept either of them. I think that situation is capable of being explained. I believe the reason that Canada does not accept the doctrine of the hon. member for Brome is because of a certain state of mind, We as Canadians are subject to a

The Budget-Mr. Bird
certain fear complex, born of the proximity of another country which far surpasses us in population and productive power. That overshadows us and it makes it very hard to convince the average Canadian of the virtues of the Cobdenite doctrine-very hard indeed. It also makes it very easy for our Tory friends to influence them in the other direction. The one wave of the flag is worth a dozen arguments to our protectionist friends. They do not need to do much arguing at all, for psychology works furiously on their behalf. Now so long as protection dominates the international situation, and so long as the gigantic trusts hide behind these tariff walls and carry on their commercial aggression, just so long will Canadians resist the eloquence, the very fine eloquence, of the hon. member for Brome. I pity him, and I pity them. On the other hand, the reason why Canadians do not accept the protectionist doctrine is purely upon economic grounds.
Canada is a predominantly agricultural country, under the necessity of exporting its products and selling them in the world markets at the world's prices; and so long as that maintains, Mr. Speaker, the average Canadian will resist the doctrine of high protection. But this brings us to a rather curious position to which I want to draw the attention of this House for a few moments, because I think it is a most significant thing in Canadian public life. The attitude of the present Liberal government on the tariff brings us to the crux of the whole situation. That policy of theirs, which is so inconsistent with their out-of-office professions is the most significant thing in Canadian, public life. Now, our Tory friends attribute it to the moral degeneracy of the Liberal politician. I think that is a very superficial way of looking at it. This thing is not due to the moral delinquency of the Liberal politicians. I think on the whole they stand up just as *well in that regard as perhaps any of us, But this thing, this strange phenomenon is due not to the moral degeneracy of the Liberal statesman, but rather to the political acumen of Liberal statesmen. That is not a theory of my own, because we have had ample demonstration of it in this debate. The Liberals no longer apologize for that attitude. This is an attitude which comes from divining that public opinion is not crystallized upon this question. For a generation or two the Liberals have pursued that policy. It is a purely political policy. It is as far removed from economics or from the science of government as it can be. It is
pure politics, unabashed politics, and for a good many years the policy adopted by the Liberals has been profitable to them. They have got away with it, and it has yielded to them the sweet and delectable fruits of office for a good many years; and after all what is policy for but to win office by? Now the Minister of Justice in his speech-yesterday was it?-alluded to this phase of the question. The Minister of Justice has the typical philosophic mind, and he made it his business to take this political attitude of the Liberals and erect it into a philosophy. I listened very attentively to him while he was trying to do it. The Liberal party from now on is going to assume the role of a centrist group, holding the balance between the Tories on the one hand and the Progressives on the other. They are going to save Canada from disruption by holding that balance. Now, while he was speaking I could not help remembering that that is just exactly what the Liberal party in Great Britain thought, that is just the role they thought they were going to play; but I would remind the hon. minister that it is a position that is getting more and more difficult to hold 'as people become more enlightened on political matters. Why just fancy this government going to the country and trying to persuade the average Canadian citizen that they are neither the one thing nor the other. We are reminded of the old revival hymn which used to say "Oh to be nothing, nothing!"

The public of Canada has undergone mighty changes since those things used to foe successful. Somebody here will very likely ask: What is the Progressive attitude on these questions, what is the Progressive attitude on protection and free trade? Well, that goes to the very root of our being, to the very root of our
The Budget-Mr. Bird

existence. The Progressives four years ago were sent here as a protest against the predominance of urban ideas in this parliament. The Progressive party has no other cause for existence but that. The tariff is not the only question that has been framed according to urban ideas; there are others too. The tariff was put over on this country, saddled upon it, long before rural Canada was organized. If rural Canada had been organized it never would have been put over. Since that time rural Canada has been organized and it stays organized; and there will be no peace in this parliament until this tariff question is settled along lines that bring something more like justice to the producers of this country.
The farmers of Canada are not unreasonable as some people try to make out. They are not sectional; they are not divisionists; they are among the most stable citizens in this country. The farmers do not think they will ever get it all their own way; they are not numerically preponderant; they never dream they will exercise autocratic political power in this country-that is not the point at all. I do not believe that the average farmer in this country thinks for a moment that he will get his own way even on the tariff question. But I will tell you what the average farmer, at any rate in the west, demands from this government, from this parliament, is a broad, constructive policy that will be designed to give him, for the first time in his existence, something like justice -justice in comparison with other elements in the community. Until now he has had no chance at all. He has been faced in this parliament with governments that were bourgeois in character, that were urbanized in their point of view and still are-governments which had their eyes everlastingly glued to the sources from which came their political power. That kind of thing cannot endure. It is no use the Prime Minister making his emotional appeals to members on this side of the House; we have long ceased to be moved by emotion. The realities of the situation will not permit us to be stirred up by eloquence of that kind. The Prime Minister in his subtle manner may try to drive us before the public mind into a position where we will be looked upon as divisionists and as sectionalists, but we have been too long in the confidence of the people who sent us here to permit him to succeed. He will have to couch his overtures in more reasonable language than he has done before he can meet with any success. What we want is not emotional appeals of the old political kind. We want a definite announcement of 
what he is prepared to do for rural Canada. He lias not given us that. He has evaded the question every time it has been put up to him. His policy has been a policy of evasion, and it is no use trying to answer the proposal that I am presenting by a peroration of the kind that he delivered to-night. I know there is a very insidious influence in that casuistic idea that if we vote against the government we will vote with the Tories, but the Liberals cannot get away with that in the fourth year of our experience here. If it had only been our first year they might have done it. The idea of trying to put us into that camp because we happen to vote against the Liberals is childish. My position is that I am not an enemy of the government. I would gladly support the government if I could see any indication of a policy that would be suited to that portion of the country which I represent. The details of the budget do not concern me very much. I do not scruple very much about the tariff this way or that in any particular budget. My conscience would not balk at that. I am voting on the budget in the way members always vote on it. I am voting on the general policy of the government and on their attitude towards the Crowsnest pass agreement and the Hudson Bay railway. In short, I am voting on their entire attitude towards the rural population of the west.

speechtext:
If I had my speech prepared, I would not hesitate to agree to the suggestion of the hon. member. I would ask the indulgence of the House for a few minutes while I discuss what seem to be the vital and important matters before us. Our attention in this debate, by reason of the amendment and the motion itself, has been attracted in two directions, first of all to the matter of economy and, second, the budget itself directs our attention to matters of finance and of fiscal policy. I dislike being put into a position where my attitude must be entirely one of criticism. If I cannot be in a position where I can helpfully criticize, I have no desire to criticize merely for the sake of criticism. So I approach what few remarks I intend to make, not with the attitude of mere captious criticism, but for the purpose of seeing if I can add anything of value to this already overburdened Hansard.
It seems to me that, with regard to the question of economy, there are two promising and fertile fields 'for investigation into our situation to-day. There is, first of all, the railway situation. The matter has been gone into at great length; but briefly, the position assumed by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) expresses so Clearly and definitely the views that I hold in the matter that I do not propose to weary the House by going into it in any detail this evening. In the first place, I am convinced that consolidation of these two railway systems must come. I am convinced likewise that that consolidation must be only under a system of national ownership. If these points are established, if they are accepted, why cannot

we take steps now to accomplish our purpose? Why wait until one or the other system gives evidence of a breakdown before we actually put our hands, as the government of Canada, to the wheel, take control of the situation and save, not millions, but tens of millions of dollars annually? After all, both railways get their money from the people of Canada; the people of Canada pay the railway transportation charges, and if one railway steadily increases its earnings, the other railway will necessarily, and to an increasing extent in the future, decrease its earnings. So, I say, if these two principles are established, why should the government, why should not this parliament, now formulate a definite proposal, present it to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and say:	Here is a proposition
for your acceptance or refusal? The Canadian Pacific will realize that if they refuse the proposal, they must face the competition of the Canadian National Railways in increasing measure in the future, with the result that, peilhaps, in a few short years it may be in a much worse position as regards deficits than the Canadian National is in to-day. So I suggest to the government that now is the opportune time, now is the appointed hour to present to the Cana dian Pacific a proposition for the consolidation of these two railways. I have not the slightest doubt that a consolidation of that character will save tens of millions of dollars yearly. It is important that the opportunity should be grasped. There is no use in trying to save money in petty ways when in. such a large way we can save such vast sums.
The next field and a very promising field for the economizing in expenditure of the public money is that of federal administration. Government, after all, is the biggest and most important business that we have in this country. The government should aim to be a model employer. The government should also, keeping this principle in mind, aim to establish economical and efficient business administration. In the field of government expenditure and administration do we reach those high standards in any particular? Some people look at the anuual expenditures; they are shocked by the amounts, and then they promptly wield the sword on the heads of any unoffending civil servants who may happen to be within their reach. That, it seems to me, is not the proper way to approach this problem. Whatever fault there may be rests, not with the individual civil servant, but rather with the system which has grown up in this country.

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
May I preface what I have to say by asking hon. members this question for example: What are the numbers of our civil servants and what is the payroll of the civil service? I am going to give you two or three figures. A Senate committee last year made a very careful examination of this and allied problems and they came to the conclusion that for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1924, the government of Canada had on its payroll 42,238 employees, the annual payroll amounting to $48,206,527. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) at the beginning of the session asked for a return showing the cost of the civil service, and the number of employees in the month of January, 1924, as well as in July of the same year. The figures submitted show that in January, 1924, there were 38,062 employees at a monthly cost of $4,746,694.90. These were the figures given Hansard to-night by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). In the month of July, 1924, the number of employees was 40,927, the monthly salary including bonus being $4,814,724. Taking these two months as the average, this would indicate that the annual payroll is $58,000,000 and not $48,000,000 as the Senate found. I turn now to the Auditor General's report for last year and I find therein that the cost of the civil service is given as not less than $74,000,000 per annum Why these vast discrepancies-forty-eight, fifty-eight, and seventy-four millions? I wonder which of these is right.

Now, we find that _in Canada we have under our system thirty-six officers holding the rank of deputy minister and enjoying an annual payroll amounting to $277,500; whereas in the United States there are only twenty-one heads of departments with an annual payroll of $157,500. months of the year in session; they are not members of congress.
Mr, SHAW: I am not talking about cabinet ministers in Canada; I am referring to deputy heads of departments. The hon. member for West Lambton discussed in some detail the bureau of the budget
1 am. as established in the United States, and I would like to give to the House, if I may, a somewhat more comprehensive survey of the situation in that country in order that we may see if it is possible to make in this country some application of a system which seems to me to have much merit I am not doing this in any spirit of criticism. Perhaps I might tell a story here. A rooster had wandered somewhat afield from his own barnyard and he discovered to his surprise a large ostrich egg. With infinite patience and with much labour he rolled it up before the gaze of his admiring flock, to whom he gave this assurance,
" This is not intended as a reflection; it only shows what can be done ", It is in that spirit that I desire to say something wTith regard to the bureau of the budget. The Budget and Accounting Act of the United States was passed in the year 1921. At that time the United States had a very large debt approximating $24,000,000,600, and they had an annual expenditure of $5,700,000,000. In the year ending June 30, 1921, their deficit was something like $80,000,000. On account of the financial chaos and the generally difficult conditions in which that country found itself, congress at that time passed the Budget and Accounting Act to come into effect on July 1, 1921. Perhaps I should say one or two things with regard to the purpose of that act, and in this connection I may read a statement made by President Harding before a group of the departmental heads in that government. He said:
I am very glad to come before you and stand sponsor for this meeting. The present administration of the federal government is committed to a period of economy and efficiency in government. The statement is not made with any thought of criticizing what has gone before. It is made in a new realization of the necessity of driving at the loose, unscientific expenditures of government. There is not a menace in the world to-day like that of growing public indebtedness and mounting public expenditures. There has seemingly grown up an impression that the public treasuries are inexhaustible things, and with it a conviction that no efficiency and no economy are ever to be thought of in public expense.
We want to reverse things. Congress, in order to aid in the change of policy, has provided, for the first time in the history of the federal government, for a bureau of the budget. It has been my privilege and my responsibility to choose the director of the budget. After a conference with him, it was

The Budget-Mr. Shaw

decided that the way to begin with an efficient system under the budget was to look to those who are in fact responsible for government efficiency and economy. Sometimes in our habits we overlook those who really do things in this world, and in the federal government there are tens of thousands of public servants who axe giving the best that is in them to bring about a satisfactory administration of affairs, but whom the public never knows.
I want to bring into this picture of a drive for efficiency and economy you servants of the government who are directly responsible for a better order of affairs, if it is to be brought about.
And so the first thing President Harding did was to appoint General Dawes to be director of the budget. General Dawes was a former controller of the United States treasury in the McKinley administration, and he knew much about the civil service. He had been chief of staff overseas of the United States army during the war, a position of tremendous importance and responsibility, and it was felt that he would be a good man, with the adequate amount of experience and training, to give the . United States a business government. The first thing he did was to select some twelve or fifteen of the best business men of the United States whom he could gather together. May I say that General Dawes agreed to stay only for a year, and that at a salary of $7,500, and he engaged, the business men at one dollar per year. They went to Washington and went into the various departments of government. General Dawes decided that he was not going to build up a new bureau, a new form of autocracy; he determined to make use of the men in the various departments; so from the departments he selected key men familiar with the work of the various government services, who were to be strictly responsible to the director of the budget, the director himself being the direct agent of the President of the United States. Now, what did General Dawes find when he commenced to investigate the service? He found a great deal of duplication of service. He found considerable over-manning. He found that as soon as a vote was granted, the departments, as a general rule, felt that it was necessary for them to spend the amount appropriated. He found that, generally speaking, government was in a very inefficient condition and working certainly at a great disadvantage.
General Dawes promptly called the meeting to which I have referred, which was addressed by President Harding from whose address on that occasion I have just read an extract. Their work in connection with the estimates would ordinarily have been concerned with the year 1923, because with the fiscal year ending on June 30, the estimates IMr. Shaw.3
had already been provided by congress for the ensuing year. But General Dawes was not satisfied with that. He said: We will look into these estimates that have already been passed by congress. Accordingly he asked the heads of the various departments to submit to him, with the assistance of the officers he had selected in each department, recommendations with a view to economizing in expenditure. Within a month he had a report, and the result was that the amounts provided by congress were reduced to the extent of some $112,000,000. Now, let me give some further figures. We have been so accustomed to dealing in millions, throwing them recklessly about here and there, that perhaps hon. members will not object if we raise it a little bit and call it billions.
For the fiscal year ending June 30, 1921, the expenditure of the United States government was $5,538,000,000, and the receipts totalled $5-,
624,000,000. For the year ending June 30, 1922, the first year of the operation of this budget, the expenditure had been decreased over $1,-
700,000,000, to the sum of $3,795,000,000. The receipts of the government, by reason of lessened taxation made possible by reductions in expenditures, were reduced to $4,109,000,000, a drop of $1,500,000,000. For the year ending June 30, 1923, the expenditure was further reduced to $3,697,000,000, and the receipts also, by reason of lessened taxes, fell to $4,007,000,-
000.	In the year ending June 30, 1924, the expenses of the United States government were further reduced to $3,497,000,000 and the receipts totalled $3,995,000,000.
Now, the estimated expenditure for the year ending June 30, 1925, was $3,083,000,000. I should say that under this system the President meets half-yearly the officers of the budget bureau heads. In his address to the gathering in June last President Coolidge asked them to reduce this expenditure to three billions, and for the current year, as the result of continued executive pressure, the estimates have been reduced to that figure. What has been the result of the bureau's activities? Putting it in percentages, before this budget scheme developed the expenditure of the United States government was 59 per cent of all governmental expenditure throughout the United States.

speechtext:
Including state and
municipal?

speechtext:
Yes, state and municipal expenditures. The figures have just been reversed, so that to-day only 41 per cent of governmental expenditure in the United States is

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
represented by federal expenditure. May I say, too, that the public debt of the United States in that period has decreased from $23,976,000,000 to $21,254,000,000, a decrease in three years of $2,722,000,000, an interest saving alone of $120,000,000 a year. Further, and as one result the tax receipts of the United States government have been decreased to the extent of $6,000,000 a day. Not only that, but the personnel of the service has been reduced in that period by 51,000; in the month of March last it was reduced by a further 2,500.
As I have indicated the director of the budget- was at first concerned primarily in revising estimates. But he soon found that he could render much more valuable service than that, so he undertook the work of co-ordinating the public services. Now, I know that a word like "co-ordinate" is not acceptable to some people in this House. I know that the right hon. leader of the opposition will object if I use the word "cooperation", and others will object if I use the word "collaboration". But I may say on the authority of General Lord that these words have been written into the United States civil service dictionary for the first time, and now that service understands fully the significance of these words.
As I say, General Dawes in his investigation found within a short period of years a tremendous overlapping in the services. What did he do? He appointed a chief co-ordinator in whom he had the utmost confidence. He then appointed assistant oo-ordinators with jurisdiction in nine areas in the United States, those areas corresponding with the existing military districts. It is the duty of these persons to see to it there that there is no overlapping, no over manning, no duplication in the service. Let me suggest one of the things discovered. The War Department of the United States had a large quantity of surplus supplies. They called for tenders and sold them to a group of speculators at figures much below the original purchase price, and the speculators promptly turned round and sold at a great advance exactly the same goods to the Naval Department. That is the sort of thing that was going on in the United States service. The director of the budget among other things organized a central purchasing department, something that is very greatly needed in this country, and generally the whole system has worked out entirely satisfactorily. As I said before, business meetings are held every six months, with the President and the members of his cabinet right on the platform, and the 1714
director of the budget talks to them just as he talks to those who come under his immediate supervision. Every few months the director of the budget calls for reports fron bureau heads and from his co-ordinating staffs and asks them: What have you done in the last few months in the direction of economy? They make their reports, and it is rather interesting to read what has been done as a matter of actual practice as the result of the application of this system.
Hon. members may be interested in knowing what this costs, because after all the cost of such an organization is an important factor. In the first year, congress appropriated the sum of $225,000 for this service. The bureau of the budget spent only $120,000 in the first year, and the estimate for the current year is just $180,000. That small expense is possible by reason of the fact that the director is using the services already provided. He stands there as the direct agent of the President, who is the chief executive officer of that nation. He has his finger upon every department, and with the co-operation of these departments with his own staff collected for co-ordination purposes he has been able to achieve the results which I have indicated.
Now there can be no doubt that this result has been largely achieved by reason of the budget bureau, and by reason too, particularly, of the splendid spirit which has animated the whole civil service. A real spirit of co-operation is certainly evidenced in the United States. Just let me read one or two words from the statement of President Coolidge on June 30, 1924. He said:
The insistent demand for economy and reduction in expenditures necessarily requires increasing * efficiency of administration. I realize that it is making an ever increasing caJll upon the administrative ability of responsible officials, but this is a call for real service. It demands a most searching inquiry into the field of your activities, so as to remove entirely from them all elements which are not essential, and so as to curtail all those which may be reduced without prejudice to the welfare of the nation.
He says further, and this I commend to the members of this House:
We must have no carelessness in our dealings with public property or the expenditure of public money. Such a condition is characteristic either of an undeveloped people or of a decadent civilization. America is neither. It stands out strong and vigorous and mature.
Further on he says:
I am for economy. After that I am for more economy. At this time and under present conditions that is my conception of serving all the people.
Now it is all very well to see what can be done, but have these facts no immediate
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

concern for us in this country? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that they have. We had in 1923 a committee appointed by this parliament for the purpose of investigating the operation of the Civil Service Act, and one of the suggestions made by that committee, whose report, however, was never adopted by this parliament, reads as follows:
Your committee is impressed with the necessity of co-ordinating and harmonizing the various departments of the public service into one efficient administrative unit in order to prevent duplication and over-lapping and to eliminate over-staffing.
Some progress has been made, but your committee is convinced that the fullest efficiency can only be secured by definitely charging some central authority with this important task. The Prime Minister, it is suggested, is the proper authority to act as the coordinating head and business manager of all government services, but the serious and grave responsibilities attached to his office, particularly with reference to government policies, would probably make it necessary that this duty should be delegated to an expert, in the same manner that the government has delegated its responsibility in connection with the management of government railways. Such an expert could be also entrusted with the duty of supervising public purchasing and contracts, with a view of securing business efficiency.
That is the recommendation of the Malcolm committee of 1923. I am not going to tell you who was responsible for writing into the report that particular provision, but I want to make what I think is a practical suggestion. First of all, the success of the United States plan has resulted from the application of executive pressure through the executive agent, the director of the budget. The Prime Minister, I think it cannot be denied, is the chief executive of this nation. He is charged, in addition to other duties, with administrative functions. He is the one who is primarily responsible. Now I say, let us give him the machinery, let us give him whatever is necessary in order to carry out his duties, and then let us hold him fully and completely responsible for economy and efficiency in all government expenditure.
We have in this country a Civil Service Commission which has two functions to perform, an examination function for the purpose of determining the qualifications of applicants for the service, and a second function, namely, the duty of organization. I am not going to discuss the first function, but in regard to the second, I claim that the Civil Service Commission have wholly failed. They have not, except in a few isolated instances, made any attempt to carry out their statutory obligations to organize efficiently the various departments of government, and what is the reason they give for their failure? The reason given is that they cannot get the co-operation of the government departments. Now I suggest the act. makes no provision about getting the co-
Mr. Shaw.!
operation of government departments. The act says it is the commission's duty, and there being no limitation, they must be held accountable for their failure in that regard.

speechtext: Did they not reorganize some departments of the government, but not all?

speechtext:
I am giving the reason for
their failure to go into all the departments of the government. I did say they have gone into one or two departments, the Printing Bureau, for instance, and the Militia department, and I think they have organized those departments efficiently, but with regard to the Interior department, for example, they have not apparently as yet developed any scheme of reorganization, and that is a department which I think stands in great need, and I say it without reflecting on anybody, of the closest scrutiny with a view to reorganization. If I may use the lurid language of General Dawes, when he found that there were some department heads he had difficulty in cooperating with, he said that it seemed like using a pile driver to kill a flea but that he was prepared to put the hook, as he called it, into these rat holes of covert hostility, and in that way secure co-operation and assistance.
Now my idea is this, that this organization branch of the Civil Service Commission should by an act of this parliament be taken away from the Civil Service Commission and be placed directly under the Prime Minister of this country. It should be made directly responsible to him as the chief executive officer of this country, and then, given his opportunity, given his duty, we should hold the Prime Minister responsible to see that there was developed in Canada an efficient business administration. If some such policy was adopted I am satisfied that there would be a tremendous saving in government expenditures and in the expenditure on the public service in this country. The saving to the country I suggest, under the consolidation of the railways would mount up to tens of millions of dollars a year. The reorganization of the public service would certainly save millions of dollars a year.
I come now to the fiscal proposals embodied in the budget. Frankly I propose to vote for the motion, and I am going to tell the House my reason. There are two or three items in the budget that I want to discuss very shortly. There is a reduction in the tariff, so far as it affects well-drilling machinery, of 22i per cent. This is a very substantial reduction. The tariff on well-drilling machinery is a tax from which western Canada has sought relief for many years. We have great hopes

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
in the province from which I come that our whole area is underlaid with oil reservoirs- I hope it is anyway-but the depth is such that the ordinary Canadian machinery is not adequate to meet the difficulties incident to deep well-drilling. The result has been that we have been forced to largely buy well-drilling machinery from Pennsylvania and pay a duty of 27J per cent, and in that way this enterprise-which under the best of circumstances must be a speculative one-this effort to develop our natural resources is hampered by reason of this heavy tariff exaction. And so I look with approval, and I am sure the people of western Canada do also, to that very substantial reduction in the tariff on well-drilling machinery.
There is another item to which I wish to direct attention, and that is the matter of the duty on slack coal. Here there has been an increase. Now, I do not pretend to be dogmatic so far as particular items in the tariff are concerned. If I felt that that increase of the duty on slack coal would solve the serious labour problems in the province of Nova Scotia, or the serious coal-mining problems in the province of Alberta, I would not hesitate for a single moment in the interests of peace and harmony in those fields to sacrifice my principles to the extent of voting for the duty on slack coal. In my opinion, regardless of what may be said, the economic unity of this country is an absolute essential, economic peace in Canada is an absolute essential; and we in a matter of this kind cannot say that we are called upon to pay too high a price or make too much of a sacrifice of principle if it has the effect suggested. Frankly I do not know. The coal miners in my province are in favour of it; the coal miners, as I understand it, in the province of Nova Scotia have assumed a noncommittal attitude, and have suggested that they want primarily a fact-finding commission for the purpose of investigating Besco. But with that reservation, with the reservation that I am not sure that the duty on slack coal will have the effect contended, I say that if it did accomplish that purpose I would have no hesitation whatever in the interests of the economic unity of this country in supporting that proposal.
Now the budget does not advance very much beyond the tariff proposals of last year. It is suggested that we have got to allow a breathing apeffl after the proposals which were incorporated in the budget of last year. There is no doubt that our revenues have fallen very much, and it may be that it is desirable that for the present at least no further substantial
change should be made. In this connection I am reminded of a speech made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) on the occasion of the liberal convention held in this city. I recall his militant language; I think, perhaps, he may have been slightly intoxicated-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: COMPARISON OF FINANCE, FISCAL YEARS 1924-25 AND 1920-21
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friends will permit me to finish. He may have been slightly intoxicated with the enthusiasm of the occasion which led him to use this somewhat militant language. He said-and apparently he pointed in a certain direction-"yonder is the castle of special privilege surrounded by the redoubts of protection." I take it he was referring to this chamber, or to the government of the day, perhaps, and then his suggestion was "Let's up and at 'em". Now when the smoke of battle cleared away I think the hon. member for Brome retired from the stricken field dismayed)-shall I say?-but yet undaunted. I have had a little experience in military matters, and one lesson which I learned was this: That where you find an enemy entrenched-imy hon. friend from Brome would indicate that the forces of special privilege were entrenched, and I think he is right-the attack .must be made by men who are like-minded and who have the one high purpose to serve. If there are deserters why of course the attack will not likely be a successful one. But in addition to that, experience shows that where specially entrenched foes of this character are attacked, the attack seldom can be made in one grand effort-it must be done by continuously exerted pressure. Every new position gained must be consolidated before a further attack is made. And so I feel with regard1 to the tariff that we must consolidate the position already secured if we hope finally to achieve the result to which all aspire. Then may I say again that in tariff matters I have tried to adopt a consistent position. I think perhaps if hon. members will examine my record on tariff matters before the House they will find that my position in supporting this budget this morning is absolutely consistent. Let me just shortly indicate-and I state this only for the benefit of my friends whose confidence and good wishes I would like to maintain: I am indifferent as to my enemies-the course which I have pursued. In 1922 I voted against the government proposals because to my recollection they went-in fact they did not go at all. In 1923 we had a slight advance, as I recall, on the budget of 1922. There was some lowering of the tariff on some important items-not con-
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

siderahtle but some; there was a turning in the direction at least of freer trade. But in conjunction with that the tariff was also raised* in some particulars. Not only that but we had the introduction of copper bounties, of hemp bounties, and I dio not know what other bounties. And I was surprised to find this year that some of my hon. friends on this side of the House were parties to the introduction at least of one of those bounties. As I say in 1923, because of the suggestion that tariff stability was the thing required and because of that more or less mixed budget I voted against the government's proposals. In 1924 we had a situation which has not persisted, a situation which did not exist before during my experience in this House. An amendment to the government proposals which went a considerable distance in the direction of freer trade was proposed by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), an amendment which represented my fiscal views on the tariff. I had no hesitation, although I found myself only in the company of sixteen or seventeen hon. members, in supporting the amendment to the budget which was then proposed, but I did not deny support to the government for the proposals such as it made. So I say that my position to-day is thoroughly consistent, if consistency be a virtue. I do not know that it always is, but if consistency be a virtue my position to-day is substantially and exactly in accord with the position I have always taken on tariff questions. More than that I am satisfied that the issue is directly between those who stand for freer trade, be the progress slow or fast, and those who stand for high protection. Personally I do not propose by my vote to give any solace or comfort whatever to the advocates of high protection in this chamber or outside of it. Under the circumstances, in voting against the present proposals of the government it seems to me that I would be directly doing what it is my purpose not to do.
I apologize to the House for having taken the time in discussing my position, but I feel, by reason of the misrepresentation which has been made as to my position, that in all fairness I should make my position perfectly clear.
There are a couple of matters I desire to speak about before I conclude. The first is the matter of rural credits. I sincerely hope that the government this year will not allow the opportunity to pass without giving effect at least to some variety of long term rural credit. We all speak about the importance (Mr. Shaw.]
of agriculture. We all stress its difficulties and its trials. I think we are all well advised in so doing. There is no problem to my mind of such consequence to the farmers to-day, particularly those in western Canada where the need is greatest, as adequate credit facilities at a low interest rate, and credit of a kind suitable to the needs and requirements of agriculture. The farmer in western Canada to-day has only two sources of supply to meet his demand. He may go to the bank, but he cannot borrow money on his real property from the bank, because that is prohibited under the terms of the Bank Act. He may go to a mortgage company but its rates of interest vary from eight per cent upwards. No farmer in western Canada can afford to pay eight per cent per annum, and the result is that the farmers find themselves in continual and increasing financial difficulties. More than that, the Canadian farmer must meet the competition of the world. He must meet competitors, all of whom enjoy rural credit facilities at a much lower interest rate than he himself enjoys, and so I say to the government, if many things must pass by the board, let not this particular subject be forgotten. I know there are interests, financial and otherwise, that are opposed to it. I know that there is propaganda abroad in the land against a system of rural credit, but I say to the government, of all the problems before us no one is deserving of prior consideration to this matter of adequate credit facilities for our farming population.
Another matter to which perhaps I may be permitted to direct the attention of the House is the matter of railway rates. Unlike the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), I do not hesitate to say that the government has, in my judgment during the whole course of this controversy beginning with the very first session of this parliament, taken exactly the correct and proper attitude with regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement. The hon. member for Nelson has apparently not studied this matter with his usual capacity and industry, because the fact is that in 1922, at the first session of this parliament, the government allowed the one section of that rate agreement covering eastbound commodities,-to come into operation, and in July last year, they allowed, by the effluxion of time and the operation of law, the section of the agreement dealing with westbound rates to go automatically into effect. What else could the government do?' They might have taken the opposite position and introduced legislation to prevent the operation of the Crowsnest pass agreement. But they did not. Along

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
came the Board of Railway Commissioners. They heard a case, and they held in October of last year that the Crowsnest pass agreement, although incorporated in a statute of this country, was not an agreement binding on the railway commission. An appeal was taken to the Privy Council in Canada, and the Privy Council held that the Crowsnest pass agreement, in so far as it had been affected by the judgment of the railway commission, should again come into effect. What else could the government do? There was nothing further they could do. This is the very application which I made before the Governor in Council when I attended here acting on behalf of the United Farmers of Alberta in November last.

speechtext:
The hon. member is quite
right. I should have said to the Privy Council of Canada. The position is that by reason of that decision of the Supreme Court of Canada the Crowsnest pass agreement has only a restricted application, and the result is a certain amount of rate chaos and rate discrimination in all parts of Canada. I am satisfied the government must take action in the matter. I trust the government will take no action which will eliminate this Crowsnest pass agreement as a rate-controlling safeguard to the people of western Canada. I think the people of eastern Canada do not realize the significance of that agreement. That agreement arose primarily because, while other parts of Canada had the benefits of water competition, thereby keeping their rates down to a minimum, western Canada, by reason of its geographical position has no such safeguard. Suppose there is a railway deficit and no maximum rate controlling agreement such as the Crowsnest pass agreement, such deficit can only be collected in rates from western Canada. In other words any deficit of the Canadian National Railways could only be made good by the people of western Canada. Now we do not want that. We want to pay our fair share, we pay now some fifteen per cent increase in the rates imposed on eastern Canada. We do not vrant, in addition, to have piled on to that, for the purpose of making our railways show a balance, any deficit that accumulates from year to year.
May I, just in conclusion, suggest that to the appeal for unity in this country, certainly I for one as a Canadian will not turn a deaf ear. We have great difficulties. We have diversities, not only in economic conditions, but in our people. We have racial differences, religious differences. It is urgent, and vitally important, that every effort should be made to weld a real nationality out of Canada as it exists to-day. Ours is a country struggling against the facts of geography; and unless we are prepared to do our part in seeking and furthering all proper plans or suggestions by which we can preserve unity, this country has a very sad future. As a Canadian I have always objected to and will continue to protest against the suggestion of secession in this country. In western Canada there are, from time to time, suggestions of that kind, and I think they should be frowned upon, not only because they are impossible of accomplishment but also because the last state would be worse than the first. This would, without question, divide the country and make impossible of success the result that we should achieve, make impossible the achievement for this country of the destiny which, I am sure, we all hope for and desire. No mere Hudson Bay railway will solve the problems of Canada. I for one quite frankly am against the Hudson Bay railway proposal. I am satisfied the people of western Canada are not a unit at all in connection with that project. I know, in the province from which I come, by reason of the opening up and development of the Vancouver route not nearly as much interest is taken in it as in other days. But this is not a plan which will solve our problems. We require the closest studentship into the great economic difficulties that surround us if we hope ultimately to secure unity, and after all political unity can be based only upon economic solidarity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker much has been said respecting the budget; it has been many times criticized and attempts have been made to uphold it. I will not take up the time of the House over it except to say that, with conditions as they have been in Canada during the past twelve months, with well-managed business houses closing their books, year after year, with a loss, is it reasonable to suppose that the business of this government, or any government, managed in an unbusiness-like way, can show a profit? -to have a surplus-I do not believe the budget, as presented to this House, represents the actual financial state of the country.
In my address before this House last session, I deplored the situation in relation to the Maritime provinces, especially regarding Nova Scotia, and I expressed the hope that some stepd might be taken by the government to discover causes and apply remedies. I hoped that my colleagues representing that province would exert themselves to disclose reasons for the depression now existing amongst us, and endeavour to improve conditions. Further, I referred to the fact that I had lived in a preconfederation period and have had personal experience of the results which have come to the province since the formation of the union. I was speaking with knowledge. I speak now with knowledge. Impressed by that knowledge, after laying the case as fairly as I could before the government and parliament, I said this:
I implore the government to rectify the grievances. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and the country, that early action is imperative. I warn you that failure will bring us all to regret, if not to disaster.
Now, after a year is passed, I ask myself if anything has been done by the government of the day to rectify the grievances which I referred to; or to insipre the people of the province of Nova Scotia with confidence in the government; or to decrease discontent and distrust, and to increase buoyancy of spirits and contentment. I am forced to say that con-

ditions are worse to-day than they were a year ago, and that the government has not taken any heed of the warnings I venture to give them.
I realize that the government has proposed a change in the tariff on coal. This is being reluctantly done after persistent representations were made to them. But it is a small measure of the justice which the province of Nova Scotia demands-which it justifiably demands-and which it should be receiving at the hands of the government.
At the time representations were made to the government in regard to the coal duties, the need of tariff assistance for the Nova Scotia steel industry was just as strongly urged upon them. But nothing is being done for it. The argument for the one is just as powerful as the argument for the other. Why, I ask, is the province being put off again with a pittance instead of substantial justice? It is a well known fact that the government's tariff changes of 1924 militated seriously against the stability and progress of the Nova Scotia steel industry. Certain of its products were the raw materials of other industrial plants in central Canada. These plants were the only markets of the Nova Scotia steel industry for such products. This government deliberately took those markets from the Nova Scotia steel industry. They did that by tariff changes which permitted the plants in central Canada to import, free of duty, products of the classes I refer to, for the purposes of their manufacturing business; and worse still, they enlarged the classes of plants which might thus import such products free of duty. This action of the government was a telling blow at the Nova Scotia steel industry. It deprived that industry of markets. It forced that industry partially to close its doors. Its men were laid off. The injury extended to the coal mining industry. The quantity of coal used in the steel plants was substantially reduced. Men who work in the mines were thrown out of employment, or put on short time. In brief, the government's decision to let foreign steel makers supply the products which should be made in Nova Scotia, and foreign labour do the work which should be done by Nova Scotia labour, contributed largely to the industrial debacle which is now being witnessed in eastern Nova Scotia and which is palsying the whole economic life of this province. When representative men a few weeks ago presented these matters to the government, and besought them to deal fairly with those two fundamental and vital industries of Nova

The Budget-Mr. Black (Halifax)
Scotia, coal and steel, the government grudgingly agreed to make a small concession to Nova Scotia in regard to coal, but turned a deaf ear to the equally convincing argument for justice in regard to the steel industry.
This government is pursuing the fetish of low cost of living as if it were a thing of substance. It is only an incident of existing conditions. Low cost of living is the evidence of few opportunities. Higher cost of living is the evidence of many opportunities. Of what advantage, might I ask, could cheap living be to the men of the coal mining industry and their families in eastern Nova Scotia when they are unable to obtain employment and earn wages? Give them steady work and good wages and they would never be heard grumbling about high cost of living. The government magnifies this fetish into a creed, apparently thinking that the acme of contentment would be reached if everything were cheap. How can everything be cheap unless wages be lowered, and people be willing to adopt primitive methods of living? Shall we emulate the nationalities that are contented to live in squalid conditions, whose spirituality finds no expression in the comforts and accompaniments of modern life as we would have it in our own country, in order that Canada may be advertised as a cheap country? I say, Mr. Speaker, that the government's policy in this regard is founded in error, and stupidly persisted in. Let prices go up, let wages go up, let opportunities increase, let prosperity grow. These things are all incidents one of the other. It is infinitely better to have a country so conditioned, than one in which a man can live cheaply, but find himself in a dead environment.

I assure you, Mr Speaker, and the hon. gentleman who has interrupted me, that I am merely following some extended notes as did the hon. gentleman, Mr. Archambault, when addressing the house two days ago. There has been a great deal of discussion in which the issue has been the state .of the country in general. On the government side, reams of figures have been put into Hansard to prove that Canada is prosperous. I may say that these figures do not prove anything. We have only to look around and see with our own eyes and know that the figures do not truly testify. If this great mass of statistics were collected and published in .one massive volume, and were placed in the hands of the people of Nova Scotia, not one mind would be convinced by them. The people would not be convinced because they know by personal experience and through personal knowledge that Nova Scotia was never, in all of its history, passing through such a gruelling period of depression as it is suffering to-day. Yet this government thinks to make Nova Scotians believe that they are really in a golden era; and that that golden era is the product of the wisdom and activity of the government. When Nova Scotians ask for bread they are handed a stone. When they ask for redress of grievances and the granting of a fair measure of justice in accordance with the undertakings given at the time of confederation and since then, they are supplied with volumes of figures, and are told tc study those figures and be satisfied that the government of the day is providing bountifully for them, and have bestowed' upon them prosperity such as they never enjoyed.
It is a tragedy in history that there should be in control of the affairs of this country a government so blind to facts, and so impervious to the force of reason, and deaf to the

The Budget-Mr. Black (Halifax)
calls of justice, as is the government now in office in Canada.
I shall) not repeat what has been often well said in regard' to the understandings and agreements which were corner-stones in the union of the provinces in 1867; which understandings and agreements, Nova Scotia claims have not been faithfully lived up to; dn respect to which Nova Scotia claims redress. These matters have been fully set before the governments of the dominions. But the people of the province are stall forced to wait for a square deal.
Let me remind the House further of that other later period of history, pregnant with interest to Nova Scotia, when the government of the day assisted the great ventures of constructing second and third transcontinental lines of railway at enormous cost. We in the Maritime provinces were again given pledges by the government. We were invited to support the government's pdlicy, with the assurance that it would mean the inauguration of national transportation on Canadian territory and through Canadian ports. Our country was to be freed from the domination in commerce and transportation of the neighboring republic. The Maritime provinces were to reap the direct and fructifying fruits of this national (policy. At last some justice was to be accorded to them. This is one of the pledges given in 1903 by Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, now Finance Minister whose continued) illness, I, in common with other hon. members, deplore:
Surely, Sir, the time has come after years of deception, humbugging and trickery about the lines of the Maritime provinces, that faith should be kept with these people, and they should have a through line running on Canadian territory from ocean to ocean.
I might refer to the national pledges which the then Prime Minister, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and his government gave to the people, speaking in the House on July 30, 1903. On one occasion he said:
Now, Sir, we lay it down as a principle, upon which we are to be judged by friend and foe, that we are to have a transcontinental railway, and that its terminus must be in Canadian waters, and that the whole line, every inch of it, must be in Canadian territory. We say further, that such a line is a necessity to our commercial independence.

I will quote again, Sir, from the speech of Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the occasion referred to. This is what he said:
Now, there is another feature of this contract to which I shall call the attention of the House. If we have gone into this contract, our intention has been, 
as stated in the preamble, to force traffic in Canadian channels and through Canadian waters. We have made it a special condition of the contract and this condition is expressed in section 42, as follows.
The section referred to, paragraph 42, reads as follows:
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and thip transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agree that all freight originating on .the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ports.
Paragraph 43 emphasizes that. It says:
The company further agrees that it shall not, in any matter within its power, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those provided above, but shall in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted, namely the development of trade through Canadian ocean ports and Canadian channels.
These two sections have been a dead letter since they were written twenty-two years ago. Again, in 1911 when the 'Canadian Northern Ontario railway was seeking assistance, we had this provision in the legislation granting that assistance:
It is hereby declared that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government for the express purpose of encouraging the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.
Then again in 1914, when that same railway was applying to parliament for $45,000,000, we had this declaration:
That at all times hereafter all freight originating on the lines of the Canadian Northern Railway, or on the lines of any of the constituent companies, or on any line or lines of railway now or hereafter owned, leased or operated by the Canadian Northern, or by any of the constituent or subsidiary companies, their successors or assigns, shall, when destined to points in Canada, be carried over the lines of the Canadian Northern or of the constituent companies, or over some other Canadian railway or railways (which term shall include the line operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company between Montreal and St. John, N.B.) and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall not be greater via Canadian ports than it would be via United States ports; and that all inward and outward ocean traffic shall be carried to Canadian ports, and that the Canadian Northern and the several constituent and subsidiary companies shall not, in any matter within their power or control, directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of any such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall in all respects, in good faith, use their utmost endeavours to further the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ports.

The Budget-Mr. Black (Halifax)
I have not taken the time to read these paragraphs in their entirety, but with the permission of the House I would ask that they be placed on Hansard.
Again I would quote from the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, as follows:
With this road built, instead of being dependent on the Canadian Pacific Railway only, St. John will have two strings to its bow. Not a pound of traffic that goes to St. John now will be taken away, and St. John will stand its chance of getting a fair share of the new traffic to be created by this road. Halifax with its peerless harbour will have advantages which it has not hitherto enjoyed. Surely, Sir, the time has come after years of deception, humbugging and trickery about the lines to the Maritime Provinces, that faith should be kept with these people, and they should have a through line running on Canadian territory from ocean to ocean.
What, may I ask, is the faith that was to be kept ; and how has it been kept? While these assurances were being given out by the leaders I have mentioned, in another place, the Hon. Mr. Scott, cabinet minister in the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was explaining the situation in these words:
Therefore, it is to our interest if we are going to have that grain go east through Halifax and ports along the St. Lawrence, to do something to induce it to go there.
It goes without saying that Nova Scotia has contributed its full share to all public works in Canada. But let us consider her position in this matter. The Maritime provinces' portion of the cost of railways and canals since confederation amounts to the huge sum of $304,745,338. Nova Scotia, having a population of a little less than one-half of the three provinces, pays, $152,372,669, or say, $150,000,000, which is equal, in round figures, to 2| millions annually. What has Nova Scotia in return for this huge expenditure? Not a foot of transcontinental railway was ever built in the province-not a canal.

Public buildings cost Nova Scotians about $150,000 annually, over and above income. Under such conditions as these, can the government of Canada ignore the demands of the Maritimes, especially those of Nova Scotia? But, Mr. Speaker, faith has not been kept. The railways have been built. First the Intercolonial railway, which was to be the special agency
for the development of the Maritime provinces by providing those provinces the means of reaching the markets of central Canada. Later the railways sponsored in 1903 were built for the purposes mentioned by the leaders of the country whom I mentioned. But instead of helping developing the Maritime provinces, instead of helping them and making them prosperous; they have been converted into agencies for the depression of those provinces. They have become millstones around the necks of the Maritime provinces. They have imposed freight rates which deny Maritime people access to the markets that were warranted to them in the days of nation building. Listen while I read the language of Premier Armstrong in regard to this matter:
The remedy for this condition undoubtedly lies in a Canadian-wide appreciation of Maritime disability, and a general realization that excessive freight rates are choking out our industrial life.
I do not preach sectionalism; such is inadvisable, in fact deplorable.
Nova Scotians are not suppliants. They ask that pledges be carried out. A policy is what they want which will benefit all sections of the country. This government has no policy that benefits any section of our Dominion.
The question of freight rates is a burning one with Nova Scotians. So exorbitant are these rates that traffic is being handled daily by other means. I give one instance:	The
freight rate on brick, less than car-loads, from Pugwash to Dorchester, is one and a half times greater than the cost of the brick. I read this morning that sugar is being Shipped from the Halifax and St. John refineries to Montreal by water-the freight and charges being less than if shipped by rail.
Western shippers complain of ocean freight rates when they reach 10 per cent of the value of the article shipped; what would they say if the rates were from 50 to 150 per cent of the value of their products?
In addition to this, the 5 per cent sales tax is a serious handicap on basic commodities used in the building trades.	*
As to the promises of 1903, not a vestige of satisfaction has been awarded to the people of Nova Scotia. The keeping of faith is still a mere figure of speech. And the grain spoken of by Hon. Mr. Scott has been pouring out through foreign ports without regard to promises made or the vital necessity of building up Canadian commerce on Canadian territory, and doing at least some of the "forcing" through Canadian ports, which Sir Wilfrid Laurier so vividly portrayed and pledged the country to see done.
