The Budget-Mr. Black (Halifax)
I do not overlook the fact that after prolonged electioneering dodging, a contract is at last let for the construction of a small grain elevator at Halifax. The government evaded its election promises in this regard as long as it could, and only took steps to have the promises made good, -in part after it was driven out of every hole of retreat. This, again, is but a slight instalment of the "good faith" promised to Nova Scotia over twenty years ago. It will not go very far towards restoring the province to its rightful place in the Canadian confederation. The government cannot excuse themselves by asserting that they do not possess understanding of the minds of the people of my province and the other Maritime provinces. It is well known that the Premier of Nova Scotia has been at Ottawa on several occasions, and that he brought back with him alleged glittering assurances from the government there. These have proved to be entirely made of tinsel, which quickly fades. If Premier Armstrong truly reported what was said to him by the Prime Minister and others of his cabinet, we are again forced to the conclusion that good faith is not being kept.
Twelve months ago, after the duty on fertilizer was reduced, a factory in Halifax closed down. The buildings are now vacant, and the machinery idle. This factory gave employment to a number of men, nearly all of whom supported families; to-day they are probably with the tens of thousands across the line, to the south of us. This factory was a further benefit to Halifax, because the company imported cargoes of raw material, such as phosphate rock, bones, and so forth, and the vessels which brought these cargoes disbursed large sums of money in the port-pilotage, for instance, hospital dues, port wardens' fees, tug-boat charges, wages earned by longshoremen in the discharging and storing of the cargoes, insurance thereon; furthermore, each of the members of the crew of the vessel, from the captain down, receives the wages due him, or at least a portion thereof, a portion at least of which is spent amongst the shopkeepers of the city. The vessel is provisioned for her next voyage and buys more or less paint, rope, canvas, and so forth, possibly going into dry-dock. Quite a large sum of money is disbursed in this operation which is now lost to our longshoremen, shop-keepers and others. This is a concrete instance of the value of one small industry to a community. After the closing of this factory, what did I find? Belgian fertilizer was imported and advertised, and as evidence, I could exhibit an advertisement, a whole page nearly, in large

attractive letters and form. Details of this kind are, perhaps, not often given in this House, Mr. Speaker, but I look upon these cases as a striking result of free trade policy in this country, and worthy of mention.
A similar factory in Sydney, was also closed down.
Now a word as to immigration. The Mari-times have not even been thought of, or mentioned, in this connection. They have no status in the Immigration department of this government. A suggestion was made to that department that half a dozen families of Hebrideans out of several hundred reported coming to Canada this spring be located in Nova Scotia, but the idea was pooh-poohed; all these people were wanted out west. Yet out of the two hundred and one-third millions of dollars spent on immigration by Canada, Nova Scotia contributed $400,000 of this amount, without a family being located in that province.
National Parks receive liberal federal aid, about $2,763,000 having been spent on such parks throughout the entire country, but the Maritime portion is insignificant.
I submit, Sir, that the Mari times are a valuable asset to Canada, contributing as they do so generously to the finance of this country, and possessing such exceptional and diversified natural resources, but apparently no place have they in the minds of this government.
Owing largely to the immigration policy of the United States, the number of steamers calling at Halifax has considerably increased. The dock facilities are insufficient, and these steamers are delayed in consequence on account of the incomplete wharf and shed accommodation at the new terminals, and although the department of the government responsible for this work has been repeatedly appealed to for completion of these different works, nothing has been done. Again is Nova Scotia ignored, as she is in so many other instances.

Very recently, however, as this House knows, a very large delegation of Maritime province men came to Ottawa to interview the government and the members of parliament; and to lay before them the case of those provinces. I am speaking in the hearing of honourable gentlemen who saw and heard this delegation; and I can safely leave it to them to say whether or not that delegation presented a powerful argument on behalf of the Maritime provinces. I am satisfied that they did; and that what was said shows conclusively that if this country is to make the progress which we all, as good Canadians, desire, measures must be adopted to wipe out the discontent which prevails in those provinces, and to give the people substantial reason for believing that they are not to be further treated with disdain. This feeling, I regret to say, prevails. I can call Premier Armstrong to witness on the point. In April, 1923, an interview with him was published in a Montreal newspaper, and he expressed himself as follows:
While dismissing any ideas of secession, however, the Premier pointed out that the people of the Maritime provinces felt keenly that they have not been fairly treated by the rest of the Dominion. They have been made to feel, he said, that they are and should remain isolated, more or less forgotten, tolerated at the best and not provided for like the more fortunate provinces to the west.
I commend these sentiments to the earnest consideration of the government. They should convince the government that the utterances of the Maritime provinces are not the catchpenny cries of a few partisans; but are the expressions of sincere convictions of the whole people. And I remind the government that it is disastrous to the whole country to have any parts of Canada imbued with the conviction that justice is not being done.
What I have just said is emphasized by the stand which the government of Nova Scotia is now taking in regard to what are deemed to be the wrongs and the rights of the province. Premier Armstrong has submitted to the legislature a series of resolutions in which he sets out these wrongs and rights as his government sees them. It is unnecesary for me to say whether I concur in all of his views. For the purposes of my argument it is sufficient to state that the government of the province, now confronted with general elections which must be held within a few weeks, is forced by existing conditions to agonize
over the distressful state of the province, and to appeal to the government of the Dominion and this parliament for the square deal which has been so long denied. It may be true that Premier Armstrong is taking this action because his government has lost the confidence of the people, and he hopes by these means to win back that confidence. The fact remains that the people are dissatisfied and discontented, that the province is not making progress, that the outlook is discouraging, and that the blame is largely placed on the shoulders of the Dominion government for neglecting to recognize the just claims of the province.
This is how the people are thinking; and it is vitally necessary to eliminate this conviction from their minds, if it be desired to have contented Maritime provinces and a united Canada. Hon. members will see that I am not exaggerating. The final proof, if any more were needed, is expressed in the attitude of the Armstrong government, the friends of the government of the Dominion. The Armstrong government would not assume the attitude I have described if thev did not feel themselves forced into the position by the overwhelming power of public conviction in the province, and their own impending destruction.
Nova Scotians are still crossing the line- the best blood of the country, skilled in all departments of work-in order that they earn a livelihood. It is said that there are more Nova Scotians in Massachusetts and the New England states than in the province itself.
I,	at times, picture our fair province with all these native born at home-Halifax, a city of 150,000 and all other parts of the country doubled or more in population. What a bee hive we would have. What numbers to feed, clothe, and so on. But alas! Industries are closed, markets are unreachable, and on all hands there is idleness.
In conclusion, therefore, I again entreat the government of the day to give heed to the warnings that come from Nova Scotia. I repeat what I said last year, that early action is imperative. I repeat the warning, that failure will bring us all regret, if not disaster.

I intend on this occasion to make a plea for economy, as I have done on previous occasions in this House. Hon. members have discussed the same question; in fact there have been pleas for economy from all sections of the chamber. But the truth is, Mr. Speaker, that we prate about economy and forget the very first principle involved in it, and that is to spend less money. I am going to make the charge that this government have failed to adopt any real policy of genuine economy, notwithstanding the excellent speech delivered by the Prime Minister to-night. He told us that we had a surplus of $11,000,000 over ordinary expenditure this year, but he admits that there was an increase in the public debt of between two and three million dollars. It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, even with my imperfect knowledge of book-keeping, that we are still in the hole, and that we have cause to worry yet. I intend to prove that this government have not enforced a policy of economy to the satisfaction of the people who have to pay the bill if not to the satisfaction of the government itself. Can I not say in truth, Mr. Speaker, that every revision of the salaries of the public servants of this country since this government came into power has been a revision upwards? Can I not say that this government have found offices for a group of favorites? In this connection I might mention Mr. Duncan Marshall, and Hon. Dr. Pugslev now deceased, not forgetting W. T. R. Preston. In 1924 it had grown to $121,905, an increase of $9,978. The Paris agency in 1923 cost $29,942, in 1924 $31,065, an increase of $1,123.
The Canadian representative in the United States in 1923 cost $10,994; in 1924, $13,008, an increase of $2,014.

I see there are travelling expenses in connection with the high commissioner's office, notwithstanding the fact that he is drawing a salary of $10,000 a year and $5,000 in lieu of house and furniture. I see he has a travelling account in 1922 of $2,913, in 1923 a travelling account of $4,168 and in 1924 of $5,265. In the Paris agency we have a man by the name of Philippe Roy. There are those who think it is a protectionist budget; there are those who think it is getting somewhere near a free trade budget; and there are those who think it is a moderate budget. have got the facts, without letting them know what we are going to do. They have gone into that country about three hundred miles back from a railway, and have freighted their supplies in there for the first few years. During the last few years most of the men hauling out wheat have been hauling it out over trails from thirty to forty miles long. They have been doing that in the hope that something better was coming, and I think it is only fair that the government with the facte in its possession should come out definitely and state its policy, whether it intends to do anything or not.

That is a

The real question back of this whole business is this, whether this Peace river country is

M-. ROBERT GARDINER (Medicine Hat):	I recognize the fact that this debate
has been continued to an extensive length, but notwithstanding that fact, Mr. Speaker, and the fact that it is almost breakfast time, I 173
still feel it is my duty to make some remarks upon the budget, even at this early hour of the morning. So far as I am personally concerned,
I am very greatly disappointed at the budget. After the government last year made some slight reductions I had hoped personally that they would continue along those lines and that this year we would get some substantial reductions that would be really worth while; but unfortunately the government have not seen fit to give us' any reductions worth mentioning. Since this House met in session this year I believe the Prime Minister has made the statement that the reductions made last year have been a great success, but he has also made the statement that notwithstanding the fact that he recognized that those reductions were a great success, we must still pause to see how much this success really amounts to. One would naturally think that when a person or a government had been successful in any line of endeavour they would continue upon that line and reach a greater success, but that does not seem to be a propensity of this particular government, and under those circumstances naturally we feel very much disappointed. I quite recognize the fact, Sir, that the protectionists in Canada are very active in pressing their demands. They can readily mobilize, they can get the ear of the government very quickly and press their demands to an ultimate conclusion. But there is one point to which I should like to draw the attention of our protectionist friends, and that is this: That while they claim they are entitled to the home market and claim also that because of the fact they are entitled to the home market they should receive such a protection as would ensure that home market for them; yet I have never heard any of the protectionists make any suggestion to put into effect a policy that while they control the prices, they would see to it that they do not take undue advantage of the protection Canada affords them. We also find our protectionist friends telling us that protection will provide employment and good wages for our workmen. This seems to be a somewhat ridiculous claim, because if you will look the world over you will find that in some of the highest protection countries in the world they have the greatest unemployment, and furthermore, if we ever go to free trade England, we find they have unemployment there, and consequently it does not seem that the question of protection or free trade is a great factor in providing employment for the people of the various countries. There is one point that always appeals to me when I hear our protectionist friends discussing the question of adequate protection, and that is this: That in my judgment pro-



The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
tection has absolutely failed to protect the purchasing power of the people in Canada. And in my judgment I believe also that the question of the purchasing power of the people of Canada is a bigger factor to-day than the question of protection or free, trade is. At the .present time naturally we pay some attention to the question of the purchasing power and the distribution of that purchasing power, and I am satisfied that our industries will never meet with the success that they should until this problem is solved. We find also our protectionist friends pointing to the United States and telling us what a great success protection has been in that country. They maintain that conditions in the United States at the present time have been brought about by the extraordinarily high protection that the United States affords to its manufacturers, and when the Speech from the Throne was being discuss.ed on February 10, 1925, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), in referring to the United States, made the following statement :
And with a 4,000-mile boundary and a tariff three times as high as ours.
In the first place the hon. gentleman's imagination runs away with him when he mentions the boundary line between Canada and the United States, but when he mentions the question of the tariff being three times higher in the United States than in Canada his imagination goes out of bounds altogether, and I propose to give to the House to-night the actual figures in that regard. I desire to give the House and to place on Hansard a comparative statement, in so far as the United States of America and Canada are concerned. The first item that I want to bring before the House is the duty collected in both of these countries. In Canada in the year 1921 there was collected a total duty of $179,667,683. The population at that time was 8,788,483. That meant a per capita duty collected in Canada for that year of $20.44. In the United States for the same year the per capita duty collected was only $2.86. In the year 1924 the per capita duty collected in Canada was $14.65 and in the United States only $4.86.
I have another table here which is very important and interesting and which deals with the average rate of duty on dutiable imports. In the year 1921, the average rate of duty on dutiable imports was 21.20 per cent in Canada and 20.30 per cent in the United States. Therefore, hon. members will notice that the average rate of duty collected on dutiable imports in that particular year was greater in Canada than in the United States. When we come to the year 1924, we find conditions somewhat changed, but this is applicable only to last year's business. In 1924, the average rate of duty collected in Canada was 22.85 per cent and in the United States it rose to 35.51 per cent. Another point with regard to these duties as between Canada and the United States and which we must recognize, because it is very important, is the average rate of duty on total imports. That includes the free, of course, as well as the dutiable imports. In 1921, the average rate of duty on the total imports into Canada was 14.49 per cent, and on the total imports into the United States it was only 8.43 per cent. In 1924, the average rate of duty on total imports into Canada had risen to 15.13 per cent, and on total imports into the United States it had risen to 15.33 per cent. That means to say that the average rate of duty collected in the United States last year was only .20 per cent higher than the average rate of duty collected in Canada. That, of course, leads us to believe that, while on certain imports going into the United States, the rate of duty is much higher than the duty on goods going into Canada, the United States has a much larger free list than we have in Canada, and the tax payers of the United States are, to all intents and purposes, rot paying much higher import duties on the average imports into that country than we are doing in Canada. Therefore, when our protectionist friends point to the United States as an example of prosperity, we must believe there is some other factor connected with their prosperity that is not within the scope of the protective tariff. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) brought down an amendment to the Dumping Act. As already stated in the House on more than one occasion, the minister proposes to withdraw this amende ment and allow the act to stand as it is at the present time. While personally I believe in the greatest freedom of trade that we can possibly get in this country, I am just as satisfied of the fact that so long as this Dumping Act remains on the statutes it will be idle for the people to think that they are getting any reductions even when such reductions have ostensibly been made. So long as the [Mr. R. Ciardiaer.l
department has the opportunity of enforcing the Dumping Act just as they see fit then I am satisfied that any reductions that are made in the duties will be of very little avail.
I am not of course in the con-5 a.m. fidence of the Acting Minister of
Finance and consequently I do not know what reason he would have for withdrawing the amendment to the Dumping Act. Possibly some pressure may have been brought to bear upon him; but whatever the reason may be I feel satisfied that he is doing the right thing in withdrawing it and I should be still further satisfied if the Dumping Act were put in such shape that it could not be applied by the officers of the department as they saw fit or to suit their particular mood.
The government proposes to establish a tariff board, or rather to employ certain men fn the departments to go into the whole question as to whether it is desirable to raise or .lower the tariff as the case may be, as circumstances warrant. There is just one point I want to raise in this connection and that is this:	if these employees of the different departments are merely to keep the information to themselves or give it only to the Minister of Finance or the government, then the tariff board will be of very little use to the people of the country. I maintain that so long as there are employees of this description in the service of the people, and so long as they are paid to perform a certain duty, which in this case would be the securing of information, the members of this House should be just as much entitled to that information as any member of the government; and I shall never be satisfied, if we are to get justice in this regard, unless the information is forthcoming from time to time. It is quite tine of course that the protective tariff is very advantageous to the manufacturing industries of Canada. But how does it affect the agricultural industry, which after all is a highly important one? Many hon. members seem to forget the importance of that particular industry, and we must therefore examine the situation to see how protection affects the farmer. It may be true that in some few cases of no great importance the farmer may derive some benefit from certain protective duties. But I am satisfied that in the long run the Canadian farmer has to bear the brunt of the protective system, -which can be so manipulated that eventually the burden will rest upon the shoulders of the agricultural community. They are the ones who have to bear the largest portion of the protective tariff.
I have said that agriculture is a very important industry in this country and I am going to quote a few figures from the De-

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
partment of Customs and Excise, being a summary of the Canadian trade for the twelve months ending March 1925. The total exports from Canada last year amounted to $1,069,067,353, while the export of agricultural products totalled $606,330,292, the exports of all other products being $452,737,061. In other words, the agricultural exports of Canada last year were in excess of all other exports to the extent of $143,593,231. So that the percentage of agricultural exports, in relation to the total exports from this country last year, was 56 per cent. Of course, some of these agricultural exports were partly manufactured, and that added to their value. Nevertheless we must recognize that those products have their origin on the farms of Canada, and just so long as agriculture is responsible for the exportation of such a large volume of commodities in comparison with all other commodities produced in Canada, then it is only fair that agriculture should be given due consideration. But when we come to consider the tariff duties in force in this country I can say very emphatically that agriculture has never been given the consideration it should have received.
I wish to refer for a few moments to the conditions of western agriculture, because that is primarily what I am interested in. I think it can be stated that, taking it by and large, the farmers of western Canada are producing at a loss. Just what the extent of that loss may be it is very hard to determine. I am aware, of course, that in certain favoured districts during the last year where they had the good fortune to have heavy grain crops, some of the farmers-and the phenomenal rise in the price of grain was also an important factor -did very well. But we cannot deal with isolated localities; we must deal with average conditions, and I believe we are justified in saying that on the. average the grain crops of Canada last year were produced at a loss.
So far as the constituency I have the honour to represent is concerned, I would like to direct attention to the conditions in that part of the province. True, they have similar conditions in other parts of the province. This land was thrown open for settlement about 1908 or 1909. It was advertised to the world as land fit for settlement, capable of producing good crops, grain, fodder and so forth. While it is true that the first few years we were in there the conditions were fairly good, in recent years the land has not been as good for agricultural purposes as we anticipated, and as we were led to believe. Before this land was thrown open for settlement I understand that the officers of the Department of the Interior used all the persuasive powers they could exert upon the minister to advise him against the opening up of this section of country on the ground that it was not first-class agricultural land. Remembering the fact, therefore, that the minister opened up this land against the advice of the officers of his department, we must hold the government responsible for the mess that that part of the country is in. I have travelled through practically the whole of my constituency during the last two years, and I can assure you that I have seen some heartrending scenes. For instance, last. fall I was on a trip and I went down to see some people -with whom I was fairly well acquainted. I found that they had left the district for good. This couple came from the United States after reading the advertisements sent out by the Department of Immigration. They have buildings on that place to-day that I will guarantee could not be built in these times for less than $20,000, and the investment they made in that property represented their entire saving of a lifetime. They are now an old couple, and last fall they left that district and the man went out to find a job. That is one of the isolated cases, and it is but representative of thousands of similar cases in that part of the country. The question that arises now is, what is the government going to do about it? The federal government cannot escape the responsibility, having invited those people there. Not only is there a large capital investment in the farms themselves, but there is a tremendous investment in the towns and vil-ages, so much so that the people in business there have been in the same unfortunate position as the farmer that is to say, they have lost everything they put into their business. I sincerely trust that the government will give some consideration to this question, because it affects a very large portion of the southeastern comer of southern Alberta as well as a portion of Saskatchewan. In justice to the people who are still there and desire to make, a living there, the government should endeavour to find out what this land is suitable? for and by what method those who are in that country can attain some measure of success'. I am satisfied that the land is good for something, but the people have not the means for carrying on experiments to find out what it is fitted for. I trust the government will lose no time in looking into the matter.

Now, the farmers of the west have been advised to go into mixed farming. The country I represent could go into mixed fanning because fodder corn can be grown there without any difficulty. But very few of the people know anything about the growing of corn, and if the government could give some lead in that respect, I am satisfied we could work out a system of agriculture that would be satisfactory in that district, and produce a tremendous volume of agricultural products. But when we attempt to go into mixed farming, when we attempt to milk cows for the cream and butter we can get, the government comes along and puts a tax on the tickets we use in that connection. During the last few days I have had more telegrams in regard to that matter than I have been able to read. The eastern farmer can deliver his own milk or cream to the factory, but in western Canada the factories are few and far between, and sometimes we have to ship our cream very long distances by express. That entails heavy expenditure to the farmer who is selling the cream, but on top of the express rates the government imposes this tax to which I have referred. I suggest that the government should give this matter also their attention and see if some remedy can be effected.
In my judgment the farmers of Canada are faced with many problems which are just as important as the tariff problems. I am satisfied of this fact, that while we might get substantial reductions in the tariff, which would be appreciated, at the same time those reductions would hardly begin to solve the problems that we farmers have to meet. If you take price levels say just prior to the war and compare them with price levels today, ;you will find that in so far as manufactured goods and services are concerned, the prices of manufactured goods to-day are much much higher than the prices of agricultural products, rand this has been the case for quite a few years. I feel that until such a time arrives as we can get price levels more equalized than they are to-day, agriculture is going to have a very strenuous time in Canada, and just so long as agriculture is having a strenuous time, industry in Canada may also expect to have a strenuous time.
The position the farmer is in is something like this. When the farmer has worked hard and produced some agricultural product, when that product is ready for the market he looks for a buyer. When he finds someone who is willing to buy his product, what is the question that he asks the buyer? It is this: What is the price you will pay me for this product? If the farmer sells his product and

gets the money for it, he no doubt goes to the general merchant to buy something that is required for the farm or the home, as the case may be, and when he sees what he requires in the store, what is the question that the farmer asks the storekeeper? It is this: What is the price? So that the farmer is in the imfortunate position that both when he sells and when he buys he has to ask that same question, what is the price? And just so long as the farmers are content to stay in that position, agriculture will never be prosperous. It is impossible for it to be prosperous under those circumstances. I will guarantee there is no business in Canada except farming that could exist for twelve months if it was placed in that same position the farmer is in of having to ask both when he buys and when he sells, what is the price?
That brings us, of course, to the problem, what are the farmers going to do under these circumstances? We have attempted in western Canada to do something to deal with this particular question. W e have organized our co-operative selling organizations for the purpose of the better marketing of the products of the farm. True, we have not them organized as extensively as we would like, but we are proceeding very satisfactorily, and I am hoping to see the day when these cooperative selling organizations will have in them every farmer in western Canada, in fact, every farmer in the whole Dominion. When that day arrives, Mr. Speaker, we can expect something worth while to happen, because when the farmer gets into that position where he will be selling co-operatively, instead of individually he will be in a very different position from what he has ever been in before in the history Of this country or of any other country in the world, for he will be in the position of having something to say as to the price of the commodity he has to sell. He will also have something to say as to the price he will pay for the commodities he has to buy. We will then be in a position to say to our manufacturing friends:	Now we will
exchange the products of the farm for the products of the factory on the basis of the units of labour contained in the various commodities, and on no other basis at all. I am satisfied of this fact, that to-day when the farmers of Canada exchange the products of the farm for the products of the factory they are giving at least five to six units of labour in exchange for manufactured products that probably contain only two and a half to three units of labour, and just so long as the farmers remain in that unfortunate position

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
those who have exploited them in the past, and who are to-day exploiting them, will continue to do so until the farmer in self-defence joins the co-operative selling organizations and does his selling co-operatively instead of individually. In my humble judgment there are greater possibilities so far as agriculture is concerned in these co-operative selling agencies than in almost any other thing I know of, and I am trusting and hoping to live to see the day when that idea will be brought to full fruition, because Mr. Speaker, I expect to enjoy a good laugh at the expense of our manufacturing friends, who have been exploiting us so handsomely and for so long.
I would like to give the House a little information with regard to the price of agricultural products, and to show to the House if I possibly can why it is that the purchasing power of the farmer to-day is to all intents and purposes gone, and why it is that industry also of course is beginning to feel the pinch as severely as it does at the present time. In the year 1918 the total value of agricultural products amounted to $1,881,718,000; in 1919, 82,109,291,000; in 1920, $2,011,201,000; 1921-and here you will note a tremendous drop from the previous year-$1,383,-95S.OOO; 1922, 81,389,289,000; 1923, $1,350,096,000; 1924, $1,453,388,000. Now if you examine those figures very closely you will find that the purchasing power of the farmer in 1924 as compared with the year 1920 dropped about
8700,000,000, and when you find the purchasing power of any class in this country drop to the extent of 8700,000,000 you can readily understand that all the other industries in Canada are going to feel the effect of that drop. That is the trouble that we find our farmers are up against to-day, and just so long as they lack purchasing power, just so long may we expect the privileged interest of Canada to come knocking at the doors of the government asking for higher protection in order that they may be able to get a little more profit if they possibly can. But that in itself is no solution. It will not solve the problems that we have to meet, and we will have to meet those problems in a different way and in a way that will be more equitable to all. We have heard a good deal of discussion since the budget was brought down as to just what is the national debt of Canada. It is very hard to find out just what that debt is. The experts that we have heard in this House all had different figures; and when we find that experts disagree we can hardly expect the ordinary member of parliament to be able to .determine what the actual debt of Canada is
at the present time. But the point I wish to make this morning is that we have a great national debt, growing a little it is true all the time. What are we doing to try and meet that national debt? No provision is being made at all for the liquidation of the national debt. We are making no provision for any sinking fund that I am aware of, nor in any other manner whatsoever, to meet the great burden that we have now upon our shoulders.
I am satisfied of this fact, however, that the people of Canada are expecting this government, or some government, to start and look into this question of trying to meet our national debt and doing so at the very earliest opportunity.

From time to time we hear a good deal of talk about secession from confederation in Canada. This is presumed to be heard in the Maritime provinces and also in the western provinces. Let me make my position very clear. I would be very loath indeed to see confederation broken up, and I would go a long way to try and retain it. But there is a point of view which must not be lost sight of, and it is this:	That people generally
speaking will only stand so much injustice, and when the pressure of injustice becomes too strong they will naturally resent it and take what means they have in hand to get away from that injustice. In so far as I am personally concerned, I have heard more talk about secession in the cities and towns of western Canada than I have in the rural districts. Now I think this is very unfortunate, but I would just like to place before the House the view that some of these people have placed before me, and they put it in this way: They say, " Suppose these nine provinces in Canada had no confederation at all, the provinces having full jurisdiction over their own affairs." And they go further and say, " Suppose the provinces of, say, Ontario and Quebec, came to the other seven provinces and said, 1 Here, let us have a confederation of these provinces and let us turn them into a Dominion.' These other seven provinces would naturally say ' All right, but under what terms do you propose to create this Dominion? ' " Now, Mr. Speaker, suppose these two provinces that I have already mentioned were to say, " These are our terms," and if they mentioned terms similar to those in existence at the present time, what do you suppose the other seven provinces would say to the two provinces? Do you presume for one moment that, say, the Maritime provinces and the three prairie provinces would accept, the conditions that we have imposed on us to-day and enter confederation on that basis? Why, the idea is simply ridiculous. If,

therefore, they would not enter confederation on the present basis, how can Canada expect to maintain confederation unless those disabilities are removed? I have stated already that I would like to see confederation kept intact, but with a full responsibility of what I say, I am just as satisfied, Mr. Speaker a3 that I am standing here this momiDg, that unless a little more serious consideration is given to the various needls of the several provinces of the different parts of Canada I am very much afraid for confederation.
We find our protectionist friends, as I have stated before, appealing to the government for higher duties. I do not think that higher duties would be of very much benefit to the industries of this country bemuse of the fact that during recent times we have had a new factor entering into the whole situation, and that new factor that we are up against is this: That industry in Canada to-day is controlled by finance, and the captains of industry are not to-day free to develop their industries as they would like to, and just so long as parliament is willing to allow industries of all descriptions, including agriculture, to remain under the throttling influence of finance, I am satisfied that neither industry nor agriculture will prosper. It is an impossibility. Now in what position do we find ourselves to-day in regard to the financial situation? First of all, let me say that parliament, either in its wisdom or otherwise, has turned over to private individuals for their own private profit the function of printing and putting into circulation money; and money in the final analysis should be used only as a medium of exchange. That is the prime function of money, but because of the supineness of governments in the past we find that the financiers of Canada, as of the world over, are not only using money as a medium of exchange, or putting into circulation as a medium. of exchange, but they also have turned it into a commodity, and because of the fact that they have turned it into a commodity and find a greater profit in buying and selling money as a commodity than they do using it purely as a medium of exchange, the circulating function of money has been made subservient to the commodity nature that the finaneies have incorporated into money. In the final analysis, the basis of the real credit of Canada rests upon the ability of the Canadian people to produce and deliver goods. That being the real basis of credit, and being ,also the real basis upon which our money comes info circulation, naturally those who are responsible for the creation of the real credit of Canada are in an almost hopeless condition when they desire to use some of the circulating medium for 'the purpose of their
business. I do not see any hope that the government will ever seriously tackle this situation. I do not think they will. But I am satisfied of this fact, that it will be tackled in a serious way in the very near future, not alone by those who are engaged in agriculture, but by those who are engaged in industry, that is if they want the industries to survive. When our industrialists in Canada realize -the position they are in at the present time because of the fact that our Canadian financiers control the circulating medium, and when they recognize how closely that control is identified with their success, I am satisfied that both industrialists and agriculturists will demand that we nationalize the money system in Canada. I am not going to say anymore about that to-night because I believe I have taken up my allotted time,.
I want, however, before I conclude, to pass a few remarks with regard to the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to-night. When he was speaking this evening, he adopted what, in my opinion, is a very peculiar attitude. In fact, if the rules would allow me, I would say that the Prime Minister adopted a very childish attitude, but if the rules of the House will not allow me to say that, I will not say it. The Prime Minister to-night thought it was quite within his privilege to lecture the Progressive members in this House 'and those who sit close by them. When I was nominated to contest the seat that I now have the honour to represent, there was a very distinct understanding as to my attitude in this House, and that distinct understanding was that I should not be guilty of engaging in political bargaining. The attitude of the people who sent me here is this, that I am to consider the measures that come before the House and to use my judgment regarding those measures. If I feel those measures are in the interest of Canada as a whole they expect me to support them; but if I feel that any measure that comes before the House is not in the interest of Canada as a whole, they expect me to oppose it. I do not propose to depart from that principle. Therefore, if the government requires my support at the present time, I shall be only too glad to give that support when I deem that the measure is one in the interest of Canada as a whole. That is the only basis upon which they can ever receive my support. It ilhbecomes the Prime Minister of this country to suggest even the possibility of political bargaining, and I was very sorry to hear him make the statement that he did to-night.

In part II, Professor Viner treats of the adjustment of the general price level and of the currency and banking systems of Canada to the above-mentioned heavy importations of capitail. In other words, he shows how the capital represented in the adverse trade balance entered Canada in the form of goods. It is in this section that he has especially broken new ground, and if his treatment is still short of finality, he has organized materials and outlined a method that will be permanently valuable. His chapters on Canadian exchange and gold movements and on the operations of the Canadian banks in the adjustment of the trade balance are a clear exposition of a process that is popularly but little understood even in Canada, especially in its theoretic aspect. The gold movement into and from Canada is a matter wholly of banking and currency, the cash reserves of the banks and the government reserves against Dominion notes being its leading index.
Now, what I wanted to do in this connection was to direct the attention of the ex-Minister of Finance, who unfortunately is not here, and the attention of members of the House, to what I regard as the proper way of approaching the discussion of problems of this sort. In this connection I should like to again express my appreciation of the valuable services of our Dominion Statistician. I would like to know who is obstructing just now. Mr. Speaker, I think that the problems confronting the Canadian people at the present time are very serious indeed, and after being here four years I must 'confess to a sense of deep disappointment at the method of approach to our serious problems. I want to say a word or two in that connection before I deal with the main topic of my remarks.
I am tempted, Mr. Speaker, to refer to an incident that occurred in my own experience when I was younger than I am now, 'and which I think illustrates the situation very well. I beg to assure you that the incident I shall narrate is absolutely authentic and accurate. There was in our neighbourhood when I was a young man an old man who used to do odd jobs around the countryside, and he frequently worked for my father, particularly in the fall of the year. I remember on one occasion we had a cow in the stable that was ailing somewhat, and I took the old man in to seek his advice. I thought perhaps he might give some suggestion as to what ought to be done for the cow. As soon as he had seen the animal he Stated with the utmost assurance that he knew the

The Budget-Mr. Good
disease very well. It was " hollow horn and wolf in the tail." I am not inventing the story; it is an actual fact. He said, "I can cure it. Get me some pepper and salt." I got him some pepper and salt, and he mixed them together, and then taking out his jack-nife cut a slit in the skin of the tail, and opening the skin up a little inserted the pepper and salt, and then closed up the wound. He told me with the utmost assurance and with the utmost confidence and sincerity that that was the cure for that particular disease, and that I need not worry about the outcome. Well now, Mr. Speaker,
I must confess to the feeling that we are dealing with an ailing Canadian economic life pretty much as the old man dealt with that cow, and I suggest the propriety of altering our attitude of mind and our methods towards a number of these problems that are vexing and worrying us, and which, unless we solve them, are going to bring us to catastrophe. In particular, I want to say that I deplore the party spirit and party politics 'as 'I see them exhibited in this House. So	far	as	the	consumptionof time goes,	so	far	as futilityand aimless effort goes, I attribute a great deal to what may disgust the House and may disgust the country to the prevalence of partisanship. I am told that the House now is better than	it used to	be;	I	do not knowas to that but	I do	think	and	I	want to submit now that if we could cast our party affiliations to the winds and get down to study questions on their merits and vote on them on their merits, regardless of who makes the suggestions, regardless of what is the attitude of this party or of that, we would be nearer a solution of our difficulties than we are at the present time. Here we have a party in power,-so-called " in power "-facing an election in the near future, and a party in opposition facing an election. So far as I am concerned I confess to a disbelief in the whole theory of partisan government. That is my growing conviction from observation in this House. I may be all wrong. I am not going into the question of constitutional methods now. I may deal with that question in the future, but not now; but I do think there is a vast amount of useless party warfare- though perhaps interesting, entertaining- across the floor of this House, because we have one party in power and one in opposition, and the opposition wants to get into office, and the government wants to stay in. Now I submit in all seriousness, that there is the strongest possible temptation to subordinate the national welfare to the welfare of parties and of individuals under this system. I need
only point to the applause which greets a clever attack, daring thrusts, shrewd defence. It is easy enough to arouse the fighting spirit; everybody knows that. It is often inevitable. But I submit, it is rarely helpful in connection with matters of this sort. We develop a good deal of hysteria in connection with our public life, and particularly in connection with our party discussions, and I want to refer to a sample of it. I presume the members on the government side will applaud this, because it has to do with the official opposition. Here is a statement which was made by the right hon. leader of the opposition-
I wish he were here at the moment-published in the campaign literature of the Conservative party during the campaign of 1921:
If this Government should be defeated-and whatever you think to-day, you will not have much fear of its d.feat if you wait three, four, or six or ten months from now-if this Government should go down,
I say here that the party that would be in office would be dominated by the men who, inspired by class consciousness, driven by agitation, led astray by distance from the real facts, have swallowed this principle of free trade. They would be in the ascendancy, along with those who are ready to take hold of free trade, or Sovietism, or semi-Sovietism, or Redism, or anything else, in order to hurl down any Government in pow'er. That is the class who would dominate the Administration if the present Government were defeated, and every single element of that class is a wrecker and a puller-down, and could never do anything to take us forward or upward.
If the right hon. gentleman were here, I would ask him now if he is not 'ashamed of making a statement of that sort in a public campaign. I cite it now as a sample of the hysteria, the folly, to which we are led in our party warfare, and as one of the reasons why I dislike and disapprove of the whole idea that seems to underlie what many people pride themselves on describing as the British constitutional method of responsible government.
Our problems are not to be solved by these methods, and I am afraid the seriousness of the situation will soon begin to force upon us a more co-operative spirit. There must be more dispassionate study, more open-mindedness, greater absence of partisanship. The problems awaiting solution are not to be solved by slamming one another, but by grappling with error, overcoming ignorance and striving to know the truth. There is a saying in the Good Book "Ye shall know the truth and the truth shall make you free." What is Liberalism if it is not an exaltation of freedom? And freedon of the proper kind certainly depends upon liberation from error and ignorance. I believe in Liberalism and I call myself a Liberal, but that does not mean that I necessarily adhere to or vote for the so-called Liberal party which is often illiberal in its attitude towards public questions.

I have already referred to the very admirable study of the question of international trade in this volume under my hand and I have suggested that we ought to make a greater use of experts in the study of our economic problems. I have my opinions and have expressed them frankly on the floor of the House, and intend to do so as long as I am here.
The next matter I want to present is a summary, or a concise statement, of the protectionist philosophy. I remarked at the outset that I proposed to deal mainly with the question as to why the free trade argument had gained so little support and why the protection argument had gained so much suppoi* and I think that ought to be of some interest to my Conservative friends. I am going to make this statement as brief as I can, and I have therefore written out my remarks in the main, so that I can be concise. I am going to state what I regard as the essential philosophy of the free trade versus protection controversy.
I think in the first place we should earnestly answer the question, should legislation be in the interests of the people generally or be in the interests of the minority of the people? If in the interests of the people generally, which is best for society, abundance or scarcity?
I am quite prepared from the standpoint of theology, morals and so on, to say tha., hardship and misery and pain and troubles may sometimes be a wholesome chastener, but I submit on the whole we agree-and there will be very little dispute in regard to my statement, that the aim of a sound national policy should be to secure abundance rather than scarcity: that is to say, a maximum of useful commodities, and services. Do I find anybody disputing that statement? And yet is not the policy of scarcity widely preached? We have our Conservative friends constantly declaiming against dumping, which gives us cheap goods. They talk about inundating this country with the products of cheap labour. Abundance is decried. There is talk about over-production on every hand. On every hand we find a direct or indirect criticism of
The Budget-Mr. Good

the philosophy of abundance. Why this enigma?
Consider the indi%ddual man in modem society. He grows richer in proportion to the return for his labours, this depending largely on the price he can get for his services or the product of his labours.
And on what does price depend? Very largely upon scarcity. Therefore we conclude that in the case of an individual producer, scarcity enriches him, provided of course that this scarcity does not equally affect his own labour products. Applying the same reasoning successively to all producers, we construct the theory of soarcity and proceed to apply it by raising prices artificially through tariffs and so forth.
We may argue in like fashion as to abundance. When any product is plentiful, it sells at a lower price, and therefore the producer gets less. If all producers are in the same situation, they all lose. Therefore, it is abundance that ruins society.
Now, what is wrong with the argument? Simply this:	It ignores the fact that man
is consumer as well as producer, and the foregoing reasoning considers him only in the latter role.
As a producer, a man may become richer by reason of scarcity. He may take advantage of other people's needs. But as a consumer he benefits by abundance, because then he buys things cheaper. By extending this reasoning to all consumers, we arrive at the *theory of plenty.
If, therefore, we consider the selfish interest of men as producers, we arrive at one conclusion:	whereas,
if we consider their interests as consumers, we arrive at the opposite conclusion. And this is natural, because as sellers we have an interest in dearness, and therefore in scarcity. But, as buyers, our interest is in cheapness and abundance.
Now, on which theory, that of abundance or that of scarcity, should public policy be based? I should like sincerely to submit this to my Conservative friends. The question is not an idle or a fantastic one. It is a burning one which confronts or ought to confront every finance minister when he is preparing his budget proposals. Nor can it be airily dismissed or lightly answered. Let us examine this matter and try to answer the question.
If a man consumed all he produced; if he did not exchange the products of his labours for the products of the labour of others, there could be only one answer: Abundance would be advantageous. It would be perceived at once that labour is a means, not

an end, and that anything that would save labour would conduce to progress and prosperity. Take the case of any farmer working for himself on his own farm. What an absurd thing it would be for him to argue in favour of or follow any policy that would lead to scarcity. Every labour saving device he could apply, anything by which he could economize, would certainly be to his advantage. But, with the division of labour, with exchange, with diversification of employment, the situation becomes complicated. In relation to any particular commodity, two interests are created and these are directly opposed to each other.
Take the case of any producer. His im-me'diate selfish interest lies in 'having the fewest possible producers in his line, and the greatest possible number of consumers. Supply limited, demand great, and up goes the price. But the immediate interest of the consumer is that supply may be increased relatively to demand, so that prices may fall. Now, as producers, our desires tempt us, and our opportunities enable us, to be anti-social. For example, as farmers we may be interested in and financially benefited by crop failures as long as they do not affect our crops. We may be financially benefited by war as long as it does not affect our farms. We may profit by the sinking of vessels, as occurred during the war, so long as our crops are not involved. If we are carpenters, masons or builders, we may be benefited financially from devastating fires or earthquakes. As lawyers we may be benefited financially by the growth of quarrels and litigation. I quote a sentence from the old French writer, Montaigne, in this connection. He said:
The shopkeeper thrives only by the irregularities of youth; the farmer by the high price of corn; the architect by the destruction of houses, the officers of justice by lawsuits and quarrels.
Producers are, of course, social in so far as they are efficient workers. For example, if a farmer grows crops above the average because of his superior intelligence or industry, and thereby receives a greater reward for his labour, his personal welfare coincides with that of society generally; but in so far as he gains by price enhancement, he does so at others' expense, and is therefore in this regard anti-social. The fact is that, as producers, some of our activities are social and some anti-social.
But when we come to consider the immediate interest of the consumer, we find that it is in perfect harmony with the general interest. As consumers, our interests are practically identical. We all want food, clothing,

The Budget-Mr. Good
housing, and many other necessaries and comforts. Though we may be divided into a hundred different occupations as producers, we all spend what money we earn through these occupations pretty much in the same way. As consumers, we desire to see the markets wtell supplied. We welcome good crops and labour-saving machinery. We rejoice in rapid and easy means of transportation and communication. We may indeed as consumers push our desires to an absurd length, without having them become antagonistic to the public welfare. Were we able to obtain necessaries and comforts of life as freely and as easily as the air we breathe, there would be nothing therein incompatible with the general interest, since all consumers would be equally benefited.
Public policy ought therefore to be based on the interests of people as consumers, rather than upon their interests as producers.
The Prime Minister went up and down this country not long ago, I think in 1921, claiming that he was going to protect the consumers. I submit to him and to the government, and particularly to the Conservative party that the interest of the consumer should be the basis of public policy. May I state again?-Public policy ought to be based on the interests of people as consumers, rather than upon their interests as producers. Only thus can it serve the general welfare and conform to the motto: "The greatest good to the greatest number." The protectionist, therefore, lands in this dilemma:	Protective tariffs
produce scarcity, or they do not. If they do, then general injury is inflicted. If they do not, then supply is not restricted and the producer does not gain. They are either harmful or useless. I am prepared to admit that there are conditions-and I shall refer to them later-under which this argument does not apply, or applies only to a limited extent. I had intended to read to the House in this connection an extract from a book which I referred to last session entitled Fallacies of Protection, by Frederic Bastiat, a Frenchman who wrote in the forties of last century.
